lessons.plain: This lesson covers the vocabulary of generative AI, the family of technologies that create new content such as text, images or code. Think of nested boxes. Artificial intelligence is the largest box. Machine learning is a method inside it, where software learns patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. Generative AI is the part of machine learning that produces new output. Large language models and diffusion models are two common kinds of generative model. Knowing which word means which thing lets you ask precise questions instead of nodding along in meetings.
lessons.guessPrompt: Without notes, what do you think separates a model that writes new product descriptions from one that only sorts incoming emails into categories, and which of the two would you call generative?
lessons.teach:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad goal of getting computers to do tasks that normally need human judgment. Natural language processing (NLP) is the branch dealing with human language, such as translation or detecting sentiment in a review. Machine learning (ML) is one route to AI: you train a model, a mathematical function with adjustable settings, on examples so it learns patterns, rather than writing rules by hand. Generative AI is machine learning that produces new content such as text, images or code, rather than only labelling items or predicting a number.

A foundation model is a large model trained on very broad data so it can be adapted to many tasks. A multimodal foundation model accepts or produces more than one type of data, such as text and images together. A large language model (LLM) is a foundation model focused on text. A diffusion model creates images by learning to turn random noise, step by step, into a picture that matches a description.

Prompt engineering means writing the instructions you give a model to get better output, without changing the model itself. Prompt tuning is a lightweight training step that learns small adjustments to the prompt while the model's main settings stay fixed.

Worked example. Step 1: a model was trained earlier on broad text, which makes it a foundation model in the model training stage. Step 2: it is an LLM because it works with text. Step 3: you ask it for a product description and specify audience and length, which is prompt engineering in the use stage. The output improves because the instructions improved, not because the model changed.

Common mistake: calling every AI system generative. A spam filter that labels email is machine learning but not generative AI.

Consequence: in a running product, treating a classifier as generative leads to wrong scope estimates and promises to customers that the system cannot keep.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a model that was trained earlier on very broad data, so it can be adapted to many tasks. Step 1: that earlier training makes it a foundation model, belonging to the model training stage. Step 2: it accepts both shipping text and photos of scanned labels, so it is a multimodal foundation model. Step 3: a staff member changes only the wording of the instruction to ask for a three-bullet summary, leaving the model itself untouched, so the output improves. Which term completes Step 3?
choices: Diffusion modelling
Prompt engineering
Fine-tuning the model's main weights
Natural language processing
questions.why: Changing only the instruction wording to improve output without changing the model is prompt engineering, as the teaching text defines it.

questions.prompt: A help-desk tool reads incoming support tickets and tags each one as billing or technical. It does not write any new text. Which description fits it best?
choices: Machine learning but not generative AI, because it labels items rather than producing new content
A diffusion model, because it processes incoming data step by step
A multimodal foundation model, because it reads tickets
Generative AI, because it works with human language
questions.why: The teaching text says a system that only labels items is machine learning but not generative AI, which matches this tagging tool.

questions.prompt: A retailer's text-only model was trained on very broad web text and is now used by staff who give it detailed instructions to draft product descriptions. Which pairing places each piece in the correct lifecycle stage?
choices: Broad training makes it a prompt tuning step in the use stage; the staff instructions are model training
Broad training makes it a foundation model in the model training stage; the staff instructions are prompt engineering in the use stage
Broad training is prompt engineering in the training stage; the staff instructions are a foundation model
Broad training is the use stage; the staff instructions are a diffusion step in model training
questions.why: Training on broad data creates a foundation model in the training stage, and writing instructions to steer output is prompt engineering in the use stage.

questions.prompt: A product manager says a new image tool is a large language model because it produces pictures from written descriptions. What is the best correction?
choices: The tool is natural language processing, because it reads the description first
Nothing is wrong, since any model that takes a text description is an LLM
An LLM is focused on text, so the tool is more likely a diffusion model, which builds images by turning noise into a picture that matches the description
The tool is prompt tuning, because it accepts written descriptions
questions.why: An LLM is defined as a text-focused foundation model, while a diffusion model is the type that creates images from a description by denoising step by step.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who thinks all AI is generative how AI, machine learning, foundation models, LLMs and prompt engineering relate to each other, and name one limit of prompt engineering.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every generative model is a kind of machine learning, and machine learning is a kind of AI, but not every AI system generates anything. A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. An LLM is a foundation model specialised in text. Prompt engineering is how we get useful output from these models by writing better instructions, and it leaves the model itself unchanged. Its limit is that it only steers behaviour the model already has. If the model lacks knowledge of our product, or we need a consistent style across thousands of requests, a better prompt can only go so far, and prompt tuning or other customisation may be needed. So I would tell my teammate that a spam classifier is AI and machine learning but not generative, while a chatbot built on an LLM is generative and depends on a foundation model underneath.
rubricPoints: Places AI, machine learning and generative AI in nested order.
Defines a foundation model and an LLM precisely, not with buzzwords.
Explains prompt engineering as changing the inputs, not the model.
Names a real limit of prompt engineering as a tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: Explaining these terms precisely to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: Machine learning means teaching a computer to find patterns in examples instead of writing every rule by hand. Researchers sort these approaches by the kind of feedback the computer gets while it learns. If the examples come with the right answers attached, that is one approach. If the examples have no answers and the computer must find structure on its own, that is another. If the computer learns by trying actions and receiving rewards or penalties, that is a third. Knowing which one fits a problem helps you ask the right questions about data, time, and cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank has ten years of past loan applications, each marked as repaid or defaulted. Another company has a huge pile of customer purchase records with no labels and wants to find natural customer groups. Which of these two situations would you expect to need answers provided in advance, and why?
lessons.teach: Supervised learning trains a model on examples where each input comes with the correct answer, called a label. The model learns a mapping from inputs to labels, then predicts labels for new inputs it has never seen. Typical tasks are classification (which category does this belong to?) and regression (what number should this be?). It works because the labels act as a teacher: the model's guesses are compared with the right answers and adjusted to shrink the gap. Unsupervised learning uses data with no labels. The model looks for structure on its own, such as grouping similar items (clustering) or finding a compact summary of many features. Nobody supplies the right answer, so the output is judged by whether the groups or summaries are useful to people. Reinforcement learning has an agent take actions in an environment and receive a reward signal. Over many trials it learns a policy, meaning a rule for choosing actions that maximises total reward over time. There is no labelled answer for each step, and feedback can arrive late. Worked example: a delivery app wants to choose routes. Past trips labelled with actual travel time make this supervised, because the model predicts minutes. Unlabelled trips grouped by driver habit make it unsupervised. Live route choices rewarded for on-time arrivals make it reinforcement. Step by step, ask whether answers exist for each example; if yes, it is supervised; if no answers but you want structure, it is unsupervised; if the system takes actions and gets rewards, it is reinforcement. Common mistake: treating any model that learns from data as supervised, or treating generative AI as a separate fourth category. Many generative models are trained by predicting parts of the data itself, and reinforcement-style feedback is sometimes used to tune them afterwards. Consequence: a team that labels data wrongly trains a model that confidently learns the wrong thing, and a reward signal that is easy to game can make a reinforcement agent score well while behaving badly. The approach is chosen by the kind of feedback available, not by how sophisticated the model is.

questions.prompt: Harbourline Freight has 200,000 past shipments. Each one is stored with the date customs actually cleared it, and the firm wants to predict clearance dates for shipments that have not cleared yet. Worked so far: Step 1: Does each past shipment already have a correct answer attached? Yes, its recorded clearance date. Step 2: Is the output a number to predict? Yes, a date treated as a count of days, so the task is regression. Step 3 (you complete it): Based on the answers from Steps 1 and 2, which ML approach fits this situation?
choices: Supervised, because each past shipment has a recorded answer the model learns from
Unsupervised, because the shipments can be grouped by route
Unsupervised, because nobody has checked the predictions yet
Reinforcement, because the firm rewards faster clearance
questions.why: Each past shipment has a known correct answer (its clearance date), which is the defining feature of supervised learning, so the approach is supervised.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain has sales records for 50 shops, with no labels attached to any record. It wants to find groups of shops that behave similarly. Which ML approach matches this goal, and why?
choices: Supervised, because the bakery wants a category for each shop
Supervised, because sales figures are numbers and numbers always need labels
Unsupervised, because there are no labels and the goal is to find structure such as groups
Reinforcement, because the shops take actions and receive sales as reward
questions.why: With no labels and a goal of finding groups, the approach is unsupervised learning, specifically clustering.

questions.prompt: A call-centre routing agent is rewarded for short calls. Over time it learns to hang up on customers early, so its reward score rises while customer service gets worse. What is the main lesson from this failure?
choices: The model was supervised on incorrectly labelled calls
Reinforcement learning cannot work unless every single call has a label
The team should have used clustering to group the short calls
The reward signal is easy to game, so the agent can score well while behaving badly
questions.why: The reinforcement agent optimised the reward it was given, and because that reward was easy to game, it scored well while behaving badly.

questions.prompt: A bank has records of past loan applicants, each marked as repaid or defaulted. It trains a model on these records to predict whether a new applicant will default. Which description is correct?
choices: Unsupervised clustering, because the model groups applicants without being told the outcome
Supervised regression, because the model predicts a number of days until default
Reinforcement learning, because the bank rewards the model for approving good loans
Supervised classification, because each past applicant has a known label and the model predicts a category
questions.why: Labelled past outcomes make this supervised learning, and predicting a category such as default or repaid is classification.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick for a new project where labelled data is scarce.
lessons.modelAnswer: Supervised learning needs labelled examples, so the model learns to map inputs to known answers, which works well for prediction tasks such as classifying tickets. Unsupervised learning gets no answers and finds structure such as clusters, which is useful for exploring data but hard to score objectively. Reinforcement learning learns by acting and collecting rewards, which suits sequential decisions but needs a simulator or many trials and a reward that cannot be easily gamed. If labelled data is scarce, I would start with unsupervised exploration to understand the data, or pay for labelling of a representative sample before any supervised training. The tradeoff is cost and time for labels versus the risk that clusters look neat but mean little to the business.
rubricPoints: Supervised learning uses labelled data to predict known answers.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data and is hard to judge objectively.
Reinforcement learning learns from rewards gathered by taking actions over time.
A named limit such as label cost, reward gaming, or unclear cluster meaning.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the three approaches and their tradeoffs back in your own words is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: The ML lifecycle is the sequence of steps a team follows to turn raw data into a model that makes useful predictions and keeps working over time. Think of a restaurant kitchen: you receive ingredients, clean and prepare them, practise a recipe, serve dishes to customers, and then keep checking quality and updating the menu. Each stage has a different job and often a different tool. Knowing which stage a problem belongs to tells you who to ask and what to check first. For this objective, you need the five stages in order and one Google Cloud tool that usually supports each stage.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a model that predicts which delivery orders will arrive late. Before any model can be trained, what work do you think must happen first, and why might a team that skips it run into trouble later?
lessons.teach:
The five stages run in order, and each one feeds the next. Data ingestion means bringing data from its sources into a place where it can be stored and reached. Object storage holds raw files, a data warehouse holds analytical tables, and a message stream carries events as they happen. In Google Cloud, Cloud Storage handles raw files, BigQuery handles tables, and Pub/Sub handles event streams. Data preparation means cleaning and reshaping that data: removing duplicates, filling or dropping missing values, converting formats, and joining sources so the data is complete and consistent. Dataflow and Dataprep by Trifacta are common tools here, and BigQuery can also transform data with SQL. Model training means fitting an algorithm to prepared examples so it learns patterns; Vertex AI provides managed training. Model deployment means making the trained model callable by applications, for example through a Vertex AI endpoint that answers prediction requests. Model management means tracking model versions, evaluating quality, and watching for drift, which is when live data slowly stops resembling the data the model learned from. Vertex AI Model Registry and Model Monitoring support this stage.

Worked example: a delivery firm predicts late orders. Ingestion: order events arrive through Pub/Sub and history sits in BigQuery. Preparation: the team removes cancelled orders, fills missing postcodes, and converts timestamps to one time zone. Training: the cleaned history trains a model on Vertex AI. Deployment: the model is placed on an endpoint so the dispatch app can request a late-risk score. Management: the team records this as version 2, tracks accuracy each week, and retrains when accuracy falls.

Common mistake: treating deployment as the finish line. A deployed model keeps facing changing data, so without management it quietly gets worse.

Consequence: the dispatch app keeps showing confident scores that no longer match reality, and nobody notices until customers complain. The lifecycle is a loop, not a straight line, because findings from management often send a team back to ingestion or preparation.

questions.prompt: A wind farm operator wants to predict gearbox faults before they stop turbines. Ingestion: turbine sensor readings stream in through Pub/Sub, and past maintenance logs sit as raw files in Cloud Storage. Preparation: the team removes duplicate readings, fills missing wind speeds, and converts all timestamps to UTC. Training: the cleaned history trains a model on Vertex AI. Deployment: the model is placed on a Vertex AI endpoint so the maintenance planner's app can request fault-risk scores. Management: the team tracks model versions and watches live readings for drift, using the Google Cloud tools for that stage, which are ____.
choices: Vertex AI Model Registry and Model Monitoring
BigQuery SQL transformations
Dataflow and Dataprep by Trifacta
Pub/Sub and Cloud Storage
questions.why: The teaching text assigns version tracking and drift watching in the management stage to Vertex AI Model Registry and Model Monitoring, while the other options belong to earlier stages.

questions.prompt: A team finds that the live inputs their deployed model receives have slowly shifted away from the data it was trained on, so its predictions are becoming less reliable. Which lifecycle stage does this concern, and what is the term for this situation?
choices: Model management, called drift
Data ingestion, called schema loading
Model deployment, called endpoint lag
Model training, called overfitting of the sample
questions.why: The teaching text defines drift as live data slowly ceasing to resemble the training data, and it belongs to the model management stage.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup receives raw GPS pings through a message stream and needs them joined with a customer table and reshaped into daily summaries before any model sees them. Which lifecycle stage is this work, and which Google Cloud tool does the teaching text name for transforming data with SQL?
choices: Ingestion, using Pub/Sub
Deployment, using a Vertex AI endpoint
Training, using Vertex AI managed training
Preparation, using BigQuery
questions.why: Joining sources and reshaping data is data preparation, and the teaching text says BigQuery can transform data with SQL.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a model to an endpoint and then considers the project finished, with no plan to track its quality over time. According to the teaching text, what is the likely consequence?
choices: Vertex AI removes the endpoint automatically after its first week of use
Training must restart from raw files because the model has no stored history
Ingestion stops because the endpoint has no record of the raw files
The model quietly gets worse as live data changes, so the app keeps showing confident scores that no longer match reality
questions.why: The teaching text warns that deployment is not the finish line, because without management a deployed model keeps facing changing data and degrades unnoticed.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the ML lifecycle is just 'get data, train, ship it.' Explain the five stages to them in your own words, name the Google Cloud tool you would associate with each, and point out one limit or tradeoff of working in these staged steps.
lessons.modelAnswer: The lifecycle has five stages. Ingestion brings data in from its sources into storage, where Cloud Storage, BigQuery or Pub/Sub can hold it depending on whether the data is files, tables or streams. Preparation cleans and joins that data so it is complete and consistent, using tools such as Dataflow or BigQuery SQL. Training fits a model to the prepared examples, which Vertex AI manages. Deployment makes the trained model callable by applications, for example through a Vertex AI endpoint. Management tracks versions and watches for drift, when live data stops resembling the training data. The tradeoff is that the stages depend on each other, so a shortcut in preparation shows up later as a weak model, and management is ongoing work and cost, not a one-time launch.
rubricPoints: Names all five stages in the correct order: ingestion, preparation, training, deployment, management.
Gives a Google Cloud tool for each stage, such as Cloud Storage, BigQuery or Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vertex AI training, Vertex AI endpoints, and Model Registry or Monitoring.
Explains that management covers ongoing monitoring and drift, not just a launch.
Notes that the stages depend on each other, so weak earlier work causes later problems.

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly a mapping of stages to named product tools, which is best learned from reading the product catalogue and stage definitions rather than from a hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large AI model trained on very large amounts of data so it can be reused for many tasks, such as writing text, answering questions, or describing pictures. Choosing one for a business is like choosing a vehicle: the right one depends on the job, the load, the budget, and the roads you must travel. You weigh what kinds of input and output the model handles, how much it can read at once, where your data goes, how reliably it responds, what each use costs, how well it performs, and whether you can adapt it to your own needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A startup wants an assistant that reads 300-page contracts and answers questions about them. Before any teaching, which two properties of a model would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Choosing a foundation model means picking the pre-trained model that fits a business need, using a short list of properties. Modality is the kind of data a model accepts and returns: text only, images, audio, video, or a mix. A model that only reads text cannot judge a photo of a damaged part. Context window is how much input the model can consider in one request, counted in tokens, which are small pieces of text, often part of a word. A 300-page contract may not fit in a small window, so the model would never see the clause you need. Security covers where your data is processed and stored, who can access it, and whether it may be used to train later models. Availability and reliability describe how often the service answers and what limits apply to request volume. Cost is usually charged per token, and output tokens often cost more than input tokens. Performance is how accurate and how fast the answers are. Fine-tuning means further training a model on your own labeled examples so its behaviour shifts. Customization is the wider set of adaptations, including careful prompting and supplying your own documents at request time, which is cheaper and easier to undo.

Worked example: a support team wants a chatbot that answers from 40 product manuals, about 200 pages in total. Step one, modality: text in and text out, so a text model suffices. Step two, context window: the manuals are far larger than a short window, so either the window must be big enough or the system must fetch only the relevant passages. Step three, cost: estimate tokens per question times questions per month. Step four, security: confirm the manuals and customer questions are handled under the company's data rules. Only then compare performance on sample questions.

Common mistake: picking the largest, most capable model by default. It often costs more and responds more slowly, and a cheaper model may already meet the requirement.

Consequence: if a long document exceeds the context window in production, parts of it are cut off and answers quietly become incomplete, while traffic growth can push spend past the budget.

questions.prompt: A regional bank wants a model that drafts replies to customer emails. Each reply must be grounded in a case file of about 90,000 tokens. Worked so far: Step one, modality: the inputs and outputs are both text, so a text model suffices. Step two, context window: the case file is 90,000 tokens, so the chosen model's window must hold that file plus the email and the reply, and a model with a 128,000-token window qualifies. Step three, security: the bank confirms that case files are not used to train other models. Step four is missing. Which step belongs there, before performance is compared?
choices: Estimate cost: tokens per reply, counting output tokens at their higher price, multiplied by replies per month.
Check which colour scheme the model's provider uses, so the drafts match the bank's branding.
Fine-tune the model on past case files before any cost check, so the answers are more accurate.
Pick the model with the highest published benchmark score, since accuracy matters more than cost.
questions.why: The sequence runs modality, context window, security, then cost, because cost is estimated from tokens per request times requests per month, with output tokens usually priced higher, before performance is compared.

questions.prompt: In the vocabulary of model selection, what does a model's context window measure?
choices: The amount of input the model can consider in one request, counted in tokens.
The number of parameters, or internal weights, inside the model.
The number of users the service can serve per minute.
The dollar price charged for each thousand tokens of output.
questions.why: The context window is the amount of input a model can consider in a single request, measured in tokens, which are small pieces of text.

questions.prompt: A transit agency wants a model that reads photographs of track damage submitted by field crews and returns a short written severity note. Which modality requirement fits this use case?
choices: Video output, because the severity note should play back as a clip.
Text in and text out only, because the final notes are written text.
Image input with text output, which is a mixed-modality model.
Audio input only, because crews may describe damage aloud.
questions.why: The inputs are photographs, so the model must accept images, and the returned note is text, so a mixed model fits; a text-only model cannot judge a photo at all.

questions.prompt: A retailer's prices change every Monday, and the chatbot must quote the current price list. Which approach is the better fit for this need?
choices: Supply the current price list inside each request, because this is cheaper to update and easier to undo.
Retrain the model from scratch every Monday so it memorises the new prices.
Raise the output token limit so the model remembers prices from earlier requests.
Fine-tune the model on each week's price list, so its behaviour shifts with every update.
questions.why: Supplying documents at request time is a customization approach that is cheaper and easier to undo, whereas fine-tuning repeatedly on changing data is costlier and slower to reverse.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a foundation model for a new internal tool, and name one limit or tradeoff you would have to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the job, not the model list. First I would confirm the input and output types, whether text, images or both, and whether our typical documents fit within the model's context window, which is measured in tokens. Next I would check security: where data is processed, who can access it, and whether it may be used for training. Then I would look at availability and request limits, cost per token at our expected volume, and quality on a sample of real questions. Fine-tuning comes last, because supplying our own documents at request time is cheaper and easier to change. The tradeoff is that the most capable model usually costs more and responds more slowly, so we may accept a somewhat weaker answer in exchange for predictable cost and latency, and we would measure that on our own test set before committing.
rubricPoints: Starts from the business task and the input and output modality
Checks the context window against real document lengths
Covers security, data handling, and availability alongside cost and performance
Treats fine-tuning as heavier than prompting or supplying documents at request time
Names a real tradeoff such as capability versus cost and latency

suggested.rationale: Choosing a model means weighing several competing properties at once, so a short exam-style scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: Generative AI is software that makes new content, such as text, pictures, code, or video, by learning patterns from very large amounts of example material. Businesses use it in four broad ways: to create things, like a draft email or a product image; to summarize long material, like a meeting transcript or a pile of customer feedback; to discover things, like finding relevant answers inside documents the company already owns; and to automate routine steps, like sorting incoming requests or drafting standard replies. Spotting a good use case starts with asking which of those jobs the business needs done, what the input is, what the output should look like, and whether a person checks the result before it matters. The skill is matching the job to the tool, not being impressed by the technology.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retail company has 40,000 customer reviews and wants a one-paragraph weekly digest of the main complaints. Before you read further, would you call this a create, summarize, discover, or automate use case, and why?
lessons.teach: Create means generating new content from a description or instruction, such as a draft marketing image or a first version of a product description. Summarize means condensing existing material into a shorter form that keeps the key points. Discover means finding and surfacing insight from large collections of material, often by asking a question in plain language and getting an answer grounded in the company's own documents. Automate means having a model carry out a repeated step, such as tagging or routing items, so fewer people handle each one. Data analysis here means asking questions of data in plain language and getting an explanation or a chart back. Personalized experience means tailoring content to an individual user, such as product suggestions or messages written for one customer's history. Why this works: a generative model learns statistical patterns in language, images, or code from huge examples, then produces output that is plausible given the input. It does not check facts against a database unless it is connected to one, so the business value depends on what it is given. Worked example: the review digest. Step 1: the input is existing text, the 40,000 reviews, so the job is not create. Step 2: the output is a shorter paragraph that keeps the main themes, so the job is summarize. Step 3: a person spot-checks a sample, because summaries can quietly drop a minority complaint. Common mistake: treating every idea as a creation use case, or trusting output because it reads fluently. Consequence: if a generated digest goes to executives unchecked and misses a rising safety issue, the business acts on a wrong picture. The first question to ask is what goes in and what the business needs back, because that decides which use case you are looking at.

questions.prompt: A regional freight company keeps 900 safety manuals as PDFs. A dispatcher types the plain-language question "What is the lockout procedure for a tipped trailer?" and a tool returns an answer quoted from those manuals. Step 1: the input is existing company documents plus a question, so the job is not create. Step 2: the business needs an answer drawn from the company's own material, so the output is an answer surfaced from existing content, not a new story. Step 3: [missing step: the job type is decided here.] Which conclusion completes the analysis?
choices: It is video generation, because the manuals contain diagrams.
It is discover, because the answer is surfaced from the company's own manuals in response to a plain-language question.
It is create, because the reply is newly written text.
It is automate, because the dispatcher asks a question that is often repeated.
questions.why: Discover means finding and surfacing insight from existing collections in response to a plain-language question, which matches the dispatcher's situation.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain receives about 3,000 supplier emails a month. The operations lead wants one short paragraph each month that keeps the main supplier problems and drops the routine replies. Which use case does this describe?
choices: Automate, because routine replies are removed by a model.
Summarize, because existing material is condensed into a shorter form that keeps the key points.
Personalized experience, because each supplier gets its own paragraph.
Create, because a new paragraph is written.
questions.why: Summarize means condensing existing material into a shorter form while keeping the key points, which is exactly what the monthly paragraph does.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm lets a generative model answer customers' policy questions, but the model is not connected to the firm's policy database. A team member says the answers must be right because they read fluently. What is the most accurate response?
choices: The answers are reliable, since fluent wording shows the facts were checked.
The fluent wording does not show accuracy; a generative model produces plausible output and does not check facts against a database unless it is connected to one.
Only image outputs can be wrong, so text answers from the model are safe to send.
The model always refers to the latest policy version, so no check is needed.
questions.why: A generative model produces output that is plausible given its input and does not verify facts unless connected to a source, so fluency is not evidence of accuracy.

questions.prompt: A museum has 80,000 photo records that each need one of 12 subject tags. A model applies the tags, and staff only review records the model marks as uncertain. Which use case fits best, and why?
choices: Create, because the tags are newly generated text for each photo.
Data analysis, because the museum asks questions of its records in plain language.
Automate, because a repeated step (tagging) is carried out by the model so fewer people handle each record.
Personalized experience, because the tags are chosen to suit each visitor.
questions.why: Automate means having a model carry out a repeated step such as tagging so fewer people handle each item, which is what happens with the 80,000 records.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague suggests using generative AI to replace our support-ticket triage team. Explain to them, in your own words, which business use cases generative AI fits in this situation, and name one limit or tradeoff we must plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Generative AI fits best in the support process as an assistant rather than a replacement. It can summarize long ticket threads so an agent reads a short version first, and it can automate first-draft replies for common, low-risk questions. It can also help discover answers by searching our own help articles so the agent sees a grounded suggestion. The main tradeoff is accuracy. The model produces fluent output that can be wrong, and it does not know our policies unless it is given them, so a person must review anything that reaches a customer, especially refunds or safety issues. We should also measure error rates on a sample before expanding automation, and keep a clear route for a human to take over.
rubricPoints: Names the right job for each part, such as summarize for ticket threads, automate for drafts, or discover for searching internal articles.
Explains that generated output can be fluent but wrong, so it needs checking.
Gives a concrete limit, such as the model not knowing internal policy unless provided.
Recommends human review or a measured rollout before increasing automation.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right use case from a short business scenario is best practised by reasoning through situations, and no listed mission or planned engine covers generative AI.

lessons.plain: Data quality means how trustworthy and usable a collection of information is for a particular job. Data accessibility means whether the people or systems that need it can actually reach it, in time, at a sensible price, and in a form they can read. A gen AI model learns from data and answers using data, so weak data produces weak answers, even when the model itself is excellent. Think of a cookbook with missing pages, mixed-up measurements and a recipe you cannot open: the chef's skill does not rescue the dinner.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a company builds a chatbot to answer customer questions about its products, but the product catalogue was last updated three years ago and half the entries have no price. Before reading further, which problem would hurt the chatbot's answers more: the model being an older version, or the catalogue being out of date and incomplete? Why?
lessons.teach: Data quality is how well a dataset fits the job it must do. Accessibility is whether the right people and systems can reach that data when they need it. The objective names six characteristics you should be able to explain. Completeness means the data has no important gaps; a customer record with an address but no postcode is incomplete. Consistency means the same fact is recorded the same way everywhere, such as one date format and one spelling for a product name. Relevance means the data bears on the question being asked; last decade's sales logs say little about this month's demand. Availability means the data can be reached when needed, not stuck in an archive or behind a slow export. Cost covers what it takes to store, clean, move and process the data, including staff time spent fixing it. Format means the data is in a shape tools can read, such as a clean table or consistent text, rather than scanned images of handwritten forms. Worked example: a retailer wants a model to draft product descriptions. Step one, check completeness: twenty percent of products lack a material field, so the model would invent materials. Step two, check consistency: colours appear as navy, Navy Blue and NVY. Step three, check relevance: descriptions from discontinued lines are mixed in. Step four, check availability and format: specifications sit in a separate PDF per product, so someone must extract them first, which adds cost. Only after these fixes is the data ready. These checks belong to the data preparation stage of the ML lifecycle. Common mistake: assuming more data is always better. A large, messy pile can produce confident but wrong answers, and it costs more to store and process. Consequence: in a running system, a retrieval step that fetches stale or duplicated records feeds the model wrong facts, and the model states them fluently. Poor data quality is usually discovered in production as customer complaints, so data must be checked before deployment.

questions.prompt: A regional bank wants a model to answer loan officers' questions using its internal policy memos from 2019 to 2024. Data quality means how well a dataset fits the job it must do, and the team checks it in the data preparation stage of the ML lifecycle (the sequence of stages a model goes through, from gathering data to running it). Step one, relevance: memos about rules that were replaced in 2020 are removed, since they would give officers outdated answers. Step two, consistency: the same policy appears as 'Mortgage Rule 4', 'MR4' and 'mortgage rule four', so the team standardises the names. Step three, availability: the memos sit in a legacy system that exports only 200 files at a time, so the team builds one scheduled export job. Step four is missing: the team must check completeness, meaning whether important gaps exist in the memos. Which finding belongs in that missing step four?
choices: Policy names appear in three spellings, which is a consistency problem rather than a completeness one.
The legacy system is slow on Monday mornings, so the export should run overnight instead.
Four percent of memos have no effective date, so the model could not tell which rule applies on a given day.
Building the export job takes engineer time, which is a cost issue rather than a completeness one.
questions.why: Completeness means the data has no important gaps, and a memo missing its effective date is a gap that would leave the model unable to answer correctly, while the other three options describe consistency, cost and availability.

questions.prompt: A library catalogue lists the same novel as 'Dune', 'dune (Herbert)' and 'DUNE'. Which data quality characteristic is most directly affected?
choices: Completeness, because some of the records are missing a publication year.
Consistency, because the same fact is recorded in different ways across entries.
Cost, because staff must spend time merging the duplicate entries.
Relevance, because the novel is no longer popular with current readers.
questions.why: Consistency means the same fact is recorded the same way everywhere, and three different spellings of one title is a direct violation of that, while the other options describe different characteristics.

questions.prompt: A team holds 10 million customer support transcripts and argues that its chatbot will improve simply because the dataset is so large. Which response best challenges this reasoning?
choices: A large dataset is unlikely to be relevant to the chatbot's current products, and if it is messy it can produce confident but wrong answers while adding storage and processing cost.
The team should store the transcripts in a single PDF so that the chatbot can read them more easily.
Ten million transcripts is too few for a modern chatbot, so the team should buy a larger archive from another company.
Large datasets are always more accurate, so the team should keep collecting transcripts until the chatbot stops making mistakes.
questions.why: Size alone does not guarantee quality: a large but irrelevant or messy pile can produce confidently wrong answers and costs more to store and process, which is why the other options, which all treat size as the main goal, are wrong.

questions.prompt: A forecasting team has a dataset that is complete, consistent and relevant, but it is stored in an archive that takes three days to restore before anyone can use it. Which characteristic is the problem, and what is the main consequence for the team?
choices: Format, because the archive stores the data as compressed files that the team must unzip before reading.
Availability, because the data cannot be reached when the team needs it, so forecasts are delayed.
Consistency, because the archive may have recorded the same sales figure in two different ways.
Completeness, because the archive is missing the most recent three days of sales.
questions.why: Availability means data can be reached when needed, and a three-day restore delay blocks the team's work, whereas the other options name characteristics the scenario does not describe.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'We have ten years of customer data, so we can skip the data cleanup and go straight to training our gen AI model.' Explain to them, in your own words, why that reasoning is risky. Name at least one data quality characteristic and one limit or tradeoff of cleaning data first.
lessons.modelAnswer: Ten years of data is a volume argument, and volume does not fix quality. Some of those years may be incomplete, for example a field added only in year six, so the model learns from blanks. Names and categories may be written inconsistently, so the same thing looks like several different things. Old records may not be relevant to how customers behave now. Cleaning has a real cost in time and staff, so there is a tradeoff: we can clean a sample first to test its value, or prioritise only the fields the use case truly needs. What we should avoid is skipping the check entirely, because the model will repeat whatever the data says, and it will say it confidently.
rubricPoints: Explains that the volume of data does not replace its quality.
Names at least one characteristic such as completeness, consistency or relevance, with an example.
Identifies a tradeoff or limit of cleaning, such as time and cost against speed.
Notes that unchecked data leads a model to produce confident but wrong output.

suggested.rationale: Judging whether data is fit for a gen AI use case and explaining the tradeoffs to others is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Data is any recorded information a computer can store. Structured data is organized into a fixed layout, like rows and columns where each value has a labeled slot, so a program can find and total things reliably. Unstructured data has no fixed layout you can count on: emails, photos, call recordings and free-text notes hold meaning, but that meaning is buried inside the content rather than sitting in labeled fields. Much of the data companies collect is unstructured, and generative AI models are good at working with it, so knowing the difference matters before you plan any project.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank stores each customer's account balance in a spreadsheet column and also keeps scanned loan application forms as image files. Which of these two is easier to add up with a single query, and why?
lessons.teach:
Structured data is information stored in a predefined schema. A schema is the agreed blueprint that names each field and says what kind of value it holds, such as a customer table with customer_id as a whole number, signup_date as a date, and balance as a decimal. Because every record follows the same blueprint, a database can filter, sort and total it quickly and predictably.

Unstructured data has no predefined schema. Its content can be meaningful, but a program cannot read a field called sender or amount directly; it must first interpret the content. Examples include email bodies, scanned contracts, photographs, audio recordings and video. Semi-structured data sits between the two. JSON logs and XML files have tags or keys, but their contents can vary from record to record.

Worked example: a retailer has two sources. Source A is a table where each row is one order with columns order_id, order_date and total. To find March revenue, you filter rows whose order_date falls in March, then sum the total column. Source B is a folder of customer support emails. To learn how many complaints mention late delivery, you must first read each email, decide whether it is a delivery complaint, and then count the matches. The second task needs an extra interpretation step, and that step is where errors and cost come from.

Common mistake: assuming that anything containing text is unstructured. A CSV file full of text values is still structured if its columns are fixed and consistent. The real question is whether the layout is predefined and reliably followed, not whether the characters are letters.

Consequence in a running system: a pipeline that expects structured fields will fail or silently drop data when unstructured input arrives, so ingestion and preparation steps must convert, tag or extract meaning from unstructured content before it is analyzed.

questions.prompt: A parking authority keeps a table of fines. Each row is one ticket, and the table has fixed columns: ticket_id (a whole number), plate (text), fine_amount (a decimal) and issued_date (a date). Its manager wants the total of fines issued in April. Step 1: confirm the table has a predefined schema, meaning every row follows the same named and typed columns, so the data can be queried directly. Step 2: keep only the rows whose issued_date falls in April. Step 3 is missing. What should it be?
choices: Add up the fine_amount values in the rows kept by step 2
Count the distinct plate values, since the total is a count of tickets
Read each scanned ticket image to decide whether it counts as a fine
Convert the fine_amount column to text before adding it up
questions.why: Step 3 is the summing of the fine_amount column, a fixed numeric field, so no reading or interpretation of content is needed.

questions.prompt: A city traffic system saves each camera frame as a JPEG image file, plus a small separate metadata file that records camera_id and timestamp for that frame. How should the image files be classified?
choices: Unstructured, because the picture content has no predefined schema of named fields
Structured, because every frame is saved in the same file format
Structured, because each file has a timestamp and a camera identifier
Semi-structured, because JPEG files contain tags that label each field
questions.why: The image content itself has no predefined schema of named, typed fields, so it is unstructured even though the separate metadata file is structured.

questions.prompt: A hospital nightly export writes lab results as JSON records. Every record has a test_name key, but for one blood panel the result is a free-text sentence, and for another it is a number. How should this export be classified?
choices: Fully structured, because each record has keys such as test_name
Unstructured, because any text value makes the whole file unstructured
Structured, because JSON is a standard file format
Semi-structured, because keys exist but the value types and wording vary between records
questions.why: Semi-structured data has tags or keys, but its contents can vary from record to record, which matches this export.

questions.prompt: A shipping firm loads a fixed-column CSV of container weights into a database where the weight column is defined as a decimal number. One week a sender types approx 12 tonnes into the weight field. What is the most likely consequence for the running pipeline?
choices: The file becomes unstructured and should be stored as images
Nothing changes, because CSV files do not enforce any types
The database converts approx 12 tonnes to the number 12 automatically
The load can fail or drop that row, so a conversion or check step is needed before loading
questions.why: A value that does not match the declared field type can make the load reject or silently lose the row, so the pipeline must convert or validate the value first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between structured and unstructured data, using one real example of each, and name one limit or tradeoff of working with unstructured data for analysis.
lessons.modelAnswer: Structured data follows a predefined schema, so every record has the same named fields with known types, like an orders table with order_id, date and total. A database can filter and sum it directly and predictably. Unstructured data, like support emails, photos or call recordings, has no fixed fields, so its meaning has to be extracted or classified before it can be counted or compared. The main tradeoff is that this extra interpretation step adds cost, takes more processing time, and can introduce errors, because a model might misclassify an email. So before we promise a dashboard built on customer feedback, we should decide how accurate the extraction needs to be and whether we can check a sample by hand.
rubricPoints: Defines structured data as following a predefined schema with named fields and types
Defines unstructured data as lacking a fixed layout, so meaning must be extracted first
Gives a concrete real-world example of each type
Names a tradeoff such as added cost, processing time or extraction errors for unstructured data

suggested.rationale: This objective is factual and definitional, and no listed mission or planned engine directly practices telling data types apart.

lessons.plain: Some data comes with a note attached that says what the right answer is, like a photo tagged 'cat'. That attached note is a label, and data with labels is called labeled data. Data without those notes, such as a pile of raw photos or unread emails, is unlabeled data. The difference matters because many systems learn by studying examples alongside their answers, and labels are how those answers get supplied. Unlabeled data is still valuable, since a system can find patterns in it without being told the answers, but getting good labels usually takes time and money. Knowing which kind you have shapes what you can build and what it will cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank has 50,000 past loan applications, and for each one it recorded whether the loan later went into default. Another team has 2 million scanned customer letters with no notes about them. Which of these two sets is labeled, and what would the default record be for one application?
lessons.teach:
Labeled data is a set of examples where each example comes with a correct answer attached. That attached answer is called a label. Unlabeled data is a set of examples with no answer attached. The raw input you observe, such as an email or a loan application, is the thing the system looks at, and the label is the thing you want it to predict.

Why this matters: a model learns a link between inputs and labels. When labels are present, the training process can compare the model's guess with the right answer and adjust itself when it is wrong. Without labels there is no answer key, so the process has to look for structure on its own, such as grouping similar items together.

Worked example. A support team has 10,000 customer messages. Step 1: they read 2,000 of them and mark each one 'billing', 'technical' or 'other'. Those 2,000 are now labeled data. Step 2: the remaining 8,000 messages have no mark, so they are unlabeled. Step 3: a second reader checks 200 of the labels and disagrees on 40, so the team fixes those and writes a labeling guide. Step 4: they now hold 2,000 trustworthy labeled examples to teach a classifier, plus 8,000 unlabeled ones that can be used later.

Common mistake: assuming that because data is plentiful it is useful for learning from answers. A pile of unlabeled data teaches a supervised model nothing until someone adds labels, and that labeling work is often the slowest and most costly part of a project.

Consequence in a running system: if labels are wrong or inconsistent, the model learns the wrong rule and becomes confidently wrong in production, for example sending billing questions to the technical queue. In the ML lifecycle, labeling normally happens during data preparation, before model training. Labeled data is therefore an investment: it costs people time, but it gives a model a clear target to learn.

questions.prompt: A city roads office has 50,000 photos taken by a camera van. Step 1: staff tag 1,500 photos as 'pothole' or 'no pothole'. Step 2: the other 48,500 photos stay untagged. Step 3: a second inspector rechecks 150 of the tags, disagrees on 15, and the office corrects those and writes a rule sheet for taggers. Step 4 is missing from this account: the office must decide which set of photos the classifier learns from. Given the account so far, which set is the right choice for training a supervised classifier?
choices: The 48,500 untagged photos, because they contain the real answers hidden in the images
The 150 rechecked tags alone, because only double-checked data can be trusted for training
The 1,500 tagged photos, which are labeled data with a known answer attached to each one
All 50,000 photos, because more examples always produce a better classifier
questions.why: A supervised classifier learns the link between inputs and labels, so it needs examples that already carry a trustworthy answer, which are the 1,500 tagged photos, while the untagged ones have no answer to learn from yet.

questions.prompt: A clinic holds 4,000 scanned intake forms that nobody has marked. Which description correctly defines these forms as unlabeled data?
choices: Forms that have been checked by a second reviewer and approved
Examples with no correct answer attached, so the system must find structure on its own
Forms that have been scanned into a digital format and stored
Forms whose answers have been removed to protect patient privacy
questions.why: Unlabeled data is defined as examples with no answer attached, and the other options describe review, digitising or privacy steps that do not define the label status of the data.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has 200,000 delivery records with no outcome field filled in. It wants to group together routes that behave similarly, without a predefined list of categories. Which approach fits this data best?
choices: Discard the records, because data without labels cannot be used by any model
Ask a reviewer to label all 200,000 records before anything else can happen
Supervised training, because the firm must first attach a delivery-outcome label to each record
Treat the records as unlabeled and look for structure, such as grouping similar routes together
questions.why: With no answer key, the approach is to find structure such as clusters among unlabeled examples; supervised training needs labels, and discarding or fully hand-labeling are not required for this goal.

questions.prompt: A team adds 10,000 unlabeled support chat logs to a supervised training run and expects the classifier's accuracy to rise because it now has more data. What is the most likely flaw in that expectation?
choices: Chat logs are always too long for a model to read, so the run will crash
The classifier automatically deletes any data that lacks an answer and so keeps none of it
Accuracy can only rise when the logs are sent to a separate reviewer, never through training
Unlabeled logs give the training process no correct answer to compare against, so they add no direct learning signal
questions.why: In supervised training the model adjusts by comparing its guess with a label, so examples without labels provide nothing to compare against and do not directly improve it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to machine learning the difference between labeled and unlabeled data, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on labeled data for a project.
lessons.modelAnswer: Labeled data is examples where each one has the correct answer attached, like a set of emails each marked as spam or not spam. Unlabeled data has the same kind of examples but no answers, like those emails with no marks. A system that learns from labeled data can check its guesses against the marks and improve, while unlabeled data forces it to find patterns without an answer key. The main tradeoff of labeled data is cost and quality: someone has to create the labels, which takes time and money, and inconsistent or wrong labels teach the wrong lesson. So before starting, I would check how many labels we really have, how reliable they are, and whether the unlabeled data could still help.
rubricPoints: Labeled data pairs each example with a correct answer or label.
Unlabeled data has inputs only, with no answers attached.
Labels let a model compare its guesses with the right answer and adjust.
Creating labels costs time and money and can be inconsistent, which harms results.
Labeling usually belongs to the data preparation stage of the ML lifecycle.

suggested.rationale: Being able to explain the difference and its tradeoffs to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Generative AI is software that creates new content such as text, images or code. Building and using it involves several stacked layers, like floors in a building. The bottom layer is the raw computing hardware. Above it sit the trained models that do the generating, then platforms that let teams use and manage those models, then agents that carry out multi-step tasks, and at the top the applications people actually touch. Knowing which layer a product or decision belongs to tells you who manages it, what it costs, and what can go wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company says it uses Gemini on Google Cloud for its new support chat. Name the separate layers you think must exist between the computer chips and the chat window the customer sees.
lessons.teach:
The five layers are a way of sorting the parts of a gen AI system from the bottom up. Infrastructure is the physical computing: specialised chips such as GPUs (graphics processors) and Google's TPUs (tensor processing units), plus the storage and networking that train and run models. Models are the trained neural networks that produce output. A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. Gemini is Google's family for text and multimodal work, Gemma is a smaller open model family, and Imagen and Veo generate images and video. Platforms are managed services that let teams access models, tune them, evaluate them, deploy them and monitor them. Vertex AI is Google Cloud's main platform. Agents are systems that use a model to plan a sequence of steps and call outside tools, such as a database lookup, to reach a goal. Applications are the finished products people use.

Worked example: a retailer builds a chat assistant that answers order questions. Chips in a data centre run the model, which is the infrastructure layer. The model writes the reply, which is the model layer. Vertex AI supplies access, logging and usage quotas, which is the platform layer. The assistant decides to look up an order and then issue a refund by calling the order system as a tool, which is the agent layer. The chat window on the website is the application.

Common mistake: calling the whole system 'the AI' and assuming one product name covers every layer. A model is not a platform, and a platform is not an application.

Consequence: a quota limit at the platform layer or an outage at the model layer stops every application above it at once. An agent with tool access can change real data, so its permissions need the same care as any other automated system.

The layers are dependencies, not a ranking: each one runs on the one below it.

questions.prompt: A shipping firm builds a tool that predicts warehouse restock needs. Its pieces are: rented GPU servers that run the model (infrastructure layer); a fine-tuned neural network that scores each product's forecast (model layer); a managed Google Cloud service that gives the team access to the model, stores their evaluation runs and monitors the deployment (platform layer); and an agent that plans steps, reads the stock database as a tool and then places a purchase order. The team's staff dashboard that shows which products are low is the last piece. Which layer does the staff dashboard belong to?
choices: Application
Platform
Model
Infrastructure
questions.why: The staff dashboard is the finished product people use, which is the application layer, while the other pieces each belong to a lower layer.

questions.prompt: A colleague says that because the Gemini family is Google's model, the managed service used to access and monitor that model must be the same layer. Which statement correctly separates the two?
choices: A model and a platform are the same layer because both are named by Google.
A model produces the output, while a platform is a managed service that gives teams access to models and lets them tune, evaluate, deploy and monitor them.
A platform is the finished product users see, and a model is the database the product queries.
A model is the managed service that stores logs, and a platform is the trained neural network that writes the output.
questions.why: The model is the trained network that generates output, and the platform is the managed service around models for access, tuning, evaluation, deployment and monitoring.

questions.prompt: A small airline's chat assistant stops answering customers because the daily usage quota on its managed AI service has been used up. Which layer's limit caused this failure?
choices: The model layer, because the network's output is too slow.
The agent layer, because the assistant's plan has too many steps.
The platform layer, because the managed service enforces the usage quota that the applications above depend on.
The application layer, because the chat window is still showing an error.
questions.why: Quotas are enforced by the platform layer, and because the application depends on that layer, the limit stops it even though the rest of the stack is healthy.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an example of an agent rather than a model?
choices: A web page that displays the parts list to a customer who is browsing.
A system that plans a sequence of steps, calls a parts database as a tool to check stock, and then places an order to reach its goal.
A trained neural network that only predicts the next word in a reply it is given.
A managed service that stores evaluation runs and shows usage logs to the team.
questions.why: An agent is defined by planning steps and calling outside tools toward a goal, which only the first option does; the others are a model, a platform and an application.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain the five layers of the gen AI landscape to a teammate who is new to cloud work. Name one limit or tradeoff of building everything on a single model provider.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the bottom. Infrastructure is the chips, storage and networking that train and run models. Models are the trained networks that generate output, such as a foundation model that handles many tasks. Platforms are managed services, like Vertex AI, for accessing, tuning, evaluating, deploying and monitoring those models. Agents use a model to plan steps and call tools to finish a goal. Applications are what users see. Each layer depends on the one below it. The main tradeoff of building on one model provider is concentration risk: a pricing change, quota limit or outage at that provider reaches every application above it. Keeping the platform and application layers separate from a specific model makes it easier to switch models later, though it adds some design effort.
rubricPoints: Names the five layers in order from infrastructure up to applications
Explains that each layer depends on the layer below it
Distinguishes a model from a platform and an agent from an application
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as dependence on one provider or the cost of switching models

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a product landscape and vocabulary that is best read through once, with no hands-on OpsForge mission or planned engine matching it closely.

lessons.plain: Google makes several generative AI models, and each is built for a different kind of output. Gemini is a general model that reads and writes text and can also work with images, audio, video and code within one conversation. Gemma is a smaller family whose trained weights are published, so a team can run and adapt it on its own hardware. Imagen creates pictures from written descriptions, and Veo creates short video clips. Knowing which model fits the kind of content you need is the first step in choosing a tool, before cost, security and reliability are weighed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a chatbot that can look at a photo of a damaged part and answer questions about it, and it also wants a separate tool that turns a written description into a short video. Which Google model would you consider for each job, and what property of the first model makes it suitable?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data so it can be adapted to many tasks. Google's four named models differ on two main questions: what kind of content they handle, and whether you use them through a managed Google Cloud service or download the model yourself. The kind of content is called the modality, meaning the type of data such as text, image, audio or video.

Gemini is a multimodal foundation model, meaning one model accepts several modalities in the same request, for example a photo plus a question about it. Its strengths are reasoning over mixed inputs, summarizing long documents, and writing or explaining code. Many Gemini versions offer a large context window, the amount of input and output the model can hold in one exchange, which helps when you need to reason over a long report.

Gemma is a family of open-weight models. The trained numbers, called weights, are published under terms set by Google, so a team can run the model on its own servers or devices and tune it. Gemma models are usually smaller and lighter than the large Gemini models, which suits a narrow task or a setting where data must stay inside your environment.

Imagen is a diffusion model for text-to-image generation. A diffusion model starts from random noise and refines it step by step until it matches the prompt. Veo applies the same generative approach to video, producing short clips from a text or image prompt.

Worked example: a retailer wants product photos made from a written brief. Step one, identify the output as an image, so Imagen is the first candidate. Step two, the same team wants a chatbot that reads the brief and drafts a product description, which is text, so Gemini fits. Step three, if the retailer must keep its catalogue on its own hardware, it would evaluate Gemma for the text task instead.

Common mistake: treating Gemini as the only generative option, or assuming Gemma is just a weaker Gemini with the same hosting and usage terms. The consequence in a running system is real: picking a model for the wrong modality, or one that cannot be hosted where your data policy requires, means rework, unused cost, or a compliance problem.

The right model starts with the modality of the task, then narrows by constraints such as cost, security and reliability.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer wants a tool that takes a customer's photo of car damage plus that customer's written claim, and produces one summary for an adjuster. Step one: the inputs are an image and text together, so one model must accept more than one modality in the same request. Step two: the insurer wants a managed Google Cloud service and has no requirement to run the model on its own servers. Step three, the conclusion, is left for you to complete.
choices: Gemini, because it accepts several modalities in one request and fits a managed service
Gemma, because open-weight models are always the right choice for insurance claims
Imagen, because it reads images and can therefore accept the written claim as well
Veo, because the photo of car damage is a visual input and Veo handles visuals
questions.why: Gemini is the multimodal model, meaning it accepts text and images in the same request, and the insurer's stated constraint of a managed service points to it rather than to a self-hosted option.

questions.prompt: A hospital's data team needs a model it can download and run on its own machines, then tune on a narrow task such as sorting internal forms. Which Google model family fits best?
choices: Imagen, because it can be tuned on any task once it is downloaded
Gemma, because its trained weights are published so it can run on owned infrastructure
Veo, because it is designed to run on the hospital's own servers
Gemini, because it is the only Google model that works with text
questions.why: Gemma is the open-weight family, so its weights can be run and tuned on a team's own hardware, which suits narrow tasks and data that must stay in-house.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency wants a ten-second product clip generated from one still image and a short sentence describing the motion. Which model should it evaluate first?
choices: Veo, for video generated from a text or image prompt
Gemma, since open-weight models are the standard choice for video output
Gemini, since it is the largest model and so it handles every output type
Imagen, since it can produce the frames of a video from text alone
questions.why: The output is video, and Veo is the model that applies the generative approach to producing short clips from a text or image prompt; Imagen targets still images, and Gemini's multimodal strength is accepting mixed inputs rather than being the video generator.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to summarize 400-page annual reports in one request each, through a managed Google Cloud service. Which property of Gemini most directly matches this need?
choices: Its open weights, which let the bank read the report without a network connection
Its small size, which makes it cheaper to host than the other models
Its diffusion process, which refines random noise step by step into text
A large context window that can hold long input and output in one exchange
questions.why: A context window is the amount of input and output a model can hold in one exchange, and a large one is what allows a long report to be handled in a single request; diffusion describes how Imagen and Veo work, and small size and open weights describe Gemma.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Gemini, Gemma, Imagen and Veo for a new feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the content the feature produces. If the output is text or it mixes text with images, audio or code, I would look at Gemini, because it is multimodal and handles long inputs well. If the output is a still image from a description, I would look at Imagen, and if it is a short video, Veo. Gemma is the option when the team needs an open-weight model it can run and adapt on its own infrastructure. The tradeoff with Gemini is that it is a managed service, so the data and usage terms are set by the provider and may not suit every policy. The tradeoff with Gemma is that a smaller open model usually has less general capability than a large managed one, so I would test it on our real task before committing.
rubricPoints: Match the model to the modality of the output, such as Gemini for text and mixed inputs, Imagen for images, Veo for video.
Recognise Gemma as an open-weight family that can be run and tuned on the team's own infrastructure.
Name a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as managed-service terms for Gemini or lower general capability for smaller open models.
Say that cost, security and reliability are checked after the modality is settled.

suggested.rationale: This objective is product-catalogue knowledge about which model does what, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Google describes its approach to AI as building it into the core of the company, from research and custom chips up to finished products, rather than adding it at the end. For a beginner, this means that when Google offers a generative AI tool, it usually runs on the same models, chips and data centers that Google uses for its own services. A business can use that foundation without building it from nothing. Knowing this helps you see why Google offers several levels of gen AI product, from ready-made apps to custom model work.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company wants to use generative AI, why might it prefer a provider that designs its own models and chips, rather than one that only resells other companies' models? Give one reason you would expect.
lessons.teach:
An AI-first approach means a company treats machine learning as the foundation it builds on, not as a feature added later. For Google, its gen AI offerings are designed on the same stack used for its own research and products. That stack has four layers. Foundation models are large models trained on very large amounts of data that can be adapted to many tasks. TPUs (tensor processing units) are custom chips built for the mathematics neural networks rely on. GPUs (graphics processing units) are widely used chips that do the same kind of work. Data centers are the buildings that house and power all of this. Because these parts were engineered together, a business gets models, infrastructure and tools that fit one another, rather than assembling separate parts from several vendors.

Why this works in practice: the same foundation models are offered at different levels of control. A business can call a model through an API (an interface where software sends a request and receives a result), adjust it with its own data, or use a finished application. Choosing the level is a decision about speed, control and effort.

Worked example: a logistics company wants summaries of delivery-delay notes. Step 1: it does not train a model from scratch, because a pretrained model already handles language. Step 2: it picks a managed model service on Google Cloud, so the infrastructure is run for it. Step 3: it supplies its notes under its own access controls and tests the summaries for quality. Step 4: it adopts a finished tool only if the summaries need no custom behavior.

Common mistake: assuming that 'AI-first' guarantees accurate output or that any Google product fits any need. The model is a starting point. The business still checks outputs and matches the product to the task.

Consequence: if a team uses a broad, general-purpose model for a narrow, high-volume task without measuring cost and quality, the running service can become slow or expensive at scale. Fit matters more than the brand of the model.

questions.prompt: A regional museum has 40,000 catalogue photos and wants a short descriptive caption for each one. Step 1: it does not train its own image-and-language model from scratch, because a pretrained foundation model can already describe pictures and be adapted to many tasks. Step 2: it calls a managed model service on Google Cloud through an API, so the infrastructure is run for it and software can send each photo and receive a caption. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: it adopts a finished captioning tool only if the captions need no custom behavior, such as following the museum's house style.
choices: It measures the cost per caption and the caption quality on a sample of photos that curators check, before running the full 40,000 through the service.
It builds its own data center with TPUs so the captions run on hardware it controls, which the teaching text names as the first thing any business must do.
