It assumes the captions are accurate because the model comes from Google, and skips review so the batch finishes sooner.
It removes the access controls on the photos so the model can read them faster, since the model is trusted by default under an AI-first approach.
questions.why: The teaching text says a business still checks outputs and measures cost and quality, so measuring both on a sample before scaling is the missing step, and the other choices are misconceptions about the approach.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text, what does it mean for a company to take an 'AI-first' approach?
choices: It hires only machine learning specialists and avoids using outside vendors for any part of its systems.
It moves all of its work to custom chips so that no general-purpose hardware is used at all.
It guarantees that every output the company's systems produce is accurate and needs no human review.
It treats machine learning as the foundation it builds on, rather than as a feature added later.
questions.why: The teaching text defines AI-first as treating machine learning as the foundation built on from the start, not as a feature added afterward.

questions.prompt: A small software firm wants a finished tool that drafts meeting summaries exactly the way the firm already formats them, with no custom behavior needed. Based on the teaching text, which level of access fits this need best?
choices: Using a finished application, because the text says to adopt one only when no custom behavior is required.
Training a new foundation model from scratch on TPUs, since that is the only way to get the firm's house format.
Calling the model through an API and writing the entire interface from the start, because the API is always cheaper.
Adjusting the foundation model with the firm's own data, because any finished tool would need that step first.
questions.why: The teaching text says a finished application is the right choice when the task needs no custom behavior, and the other options describe more effort than this need requires.

questions.prompt: A team assumes that because its gen AI service is built on Google's AI-first stack, it does not need to measure output quality or cost. It runs a broad, general-purpose model on a narrow, high-volume task. What is the most likely consequence for the running service?
choices: The service becomes slow or expensive at scale, because the team has not checked cost and quality for this task.
The service is protected from errors, because the AI-first design guarantees correct output on any task.
The service becomes more accurate over time, because the foundation model improves automatically with each request.
Nothing changes, because the brand of the model determines fit, so the choice of model needs no review.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a broad model used for a narrow, high-volume task without measuring cost and quality can become slow or expensive at scale, and that fit matters more than brand.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate in your own words what 'AI-first' means for Google's gen AI offerings, and name one limit or tradeoff a business should keep in mind when using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: AI-first means Google designs its gen AI around machine learning from the start, so the models, custom chips, GPUs and data centers were built to work together. For a business, that means access to a mature foundation without building it. The tradeoff is control. A business can use a model through an API, customize it with its own data, or use a finished app, and each step up gives less control over behavior and data handling. Another limit is that a strong underlying platform does not guarantee correct answers for a specific task. The business still has to test outputs, check quality, and choose the level of product that matches the job. Cost also scales with usage, so a broad model used for a narrow, high-volume task may be the wrong fit even though it is capable.
rubricPoints: Defines AI-first as building machine learning into the foundation of the stack, including models, chips and data centers.
Explains the benefit: a business uses a ready foundation rather than building its own.
Names a tradeoff, such as less control at higher levels of abstraction or cost that grows with usage.
States that the business must still test output quality and match the product to the task.

suggested.rationale: This objective is conceptual, and the core skill is explaining how the AI-first stack shapes the products and their tradeoffs in your own words.

lessons.plain: When a company puts an AI system into real work, it needs more than a clever model. It needs the surrounding platform to be safe with customer data, to behave predictably, to stay up under load, and to grow as demand grows. Enterprise-ready means a platform that meets those needs for an organization, not just for a demo. Think of the difference between a prototype car and a vehicle with brakes, insurance, service records and a warranty. Both can drive, but only one is fit to carry a business's daily work. This lesson describes the qualities that make an AI platform fit for that kind of use.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a bank wants to use an AI assistant to answer questions about customer accounts. Before anything else, what would you worry about that a hobby chatbot would never need to handle?
lessons.teach:
An enterprise-ready AI platform is one that an organization can trust with its real data, real customers and real uptime requirements. Five qualities are usually named: responsible, secure, private, reliable and scalable.

Responsible means the platform helps the organization use AI fairly and safely, with tools for checking outputs, filtering harmful content, and documenting how a system is meant to be used. Secure means access is controlled, so only authorized people and services can reach models and data, and activity can be logged. Private means an organization's data is not used to train shared models without permission and stays under its control. Reliable means the service stays available and behaves consistently when something goes wrong. Scalable means capacity grows or shrinks with demand, so a busy day does not cause failures.

Worked example: a retailer launches a product-description generator. Step one, its staff sign in through the company's identity system, so only approved users can call the model (secure). Step two, prompts and outputs stay within the company's cloud project and are not used to improve public models (private). Step three, a safety filter blocks offensive text before it reaches a customer (responsible). Step four, when a holiday sale triples traffic, the service adds capacity automatically (scalable). Step five, if one data center has a problem, traffic moves elsewhere (reliable).

Common mistake: assuming enterprise-ready is a single feature you switch on. It is a combination of settings, access rules, data handling choices and operational design, and each must be set up deliberately.

Consequence: a platform that is not private can leak sensitive records into outputs visible to others, and one that is not reliable can stop a customer-facing service mid-sale. Those failures are why these qualities matter as much as model quality.

questions.prompt: A regional bank deploys an internal assistant that summarizes loan files for its underwriters. Here is the setup so far. Step one: only underwriters who sign in with the bank's own staff accounts can call the model, so access is controlled (secure). Step two: loan files stay inside the bank's own cloud project and are not used to improve shared models (private). Step three is missing. It is a filter that checks each summary for harmful or unfair wording before a loan officer sees it, which is a responsible-AI safeguard. Step four: at month-end, when submissions double, the service adds capacity without manual changes (scalable). Which completion best fills the missing step three?
choices: Each underwriter's sign-in session is recorded and kept for audit, so later reviewers can see who called the model.
The model is retrained every night on all loan files so its wording improves over time.
Summaries are stored for ninety days so that repeat lookups run faster.
Before a loan officer sees a summary, tools check it for harmful or unfair wording, which is the responsible-AI safeguard the list is missing.
questions.why: The missing step is the responsible-AI check on outputs, and only the last choice describes filtering or checking content before it reaches a person, while the others describe logging, storage or retraining, which belong to other qualities or are not qualities at all.

questions.prompt: A school district sets up a no-code tool that drafts parent newsletters. The district wants to be sure that the teacher-written drafts and the tool's outputs are never used to train a model that other customers can use. Which of the five enterprise-ready qualities addresses this concern?
choices: Secure, because only authorized staff can open the tool.
Responsible, because the tool checks its drafts for fairness.
Private, because the district's data stays under its control and is not used to train shared models without permission.
Scalable, because capacity grows when many schools use the tool at once.
questions.why: Private is the quality that keeps an organization's data under its own control and out of shared model training, which is exactly what the district is asking for, while the other three qualities concern capacity, access and content safety.

questions.prompt: A ticket seller runs a chatbot that answers buyers during a major concert sale. Its only serving location loses power for two hours, and no other location takes over, so buyers see errors. Which enterprise-ready quality was missing from this setup?
choices: Reliable, because the service did not stay available or keep working when one location failed.
Private, because the buyers' questions were exposed during the power failure.
Secure, because unauthorized buyers reached the chatbot during the outage.
Scalable, because the chatbot could not add capacity during the sale.
questions.why: Reliable means the service keeps running and behaves consistently when something goes wrong, and here the failure of a single location took the service down with no fallback, whereas scalability concerns demand, not failure, and security and privacy were not the problem described.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm lets only its regional dispatch managers use an AI tool that proposes delivery routes. The firm also needs a record of which account made each request, so it can review usage later. Which quality most directly covers both of these needs?
choices: Secure, because access is restricted to authorized people and their activity can be logged.
Private, because the firm's route data stays under its control.
Reliable, because the tool stays available during peak dispatch hours.
Responsible, because the tool documents how routes should be used.
questions.why: Secure covers both controlled access and logged activity, which are the two needs in the scenario, while private concerns data handling, reliable concerns availability, and responsible concerns fair and safe use of outputs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes a cloud AI platform 'enterprise-ready' compared with a model that works well in a demo. Name one limit or tradeoff a team should still consider, even on an enterprise-ready platform.
lessons.modelAnswer: Enterprise-ready means the platform can safely handle an organization's real work. The model may be strong, but the company also needs access control so only authorized people and services can use it, and it needs to know its prompts and data stay private and are not used to train shared models. It also needs responsible-use tools such as safety filters, reliability so the service stays up, and scalability so it handles peak load. A demo usually skips all of this. One tradeoff remains: an enterprise platform reduces risk but does not remove it. The team still has to configure access correctly, decide what data should go in, check outputs for accuracy, and plan for failures.
rubricPoints: Defines enterprise-ready as meeting real organizational needs, not just producing good demo output
Names at least three of: responsible, secure, private, reliable, scalable, with a plain meaning for each
Explains that the platform reduces risk but the organization still must configure and govern it
Gives a concrete example such as access control, data privacy, or scaling under load

suggested.rationale: This objective is a set of qualities and facts about the platform that are best learned by reading and recalling, with no hands-on mission in the current list that covers enterprise AI platform qualities.

lessons.plain: An integrated ecosystem means many AI tools from one provider are built to work together rather than as separate, unconnected products. Think of a kitchen where the oven, fridge and sink share one power supply and one set of safety rules, instead of three appliances you wire up yourself. When the pieces share the same data access, sign-in and security settings, a business can add or change a tool without rebuilding everything. Recognizing this advantage means knowing why a company might choose a connected set of AI services over assembling many separate ones from different vendors.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company buys three separate AI tools from three different vendors: one for drafting emails, one for searching internal documents, and one for a customer chat assistant. Each tool keeps its own copy of the company's files and its own list of who can log in. What problems would you expect to appear over the first year, and what would a single connected set of tools change?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. An ecosystem is a group of products that work with one another. Integration means the products share something important, such as the same sign-in system, the same data access rules, the same underlying AI models, and the same logging and billing. A managed service is one the provider runs for you, so you do not maintain the servers yourself. Grounding means tying a model's answers to specific trusted documents or data, so it answers from the company's own information rather than from memory alone.

Why it works. When the products share identity and permissions, a rule set once applies everywhere. When they share data connections, a document indexed for search can also feed a chat assistant without a second copy being made. When they share models, a team can try a different model or product without rewriting its connections from scratch. Less glue code between products means fewer places where things can break.

Worked example. A retailer wants an assistant that answers staff questions from its returns policy documents, plus a weekly report on common customer complaints. Step one: the policy documents sit in one governed storage location. Step two: a search-and-grounding service indexes them, using the company's existing sign-in so only staff can query. Step three: a chat assistant uses that same index to answer questions. Step four: call summaries from the same support data feed the weekly report under the same permissions. One access policy covers all four steps.

Common mistake. Learners often read integration as meaning every product in the ecosystem is automatically right for every need, or that it removes the need to check where data is stored and who can see it. You still choose the product that matches the business need, and you still set the permissions.

Consequence. In a running system, a separate copy of the policy documents in each tool drifts out of date, so the chatbot and the report disagree. Connected products that read from one governed source keep answers consistent, and a revoked permission takes effect everywhere at once.

questions.prompt: A freight company wants a dispatcher assistant that answers questions from its shipping manifest files, plus a weekly summary of delivery delays. Step one: the manifest files sit in one governed storage location. Step two: a search-and-grounding service indexes them, using the company's existing sign-in so only dispatchers can query. Step three is missing. Step four: delay records from the same operations data feed the weekly summary under the same permissions, so one access policy covers the whole flow. Which completes step three?
choices: The assistant is given its own copy of the manifests, exported nightly so it can work offline.
The team rebuilds the index from scratch in a new product before the assistant can connect.
The chat assistant uses that same index to answer dispatcher questions, so no second copy of the manifests is made.
The assistant is given a separate sign-in so it can answer questions from any account.
questions.why: Step three must reuse the shared index so the assistant and the search service draw on one governed source, which is the point of connected products in this ecosystem.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does integration mean across a group of cloud AI products?
choices: Each product keeps its own copy of the data so that no tool depends on another.
Every product in the group is the best choice for every business need.
The products share something important, such as sign-in, data access rules, underlying models, and logging and billing.
The products run on separate servers that are maintained by the customer.
questions.why: The teaching text defines integration as sharing key elements like identity, data access rules, models, and logging and billing, and the other options contradict or misstate it.

questions.prompt: A school district wants a tool that answers teacher questions from its curriculum guides, and a monthly summary of parent email themes. It wants both to follow the same access rules. Which benefit of an integrated ecosystem best explains why this setup helps?
choices: The summary must be rewritten by hand each month because the two tools cannot share permissions.
Each tool keeps its own copy of the guides, so a change in one tool cannot affect the other.
A permission change made once on the shared access rules takes effect in both tools at the same time.
The district can skip setting permissions because the ecosystem applies its own default rules.
questions.why: Shared permissions mean one rule set applies everywhere, so revoking or changing access updates both the assistant and the summary together.

questions.prompt: A clinic team assumes that because its scheduling tool and its records tool belong to the same ecosystem, the scheduling product is automatically the right fit for a new patient-intake need. What is the main flaw in that reasoning?
choices: Integration means every product is automatically right for every need, so the team should not check fit.
Managed services always require the customer to maintain the servers, so the scheduling tool cannot be used.
Integrated products cannot share sign-in, so the clinic must manage two separate logins.
Integration does not remove the need to choose the product that matches the business need or to set permissions and check data location.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that integration does not mean every product fits every need, and you still choose the right product and set permissions and data location checks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a business might prefer one connected set of Google Cloud AI services over several separate tools from different vendors, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: A connected set of AI services lets us share one set of sign-in rules, one governed data source and one logging setup across the search tool, the chat assistant and the reporting, so we do not maintain three copies of our documents or three permission lists. A change to someone's access applies everywhere, and answers stay consistent because they come from the same source. The tradeoff is dependence. If most of our workflow runs on one provider's services, moving to another provider later costs more, and each product still has to be the right fit for its task. So before committing, we would check that the integrated option meets our data location and cost needs, and we would keep our data in formats we can export.
rubricPoints: Names a concrete advantage such as shared sign-in, shared data access or a single source of truth.
Explains why shared permissions or data reduce inconsistency or duplicated effort.
States at least one limit, such as dependence on one provider or the need to still match each product to the task.
Notes that the choice still needs checks on data location, security settings or cost.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which connected service fits a business scenario is best practised by reasoning through a situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: An open approach to AI means a platform that lets you choose from many models, including open models whose design and trained settings are published so others can download, inspect, run and adapt them. It also means working with widely used tools and standard interfaces instead of forcing one closed path. Think of building a kitchen: an open setup lets you pick the oven, knives and fridge from different makers, and they still fit together, so you can replace one later without rebuilding the room. For a business, this keeps options open on cost, quality, privacy and future changes, and lowers the risk of being locked into one vendor's model or tooling. The benefit is flexibility and control, not a promise that everything is free or automatically better.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company builds an assistant on one vendor's closed model, then wants to switch to a different model a year later. What would make that switch easy, and what would make it hard?
lessons.teach:
An open model is an AI model whose trained settings, called weights, are published so that others can download, run, inspect and adapt it, usually under a licence that sets the rules of use. A proprietary or closed model is kept by its owner, and you reach it only through the owner's service. Vendor lock-in is the situation where moving away from one provider is costly because your data, code, prompts or staff skills are tied to that provider. Portability is how easily you can move a workload to another model or platform. The open approach works because it separates the model from the platform: when the interface is standard and the tools are widely used, you can change the model behind it while the rest of the system stays put.

Worked example. A support team builds a feature that summarises customer tickets. Step 1: the application calls a model through a standard API, a defined way for programs to send requests. Step 2: the team runs the same 200 past tickets through a proprietary model and an open model and compares summary quality and cost. Step 3: the open model meets the quality bar at lower cost, so the team changes the model name in configuration. The prompts, data pipeline and dashboards do not change.

Common mistake: treating open as meaning free, secure or automatically compliant. Licences differ, and running a model yourself brings hosting cost and responsibility for security.

Consequence in a running system: a model swap is a production change. Output quality can shift even when the code is untouched, so the new model must pass the same evaluation and staged rollout as any other release.

questions.prompt: A freight insurer builds a feature that drafts replies to claim-status emails. Step 1: the application sends each draft request through a standard API, a defined way for programs to send requests. Step 2: the team runs 120 past emails through its current proprietary model and through an open model, then compares reply accuracy and cost per thousand emails. Step 3 is not shown in this write-up. Suppose the open model scored higher on accuracy and lower on cost. Which action comes next, before the open model handles live customer emails?
choices: Change the model name in configuration and switch all customers over at once, since the offline scores already passed
Run the new model through the same evaluation and staged rollout as any other release, because output quality can shift even when the code is unchanged
Rewrite the email prompts for the open model and skip further testing, since the prompts are the only part that changes
Publish the open model's weights on the company website so customers can inspect how the drafts are produced
questions.why: A model swap is a production change, so the new model must pass the same evaluation and staged rollout as any other release, because output quality can shift even when the code is untouched.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes an open model?
choices: A model whose trained settings, called weights, are published so others can download, run, inspect and adapt it under a licence that sets the rules of use
A model hosted by a cloud provider that automatically meets every compliance rule
A model whose trained settings are kept secret and reached only through the owner's paid service
Any model that costs nothing to use, because open means free of charge
questions.why: The teaching text defines an open model as one whose weights are published for others to download, run, inspect and adapt, under a licence that sets the rules of use.

questions.prompt: A startup chooses an open model and concludes that its customer data is now automatically compliant with privacy rules. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: Open models cannot be used with any customer data at all
Open models are always cheaper to run, so compliance costs disappear
The licence of an open model always forbids commercial use
Open does not mean automatically compliant: licences differ, and running a model yourself brings hosting cost and responsibility for security
questions.why: The teaching text warns that open should not be treated as meaning free, secure or automatically compliant, because licences differ and self-hosting carries security responsibility.

questions.prompt: A company wants to keep the option of leaving its current AI provider without a costly rebuild. Which design choice most directly improves its portability?
choices: Store all prompts only inside the provider's proprietary console so they stay in one place
Train all staff only on one provider's tools so they remain productive during any change
Hard-code the provider's private interface into every service so the connection is consistent
Call the model through a standard API so the model can be changed behind it while the rest of the system stays the same
questions.why: Portability is how easily a workload can move to another model or platform, and a standard interface lets the model change while the surrounding system stays put, whereas tying prompts, code or skills to one provider raises lock-in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the benefits of Google Cloud's open approach to AI are for a business, and name one limit or tradeoff we should still watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: The main benefit is choice without rebuilding everything. Because the platform offers many models, including open ones whose design can be inspected, we can compare options on quality, cost and where the data is processed, then pick what fits. Standard interfaces and widely used open tools mean the application code and workflows can stay the same when we change models, which lowers vendor lock-in and keeps our future options open. The tradeoff is that open does not mean free or automatically safe. Each model has its own licence terms, and if we host or customise a model ourselves we take on operating cost, security work and upkeep. Whichever model we pick, we should re-run our evaluation before switching, because output quality can change even when our code does not.
rubricPoints: Open approach means choice among models and tools, including open models whose design can be inspected.
Standard interfaces let a business change models with less rework and less vendor lock-in.
Open does not mean free, secure or compliant by default; licences and operating responsibilities still apply.
A model change should be evaluated and rolled out carefully because output quality can shift.

suggested.rationale: The objective is descriptive, and the core skill is explaining the benefits and tradeoffs of openness in one's own words, which explaining back practises directly.

lessons.plain: Training and running a large AI model takes an enormous amount of arithmetic done in parallel. Google Cloud packages the hardware and supporting software for that work under the name AI Hypercomputer, which bundles chips, networking, software, and buying options that were designed to work together. The main chip types are Google's own custom chips, called TPUs, and graphics processing units, called GPUs, which several companies make. All of it runs inside data centers, the large physical buildings full of servers, power, and cooling. Think of this as the engine room under AI products. You rarely touch it directly, but knowing its parts helps you choose the right option for a workload.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants to train a large image model as fast as possible. Would a room of ordinary general-purpose processors or a set of chips built only for repeated matrix arithmetic be the better starting point, and why?
lessons.teach: An accelerator is a chip built to do one kind of work very fast. A CPU, or central processing unit, is a general-purpose processor good at many different tasks in sequence. Training a neural network, the kind of model behind most gen AI, mostly means multiplying huge grids of numbers (matrices) over and over. Accelerators do thousands of these small multiplications at the same time, which is why they are far faster than CPUs for this job. A TPU, or Tensor Processing Unit, is Google's custom accelerator designed for exactly this pattern; Cloud TPU is the form you rent. A GPU, or graphics processing unit, began as a chip for drawing images and is also strong at parallel arithmetic; Google Cloud offers GPUs made by third-party vendors. A data center is the physical facility holding these machines, along with power, cooling, and networking. AI Hypercomputer is Google's integrated approach that joins accelerators, a high-speed network linking many of them so they act like one machine, open software frameworks and orchestration tools, and flexible ways to consume capacity. Worked example: a team needs to train a model. Step 1: confirm the work is matrix-heavy training. Step 2: choose an accelerator family, TPU or GPU, based on the framework and cost. Step 3: choose how many chips, and confirm the network links them. Step 4: pick a consumption model, such as reserved or on-demand capacity. Step 5: pick a region, since the data center location affects latency and data residency. Common mistake: assuming the fastest single chip is always the answer. If the chips wait on a slow network or a starved data feed, you pay for idle accelerators. The consequence in a running system is that throughput is set by the slowest link in the whole stack, not by the chip alone.

questions.prompt: A small insurer runs a model that summarizes claim files. Its neural network does mostly matrix multiplication, so the team confirmed the work is matrix-heavy. They chose GPUs because their existing framework runs well on them. They then chose a region close to their claims database so that customer data stays where their rules require. Their last open step is the consumption model. Their claim volume is steady around the clock, and they want predictable cost for the next year. Which choice completes this step?
choices: Switch to CPUs, because a steady claims workload does not need accelerators
Buy more GPUs than needed so the consumption model no longer matters
Use on-demand capacity only, because it is always the cheapest option for any workload
Reserve accelerator capacity for the year, because steady 24-hour demand makes reserved capacity the better fit for predictable cost
questions.why: Reserved capacity suits steady, predictable demand and gives predictable cost, which is the consumption choice the scenario calls for.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does Cloud TPU refer to in Google Cloud?
choices: A physical building that holds machines along with power and cooling
A third-party graphics chip sold by an outside vendor
A general-purpose processor that handles many tasks in sequence
Google's custom accelerator for matrix-heavy neural network work, offered as a rentable service
questions.why: A TPU is Google's custom accelerator built for the parallel matrix work of neural networks, and Cloud TPU is the form you rent.

questions.prompt: A training team rents 64 fast accelerators, but they sit idle about 70 percent of the time. The team's chips are not the problem and the model is matrix-heavy. Which explanation best fits the teaching idea about throughput?
choices: The region was chosen too close to the data center
The chips are waiting on a slow network link or a starved data feed, so throughput is limited by the slowest link
The model should be moved to CPUs because accelerators only help with images
The accelerators are too slow and should be replaced with a faster single chip
questions.why: Throughput is set by the slowest link in the stack, so idle accelerators usually point to a network or data-feed bottleneck rather than the chip itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement about where a data center is located is correct?
choices: Location only affects the price of electricity and nothing else
Location has no effect once the accelerator family has been chosen
Location is only relevant for CPUs, not accelerators
Location affects latency and data residency, so it is a deliberate choice when setting up AI infrastructure
questions.why: The data center location affects latency and where data is kept, so it must be chosen deliberately rather than treated as irrelevant.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AI Hypercomputer is, how TPUs and GPUs differ at a high level, and one limit or tradeoff a team should consider before choosing this infrastructure.
lessons.modelAnswer: AI Hypercomputer is Google Cloud's combined setup for AI work. It brings together accelerator chips, a fast network that links many of them, open software frameworks, and flexible ways to rent capacity. TPUs are Google's custom chips built for the matrix arithmetic that neural networks use, while GPUs are more general-purpose parallel chips that Google Cloud offers from third-party vendors. A tradeoff to raise is that specialized hardware can lock a team into certain frameworks or ways of working, and a fast chip only helps if the network and data pipeline keep it busy. Cost is another limit, because accelerators sitting idle still cost money. So the choice should be checked against the actual workload, the software the team already uses, and the region where its data must live.
rubricPoints: Describes AI Hypercomputer as an integrated bundle of chips, networking, software, and consumption options
Explains that TPUs are Google's custom accelerators and GPUs are general-purpose parallel chips offered by vendors
Notes that throughput depends on the whole stack, including network and data feed
Names a tradeoff such as framework fit, cost of idle capacity, or data location

suggested.rationale: This objective is product and hardware catalogue knowledge with no hands-on mission or planned engine that would teach it better than reading.

lessons.plain: When a company uses AI that writes or answers questions, it needs to know where its information goes, who can see it, and whether the AI provider learns from it. Google Cloud's AI platform is designed so the customer stays in charge of those answers. Think of renting a secure office in a shared building. The building owner maintains the locks and alarms, but you decide who gets a key, which rooms they can enter, what gets recorded, and whether your papers ever leave. This lesson explains the main levers: access control, encryption, privacy terms, logging, and choice of models, from ready-made tools to customised agents that can act on company systems.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company wants an AI assistant that answers questions using internal HR documents. Before any teaching, list three things you would want to control about that setup, and say who in the company should be able to change each one.
lessons.teach:
Data control means you decide where your data is stored, who can read or change it, what is recorded about its use, and whether it is used to improve anything beyond your own project. Access control, usually handled by Identity and Access Management (IAM), is the rule set that says which user or service account (a non-human identity used by software) may perform which action on which resource. Encryption protects stored data (at rest) and moving data (in transit). Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) let you hold the key material yourself. Data residency is the physical region where data is kept. Governance is the ongoing system of policies, approvals and audit logs that shows who did what. A foundation model is a large pre-trained model. A first-party model is one built by Google, such as Gemini. An open model publishes its weights so it can be inspected and run more freely; Model Garden is the catalogue where you browse and deploy models. An agent is a model that can call tools, such as a function, a data store lookup or a plugin, to act on external systems.

Worked example: an HR team stores policy PDFs in a storage bucket in one region. IAM grants the HR assistant's service account read-only access to that bucket. A prebuilt search-and-answer option is pointed at the bucket as a data store, so answers are grounded in those documents. Audit logs record each query. Finally, a lookup tool lets the agent check leave balances, using a service account limited to that single read operation.

Common mistake: giving the agent's service account broad project permissions because it is quicker to set up. An over-permissioned agent that can read everything or write to production systems turns one prompt-injection trick into a real data leak.

The platform gives you these levers, but the permissions you set are the ones that actually govern your data.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's compliance team keeps client account statements in a storage bucket located in Frankfurt, so the data stays in Germany. They want a prebuilt search-and-answer option that answers staff questions from those statements, and an agent that can look up a single customer's current balance from the core banking system. Step 1: the bucket is in Frankfurt, which sets data residency. Step 2: IAM grants the summary assistant's service account read-only access to that bucket, so it can read but not change statements. Step 3: the search-and-answer option is pointed at the bucket as a data store, so answers are grounded in the statements. Step 4: audit logs are enabled so every query is recorded. Missing step: the balance-lookup tool needs its own service account, and the team must decide what that account is allowed to do.
choices: Give it write access to the core banking system so it can correct mismatched balances
Give it read-only permission for the one balance-lookup operation and nothing else
Give it project Owner rights so the tool never fails with a permission error
Share the summary assistant's service account with it so only one identity needs managing
questions.why: Least privilege means the tool's service account gets only the single read operation it needs, which limits damage if the agent is manipulated.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK) let an organisation do?
choices: Make stored data unreadable to every user in the project, including administrators
Hold the key material yourself rather than relying only on keys the provider manages
Remove the need for IAM rules because the key itself controls access
Let Google rotate and store keys on the organisation's behalf with no visibility
questions.why: CMEK means the customer holds the key material, which is the defining point of the option; the others misdescribe encryption or confuse it with access control.

questions.prompt: A small logistics startup wants a generative AI system that can answer a dispatcher's question about which trucks are free right now by calling its own fleet-status API and then explaining the result. Which concept best fits this need?
choices: A foundation model used alone, with no connection to any outside system
An open model downloaded from Model Garden and run on a laptop with no tools
A governance policy with audit logs, which records activity but does not answer questions
An agent, which is a model able to call tools such as an API to act on external systems
questions.why: An agent is defined as a model that calls tools to act on external systems, which is exactly what checking live fleet status requires; the other options either lack tool calls or are not answering components.

questions.prompt: A team gives its customer-support agent's service account project-wide Editor rights so the agent never hits a permission error during testing. What is the main risk of leaving this in place in production?
choices: A successful prompt-injection trick could make the agent read or change data far beyond its job
Audit logs will stop recording the agent's queries
Encryption at rest will be switched off for every bucket in the project
The agent will become a foundation model rather than a tool-using agent
questions.why: Over-broad permissions turn a manipulated prompt into a data leak or unauthorised write, which is the failure case the teaching text warns about; the other options describe effects the permissions do not cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: A colleague says the AI platform is secure, so we don't need to think about who can access our data. Explain to your teammate what control Google Cloud's AI platform gives you over data and access, and name one limit or tradeoff that remains our responsibility.
lessons.modelAnswer: The platform gives us several controls rather than one switch. IAM lets us decide which users and service accounts can call models, read data stores or invoke agent tools, and we can keep each role narrow. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit, and customer-managed keys let us hold the key material. Audit logs show who queried what. We can choose between Google's own first-party models, open models from a catalogue, and prebuilt or custom solutions, so we match the tool to our sensitivity needs. But the platform cannot decide for us. We still have to design least-privilege roles, pick the right region for residency, and review what an agent is allowed to do with its tools. A broad permission on an agent is our mistake, not the platform's.
rubricPoints: Names concrete controls such as IAM roles, encryption and audit logs
Explains that customers choose the model type and data location
States that permission design and least privilege remain the customer's responsibility
Notes that agents need tightly scoped tool access

suggested.rationale: Working through who may access which data under a policy is the core skill, and a planned authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test that directly.

lessons.plain: Democratizing AI means putting it within reach of people who are not specialist AI researchers. Google Cloud offers several levels of help. Low-code and no-code tools let you build with visual screens and little or no programming. Pre-trained models are models that someone has already trained on huge amounts of data, so you can use them without gathering data and training one yourself. APIs, short for application programming interfaces, are agreed-upon ways for one program to ask another program to do a job, so your existing software can use AI with a few requests. A business can start with the skill it already has and move up only when it needs more control.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small retail team with no machine learning engineers wants a chatbot that answers questions from its own product manuals within a month. Before reading anything, which would you guess is the faster starting point: training a new language model from scratch, or using an existing model through a managed service, and why?
lessons.teach:
A pre-trained model is a model whose learning has already been done by its maker, so you use it rather than building it. A managed service is a cloud offering where the provider runs the servers, scaling and updates for you. An API is the request format your software uses to send input to that service and receive output back. Low-code tools reduce programming to configuring settings and connecting blocks, and no-code tools replace most code with visual forms and uploads. The reason this works is that most business tasks need general language or image skills, which large pre-trained models already have. You only add your own data where the general model falls short.

Worked example: a support team wants incoming emails sorted into billing, technical, or other. Step one: send sample emails to a pre-trained language model through an API, with plain-English instructions and a few examples in the request. Step two: run it on about 200 past emails with known answers and measure how often it is right. Step three: if accuracy is poor, use a no-code training tool to upload labelled examples and train a custom classifier. Step four: write custom code only if neither option fits. Each step is chosen only when the previous one fails.

A common mistake is believing that no-code means no testing. You still need real examples with known answers, because a model can sound confident and still be wrong.

In a running system the choice has consequences. Each API call costs money and adds delay, and the service may limit how many requests you can send per minute, so a traffic spike can cause failed calls. Design for those errors from the start.

The simplest option that meets the measured need is almost always the right first choice.

questions.prompt: A hotel group wants guest reviews sorted into positive, negative, or mixed. The team follows these steps. Step one: send sample reviews to a pre-trained language model (a model whose learning was already done by its maker) through an API (the request format software uses to send input to a service and get output back), with plain-English instructions. Step two: run the model on 150 past reviews with known labels and measure accuracy, which comes out at 91 percent against a 95 percent target. Step three: upload 1,200 labelled reviews to a no-code tool (one that replaces code with visual forms and uploads) and train a custom classifier, which reaches 96 percent. Step four is missing. The team is about to send 40,000 reviews a day through the service. Which step fits next?
choices: Stop testing and launch, because 96 percent accuracy on past reviews guarantees the live results will match.
Switch to a larger pre-trained model to avoid any need for limits or retries, since larger models do not get rate-limited.
Plan for the service's per-minute request limit and the cost per call before launch, and design retries for failed calls from the start.
Write custom code to host the trained classifier on the group's own servers, since custom code is the most flexible option.
questions.why: At 40,000 reviews a day the service's per-minute request limit and per-call cost become real constraints, so the team must plan for both and handle failed calls before going live.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a managed service mean in a cloud offering?
choices: A service where you install and patch the software yourself on servers you rent by the hour.
A service where the provider runs the servers, handles scaling and applies updates for you.
A service that only works when a human operator approves each request before it runs.
A service that is free of charge because it is funded by advertising.
questions.why: A managed service means the provider operates the underlying servers, scaling and updates, so the customer does not do that work.

questions.prompt: A small bakery wants short product descriptions written for its website. Its developer has no machine learning background and a one-week deadline. Which approach best fits the need?
choices: Hire a team to write custom model code, since only custom code can produce good descriptions.
Buy dedicated servers and install an open model, since using a managed service would mean giving up control.
Collect 50,000 past descriptions and train a new language model from scratch before writing anything.
Send a few example descriptions and plain-English instructions to a pre-trained language model through an API, then check the output on sample products.
questions.why: A pre-trained model with an API and a few examples meets a common writing need quickly, and the team then checks output quality rather than building anything new.

questions.prompt: A online ticket shop calls a pre-trained model through an API during a flash sale and many requests fail. The team's first reaction is that the model is broken. What is the most likely explanation and sensible response?
choices: The model has learned wrong answers, so the team should retrain it before the next sale.
The API is always free, so the failures must come from the shop's own internet connection, which should be upgraded.
The model cannot handle more than one customer at a time, so the team should delete the API integration entirely.
The service limits requests per minute, so the spike triggers failures; the team should design for these errors, such as retrying with a short wait and budgeting calls.
questions.why: Services often cap requests per minute, so traffic spikes cause failed calls, and designing for those errors from the start is the sensible response.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud AI how low-code, no-code, pre-trained model, and API options let a team add AI without building it from scratch. Name one limit or tradeoff of choosing the simplest option.
lessons.modelAnswer: The idea is that most teams do not need to build AI from nothing. Google Cloud provides pre-trained models that already understand language and images, and you reach them through an API, which is just a standard request your software sends and a response it gets back. If you need your own categories or behaviour, low-code or no-code tools let you train on your examples with little programming. The simplest path is to try the pre-trained model first, measure its accuracy on real examples, and only add custom training if that falls short. The main tradeoff of the simple route is control. You depend on the provider's model, its pricing, its rate limits and its update schedule, and you may not be able to tune its behaviour as precisely as with code you own. So you should plan for failed or slow calls and keep checking quality over time.
rubricPoints: Defines pre-trained models and APIs in plain terms
Explains that low-code and no-code tools allow customization with little programming
Describes starting with the simplest option and measuring before adding custom training
Names a concrete tradeoff such as less control, dependence on the provider, or per-call cost and rate limits

suggested.rationale: This objective is product recognition and catalogue facts, which no listed mission or planned engine currently covers, so reading the product descriptions is the best fit.

lessons.plain: The Gemini app is a chat assistant you open in a browser or phone app. You type a request in ordinary language, such as asking for a draft email, a summary of a long document, or an explanation of a concept, and it writes a reply you can refine in follow-up messages. Gemini Advanced is the paid tier of that same kind of assistant, with access to a more capable model and higher usage limits. Gems are custom versions you build by writing standing instructions and optionally attaching reference files, so you do not repeat the same setup in every chat. Think of a Gem as a saved job description for the assistant.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project lead wants the same instructions (tone, audience, output format) applied every time her team asks the assistant to draft status updates. Without reading further, what feature would you expect to save that setup, and what would you expect a paid tier to add on top of it?
lessons.teach:
The Gemini app is Google's chat interface to its Gemini models. A model is a large generative AI system that produces text, images and other content from a written instruction. That instruction is called a prompt. You type a prompt, the model returns a response, and you refine it in follow-up messages. Gemini Advanced is a paid tier of the same app that gives access to a more capable model and higher usage limits. Gems are reusable custom versions of the assistant. You write standing instructions describing a role, tone and output format, and you can attach reference files, so each new chat starts already configured.

Why it works: the saved instructions and files are included with every request made through that Gem, so the model is steered the same way each time without you retyping the setup. A Gem does not retrain the model and does not learn from your later chats.

Worked example: a support lead creates a Gem named Release Note Writer. Step 1: she writes instructions asking for plain language, three sections (new, fixed, known issues) and under 150 words. Step 2: she attaches the product style guide. Step 3: she opens a new chat with that Gem and pastes raw bullet points from engineering. Step 4: the reply follows the saved format, and she edits it before sending.

Common mistake: treating a Gem's output as verified fact. The assistant can produce confident but wrong statements, so a person still checks claims before they reach customers.

Consequence: if the attached style guide is out of date, every draft inherits the old rules, so each Gem needs an owner who keeps its instructions and files current. For business use, the edition you have and its data terms decide whether confidential material should be pasted in at all.

A Gem is a saved, reusable instruction set for the Gemini assistant, and its value is consistency, not extra knowledge.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm wants its customer service staff to send consistent shipment delay notices. A team lead builds a Gem called Delay Notice Drafter. Step 1: she writes standing instructions asking for a calm tone, a greeting, a revised delivery window, and under 100 words. Step 2: she attaches the carrier's current delay-policy document. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the reply follows the saved tone and length, and a dispatcher checks the dates and facts before the notice goes to the customer.
choices: Opens a new chat with the Delay Notice Drafter Gem and pastes in the specific delay details for one shipment
Copies the full history of past chats into the Gem's instructions so the model remembers every earlier customer
Retrains the Gemini model on the delay-policy document so it permanently learns the firm's wording
Upgrades the whole team to Gemini Advanced so the Gem's instructions are no longer needed
questions.why: Step 3 is the point where a new chat is opened with the Gem and the shipment-specific details are pasted in, which matches how a Gem is used as a reusable configured assistant.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does a Gem add to the Gemini assistant?
choices: A saved set of standing instructions and reference files that is included with each request made through it
A paid subscription tier with higher usage limits than the free app
A larger memory of every chat you have ever had, shared across all users
A separate, retrained model that is more accurate than the standard Gemini model
questions.why: The teaching text defines a Gem as reusable standing instructions plus attached files that are sent with every request in that Gem, which is about consistency rather than new knowledge or a separate model.

questions.prompt: A procurement manager believes that each time her team's Gem is used, it gets a little smarter about their supplier list because it learns from later chats. Which statement corrects this misunderstanding?
choices: The Gem learns from every chat, so its answers improve automatically over time
The Gem does not retrain the model or learn from later chats; its behaviour only changes when someone edits its instructions or files
The Gem learns only when a Gemini Advanced subscription is active
The Gem stores each chat as a training example that is applied the next day
questions.why: The teaching text states that a Gem does not retrain the model and does not learn from later chats, so its steering changes only when its saved instructions or attached files are changed by a person.

questions.prompt: A small finance team uses the free Gemini app and keeps hitting usage limits during heavy daily analysis of long reports. Which change best matches the paid tier described in the teaching text?
choices: Turn on follow-up messages so each prompt covers more reports at once
Subscribe to Gemini Advanced, which gives access to a more capable model and higher usage limits
Switch to a Gem that writes its own instructions to save usage
Build a Gem with the report template attached so each chat has fewer limits
questions.why: The teaching text says Gemini Advanced is the paid tier of the same app offering a more capable model and higher usage limits, which addresses the stated limit problem, while the Gem options only change how instructions are stored, not the limits.

lessons.explainPrompt: You are advising a team that wants to use the Gemini app to draft customer emails. Explain to a teammate what a Gem is, when a paid Gemini Advanced tier might be worth it, and one limit the team must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Gem is a saved version of the Gemini assistant with standing instructions and optional reference files attached, so the team does not retype the tone, audience and format for every chat. We would create one Gem for customer-email drafts, with the brand voice and a sample of approved replies attached. Gemini Advanced is the paid tier of the same app with a more capable model and higher usage limits, so it is worth considering when the team hits limits on the free tier or needs better quality for long or complex drafts. The limit to watch is accuracy: the model can write fluent but wrong statements, such as an incorrect refund policy, so a person must check every draft before it is sent. Also, a Gem does not learn from later chats, so when policies change, someone must update its instructions and files. Finally, we check the data terms of our edition before pasting any customer details into it.
rubricPoints: Defines a Gem as a saved, reusable set of instructions and attached files for the Gemini assistant.
Explains that Gemini Advanced is a paid tier with a more capable model and higher usage limits.
Names human checking of generated drafts as a limit on accuracy.
Notes that Gems must be updated when policies or reference files change, since they do not learn from later chats.
Mentions checking data terms before entering confidential customer information.

suggested.rationale: This objective is product facts and feature tiers, which a reference read covers better than any hands-on mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Gemini Enterprise is a business-facing offering from Google Cloud that lets a company's staff use generative AI on the company's own documents and systems. Think of it as a shared assistant that can search across internal content, answer questions with sources, and be extended with custom helpers called agents. This lesson covers three capabilities that may be named in exam questions: a notebook-style workspace for working with a chosen set of sources, search across mixed content types such as text, images and audio, and building task-focused agents. The goal is to match each business need to the right capability, not to memorise every setting.
lessons.guessPrompt: A regional sales team has hundreds of PDFs, slide decks and recorded calls about one product line and wants staff to get answers quickly. Before any teaching, what would you expect a useful AI tool to need to do with that material, and what would worry you about letting it do so?
lessons.teach: Definitions first. Generative AI means models that produce new content such as text, images or summaries. A grounded answer is one whose facts come from specific sources you supply, rather than only from what the model learned during training. Multimodal means the system handles more than one type of content, such as text, images, audio and video. An agent is a system that works toward a goal by taking steps, and a tool is anything outside the model that it can use to look things up or act, such as a data store or an action in another system. A notebook-style workspace is a bounded set of sources you choose, so answers can be traced back to them. Why it works: at question time the system retrieves relevant passages from your sources and gives them to the model, so the answer reflects your content and points to where it came from. Worked example: a sales team adds 300 files to a workspace. Step one, the files are indexed, including the text and the images inside slides. Step two, someone asks what warranty applies to model X. Step three, the system retrieves a passage from a PDF and a diagram from a slide, and the answer cites both. Step four, for a request to draft follow-up emails for each lead, a custom agent with a tool that reads the CRM and an email template produces drafts for a person to approve. Common mistake: assuming the assistant knows facts outside its sources, or granting broad access without checking permissions. Consequence: if access is set too loosely, staff can receive answers built from documents they were never allowed to open, so permissions should mirror existing access rules. The objective also names a Notebook API; treat it as the programmatic way other software works with such a workspace. Feature names and availability change, so confirm current details in official documentation. The business value is faster answers from knowledge the company already owns, with traceable sources and little custom code for common cases.

questions.prompt: A regional hotel group loads 80 documents into a workspace: a parking policy PDF, a property floor plan image, and a pool schedule slide deck. Step one: the system indexes the text and the images inside the slides and PDFs. Step two: a front-desk employee asks, "Where can guests park overnight at the Porto property?" Step three: [missing step]. Step four: the answer states the overnight parking rule and cites both the parking PDF and the Porto floor plan image.
choices: The system retrieves relevant passages and the floor plan from the workspace sources and gives them to the model to build the answer.
The question is sent to an email template that drafts a reply for a manager to approve.
The model answers from general knowledge about hotel parking rules it learned during training, without consulting the workspace.
The parking PDF and floor plan are copied into the model's training data so future answers will remember them.
questions.why: The missing step is the retrieval step, where relevant passages from the chosen sources are fetched at question time and handed to the model so the answer reflects and cites that content.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for an answer to be grounded?
choices: The answer is produced only by the model's general training and never uses any files.
The facts in the answer come from specific sources you supply, not only from what the model learned in training.
The answer is checked by a human reviewer before it is shown to anyone.
The answer is written quickly because the system has very little content to search.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a grounded answer as one whose facts come from specific sources you supply rather than only from training.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm sets its shared workspace so that every employee in the company can open every uploaded contract, including ones marked for the legal team only. Which outcome is the most direct consequence described in the teaching text?
choices: Staff may receive answers built from documents they were never allowed to open, so access should mirror existing rules.
The custom agent will refuse to draft any emails until the legal team approves each contract.
The workspace will stop indexing images inside the contract PDFs automatically.
The model will forget the contracts after a few weeks because the workspace is too large.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that loose access can give staff answers built from documents they were not permitted to open, so permissions should mirror existing access rules.

questions.prompt: A support team wants an agent that reads new help tickets, looks up the customer's order history in a ticketing database, and writes a reply draft for an agent to approve before sending. Which part of this setup is the tool?
choices: The reply draft that the support agent approves before sending.
The overall goal of resolving tickets faster across the company.
The model's general knowledge of customer service language.
The ticketing database lookup, because it is something outside the model that the agent can use to look things up.
questions.why: A tool is anything outside the model that the agent can use to look things up or act, and the order history database lookup fits that definition.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never used it what Gemini Enterprise's notebook-style workspace, multimodal search and custom agents each do for a business. Then name one limit or tradeoff a sponsor should weigh before rolling it out.
lessons.modelAnswer: The notebook-style workspace is a bounded set of company sources, such as policy documents and product files, that the assistant answers from, and it cites where an answer came from. Multimodal search means the same question can pull a relevant passage from a PDF, a diagram in a slide or a clip from a recording, so staff do not need to know which file type holds the answer. Custom agents take a goal and carry out steps, using tools such as a CRM lookup, then return a result for a person to check. The main tradeoff is access control. The assistant can only be as safe as the permissions on its sources, so a sponsor should confirm that existing access rules carry over before broad rollout, and should check answers on sensitive topics before relying on them.
rubricPoints: Describes the notebook-style workspace as a chosen set of sources that answers are grounded in and traced to.
Explains multimodal search as finding answers across text, images, audio or video.
Explains custom agents as systems that take steps toward a goal using tools.
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as access permissions or the need to verify answers.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and business-fit recognition, which the course covers as reading rather than a listed hands-on mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Gemini for Google Workspace is an AI assistant built into the everyday office tools many companies already use, such as email, documents, spreadsheets, slide decks, video calls and shared drives. Instead of copying your work into a separate chatbot, you ask the assistant from inside the app you are already using. It can draft or rewrite text, summarize a long email thread or meeting, pull key points out of a spreadsheet, and help build a first version of a presentation. Think of it as a capable colleague sitting beside you in the document, not a new place you have to go.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team lead missed a 90-minute meeting and has 40 unread email threads waiting. What would you want an AI assistant to do for them inside the tools they already use, and what would make you hesitant to let it read those messages?
lessons.teach: Gemini for Google Workspace is a generative AI assistant added to Google Workspace, the bundle of collaboration apps that includes Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Meet, Chat and Drive. Generative AI means a model that creates new text, images or summaries in response to a prompt, which is a plain-language instruction you type. For organizations it is usually sold as a per-user add-on or as part of certain editions, and it works inside each app rather than as a separate tool. Why it works: the assistant can see the content already in the app you are using, such as the open document, the email thread or the spreadsheet range you select, and it uses that context to respond. Because the work stays where it already lives, people skip the copy-and-paste step that makes generic chatbots awkward for routine office tasks. Typical functions include drafting and rewriting text in Docs and Gmail, summarizing long threads, producing meeting notes and catch-up summaries in Meet, answering questions about data in Sheets, and generating a first draft of slides. Business value comes from less time spent on blank pages and routine rewriting, faster catch-up after absences, and quicker analysis for people who are not spreadsheet experts. Worked example: a sales manager opens a long Gmail thread about a delayed order and asks the assistant for a summary and a list of open questions. Step 1, the assistant reads the thread she has open. Step 2, it condenses the back-and-forth into a short summary. Step 3, it lists the three questions no one has answered. Step 4, she checks the summary against the thread before forwarding it, because the output is a draft. Common mistake: treating the output as verified fact. The model can miss a detail or invent one, so a person must review anything that goes to customers, leadership or regulators. Consequence: if an unchecked summary is sent on, a wrong date or amount reaches people who act on it, so organizations keep a human reviewer in the loop and set admin policies on who can use the feature and what content it can reach.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a business wants an AI assistant that answers questions from its own documents, or that checks its answers against current public information. Google Cloud offers external search for both needs. One kind searches a company's own content so the AI can find the right passages and answer from them. The other lets the AI look up live public web results to support what it says. The core skill is recognizing which source a business need calls for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a chatbot that answers employees' questions using only its internal policy documents, and separately wants answers about today's public news checked against current sources. Before any teaching, which kind of search would you connect to each need, and why?
lessons.teach:
Grounding means tying a model's answer to real source material so it is less likely to invent facts. Retrieval is the step where a system finds relevant passages from a body of content before the model writes its reply. Together these form retrieval-augmented generation, usually called RAG.

Agent Search on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is a managed search-and-retrieval service over your own content, such as documents, web pages, and data you connect to it. It indexes that content, retrieves the passages that match a question, and passes them to an agent or model so the answer comes from your sources. Its business value is that employees and customers can find answers in company knowledge without a team building a search system from scratch.

Google Search, as an external search offering, works in the opposite direction. It grounds a model's answer in current results from the public web. This suits questions whose answers depend on recent or general public information rather than private files.

Worked example: a claims team asks what its policy says about flood damage in section 4. Agent Search retrieves section 4 from the indexed policy library, and the model answers from that passage. A second question asks for current public guidance on flood insurance rules. That calls for web grounding, so Google Search supplies recent public results.

Common mistake: sending questions about private content to web grounding. Public results cannot see your internal files, so the answer will be generic or wrong for your business. In a running system, that means confident answers that contradict internal policy, which quickly destroys user trust.

The rule to remember: match the source of truth to the need. Internal knowledge goes to Agent Search, and current public information goes to Google Search.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm wants two kinds of answers for its dispatchers. Case one: a dispatcher asks what the firm's own forklift manual says about charging batteries in cold storage. The firm has already connected and indexed the manual, the system finds the matching section, and the model answers from that section. Case two: a dispatcher asks what the current national hours-of-service limit for truck drivers is. Case one is internal knowledge, so Agent Search handles it. For case two, the missing step is choosing the product that matches the source of truth. Which product should answer case two, and why?

Google Search, because the rule is current public information rather than the firm's private files
No grounding at all, because the model's own built-in knowledge is recent enough for a regulation
Agent Search with a faster index refresh schedule, so the regulation is added to the company library
questions.why: The regulation is current public information that is not in the firm's private files, so the source of truth is the public web and Google Search is the matching product.

choices: A model with no grounding, because the theses will be learned during the model's own training
A general chat assistant with no connection to any content, because students only need fluent writing
Google Search, because it grounds answers in the public web and the theses are published online
Agent Search on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, because it indexes the library's own content and retrieves matching passages
questions.why: The answers must come from the library's own indexed content, which is the job Agent Search is designed for, while Google Search covers public web information.

Agent Search can answer because it indexes every page on the internet once it is connected to a catalogue
Agent Search will automatically browse the rival's website to confirm the price during the answer
questions.why: Agent Search retrieves only from content connected to it, so information on a rival's live website falls outside its reach and calls for public web grounding.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the business value of Agent Search on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform?
choices: It guarantees that every answer is correct, so staff no longer need to check sources
It removes the need for any model, so answers come directly from stored files without generation
