It lets employees and customers find answers in company knowledge without a team building a search system from scratch
questions.why: Agent Search is a managed retrieval service over an organisation's own content, so its value is faster access to company knowledge without building a custom search system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between Agent Search and Google Search in Google Cloud, and name one limit or tradeoff of choosing each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Agent Search is for answering from our own content. We connect it to documents and data sources, it indexes them, and when someone asks a question it retrieves the matching passages and gives them to the model, so the answer is grounded in our material and can point back to the source. The limit is that it is only as good as what we index. If a document is missing, outdated, or badly structured, the answer will reflect that, so we need someone to own content freshness. Google Search grounding is for questions that depend on current public information. It brings in live web results, so it covers things our files cannot know. The tradeoff is that it cannot see private content, and public sources may not match our internal policy. So for a company policy question I would choose Agent Search, and for a question about today's public regulations I would choose Google Search.
rubricPoints: Agent Search retrieves answers from the organization's own indexed content, so answers are grounded in internal sources.
Google Search grounding draws on current public web results, which suits questions about public or recent information.
A key limit of Agent Search is dependence on the quality and freshness of indexed content.
A key limit of web grounding is that it cannot access private files and may conflict with internal policy.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product facts and matching products to business needs, which a focused reading of the product catalogue covers better than any listed mission or engine.

lessons.plain: Customer Engagement Suite is Google Cloud's bundle of AI tools for businesses that talk with customers through chat, voice, or messaging. It covers four jobs: a virtual assistant that answers customers itself, a helper that quietly feeds suggestions to human agents during a live conversation, an analytics layer that reads past conversations to show what customers keep asking about, and a complete hosted contact center that routes calls and messages. Each piece solves a different business problem, and the skill is matching the need to the right piece.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank has thousands of recorded customer calls it has never listened to, and leaders want to know why the same few complaints keep coming in. Which part of the suite would you reach for first, and what would it produce?
lessons.teach:
A contact center is the team and systems that handle customer calls, chats, and messages. Customer Engagement Suite is Google Cloud's set of AI products for that work. Conversational Agents are virtual agents: software that holds a conversation with a customer, works out their intent (what they want, such as changing an address), and can take actions through connected back-end systems. Agent Assist works alongside a human agent in real time, reading the live conversation and suggesting answers or relevant knowledge-base articles. Conversational Insights analyzes conversations after they happen, turning transcripts (text versions of calls) into topics, trends, and sentiment (the emotional tone of the customer). Contact Center as a Service is a hosted contact center platform, so the business rents routing and telephony from the provider instead of running its own phone infrastructure.

Why it works: the suite separates the customer-facing side, the agent-facing side, the learning-from-history side, and the platform under them. Worked example: a customer calls to change a delivery address. First, a Conversational Agent answers, identifies the intent, collects the order number, and updates the address through a connected system. Second, when the customer asks for a person, the call is routed through the contact center platform to a free agent. Third, Agent Assist watches that live call and surfaces the address-policy article the agent needs. Fourth, the following week, Conversational Insights shows that address-change calls rose after a carrier change.

Common mistake: treating Agent Assist and Conversational Agents as the same thing. One supports a human during the call, while the other can handle some conversations without a human at all. Consequence: if a virtual agent cannot hand off cleanly to a person, customers repeat themselves and abandon the call, so the handoff design matters as much as the bot.

Step 1: Conversational Insights reviews last quarter's call transcripts and finds that damaged-item calls cluster after deliveries from one courier. Step 2: BrightCart adds a Conversational Agent flow that takes a photo link and order number from customers reporting damaged items, then opens a claim in its order system. Step 3: [MISSING STEP: For the damaged-item calls that still reach a staff member, the product that watches the live call and suggests the refund-policy article to the staff member is the one to name here.] Step 4: Six weeks later, the team compares average handling time for claims that reached staff before and after the change.

Conversational Agents, because a virtual agent is what suggests articles to a staff member during a call
Conversational Insights, because it reads the live call and suggests policy articles during the conversation
Agent Assist, because it works beside the human agent during the live call and surfaces knowledge-base articles
questions.why: Agent Assist is the product that works alongside a human agent in real time, reading the live conversation and surfacing relevant knowledge-base articles, which is exactly the missing step.

questions.prompt: A dental practice wants a hosted phone system so it does not have to buy and maintain its own switchboard hardware, while still getting call routing to the right front-desk staff. Which Customer Engagement Suite offering fits this need?
choices: Conversational Insights, because it routes calls to the right staff member based on call topics
Contact Center as a Service, because it is a hosted platform where the business rents routing and telephony from the provider
Conversational Agents, because a virtual agent handles all routing without any phone infrastructure
Agent Assist, because it provides the hosted telephony and routing for the practice
questions.why: Contact Center as a Service is the hosted platform that rents routing and telephony from the provider, so the practice does not run its own phone infrastructure.

The agency removes the option to reach a person, and complaints about repeated questions rise. What is the most likely consequence this scenario illustrates?
choices: The contact center platform will automatically reroute the chats to a different country

questions.prompt: A home-tree-service company wants to review every recorded call from last year to find out which topics, such as storm damage quotes or late arrivals, are growing over time and how callers' emotional tone changes. Which product should it use?
choices: Agent Assist, because it analyzes recorded calls after they end to show trends
Conversational Agents, because they replay past calls to measure topics and tone
Contact Center as a Service, because the hosted platform produces topic and sentiment reports
Conversational Insights, because it analyzes conversations after they happen, turning transcripts into topics, trends, and sentiment

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what each of the four parts of Customer Engagement Suite does, and name one limit or tradeoff a business should weigh before replacing some human agents with a virtual agent.
lessons.modelAnswer: Conversational Agents are virtual agents that talk to customers directly, understand what they want, and complete simple tasks through connected systems. Agent Assist sits beside a human agent during a live conversation and suggests answers or knowledge-base articles. Conversational Insights reviews past conversations, so the business can see recurring topics and sentiment trends. Contact Center as a Service is the hosted platform that routes calls and messages. The main tradeoff with a virtual agent is that it works well for predictable requests but can frustrate customers with unusual problems, so a business must design a smooth handoff to a person and measure whether customers are actually resolved. Good deployments usually start with a narrow set of high-volume requests.
rubricPoints: Conversational Agents handle customer conversations directly and can take actions in connected systems.

Contact Center as a Service is the hosted platform that routes calls and messages.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company that wants AI help with its work but does not want to build every piece from scratch. Google Cloud offers the Agent Platform, a managed environment where teams pick models, connect them to their own documents, and build AI helpers called agents. Three parts matter for this lesson. Model Garden is a catalog of ready-made models you can browse and choose from. Agent Search helps an AI answer questions using your organization's own documents, so answers are based on real sources. AutoML lets you train a custom model on your own labeled examples with little or no coding. Knowing which part fits which business need is the skill being tested.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retailer wants a chatbot that answers customer questions using only its own product manuals, and it has no AI specialists on staff. Before reading on, which of the three parts would you reach for first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A model is a trained program that takes an input such as text or an image and produces an output such as an answer or a label. Model Garden is a catalog inside the Agent Platform where you browse available models, including Google's own models, open models, and some third-party models, then choose one to try or deploy. Agent Search is a search product that lets a generative model answer from your organization's documents. This pattern is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, meaning the system first retrieves relevant passages from your documents and then hands them to the model together with the question, so the answer is grounded in your sources. AutoML, short for automated machine learning, trains a custom model on your own labeled examples, where a label is the correct answer you supplied for each example, such as this photo shows a damaged box.

Why it works: a general model knows broad language but not your private manuals. Retrieval supplies the missing facts at question time, so you do not have to retrain when the manuals change. Training is the right tool when you need a specific prediction that a general model cannot make well and you have enough labeled examples.

Worked example: a retailer wants a chatbot that answers questions from its product manuals. Step 1: the need is answers drawn from the company's own documents, so Agent Search fits. Step 2: the team picks a language model from Model Garden to write the reply. Step 3: no labeled training set is needed, so AutoML is not part of this answer.

Common mistake: reaching for AutoML because it sounds like the custom option. It trains prediction models and does not make a document collection searchable. Consequence: a model trained on last year's manuals keeps giving old answers until someone retrains it, while a retrieval setup picks up new documents once they are indexed.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain has 9,000 past customer emails, and staff have already tagged each one as 'delivery', 'allergen', or 'refund'. The chain wants each new incoming email sorted into one of those three tags automatically. Step 1: the output is one tag chosen from a fixed list, and the correct tags for past emails are already known, so AutoML fits this need. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the tagged emails are uploaded as the training set and a custom classifier is trained on them.
choices: Pick a language model from Model Garden to write a reply to each incoming email, since AutoML cannot produce text.
Skip the existing tags and let the model group emails by topic on its own, since AutoML needs no supplied answers.
Confirm that each of the 9,000 past emails carries a correct tag, because those tags are the answers the model learns from.
Index the 9,000 emails with Agent Search so the tagger can retrieve the closest past email before choosing a tag.
questions.why: AutoML learns from the labels supplied with each example, so verifying those labels is the step that must come before training, while the other choices either describe a different product or skip labels AutoML depends on.

questions.prompt: A startup wants to compare several candidate models, including open models and models from outside vendors, before choosing one to try. Which Agent Platform feature fits this need best?
choices: A custom retrieval index, because it stores the startup's documents so any model can read them.
AutoML, because it trains a new custom model from the startup's own labeled examples.
Model Garden, because it is a catalog where models can be browsed, compared, and selected to try or deploy.
Agent Search, because it lets a model answer questions from the startup's internal documents.
questions.why: Model Garden is the catalog for browsing and choosing among available models, including Google, open, and some third-party models, which matches the startup's comparison need.

questions.prompt: A law firm has 3,000 client contract PDFs. Lawyers want to type a question and receive an answer that is drawn from those contracts, with the answer updated automatically when new contracts are added, and without retraining any model. Which product best matches this?
choices: AutoML with a labeled set of past lawyer answers, so the model learns the firm's wording.
Model Garden alone, by choosing a large model and relying on its general knowledge of contracts.
AutoML, retrained each time a contract is added so the model stays current.
Agent Search, which retrieves relevant passages from the contracts and gives them to a model with the question.
questions.why: Agent Search uses retrieval-augmented generation, so new contracts become available once indexed and answers stay grounded in the firm's own documents without retraining.

questions.prompt: A company built an AutoML model to answer employee questions from its HR handbook. The handbook is revised every quarter, and the bot keeps giving answers from an old version. Which change most directly fixes the cause?
choices: Add more labeled examples and retrain the AutoML model, so it memorizes the newest handbook wording.
Use Agent Search over the current handbook, so the latest revision is retrieved at question time without retraining.
Keep the AutoML model but turn off answers for any question that mentions policy or benefits.
Switch to a larger model in Model Garden and keep the AutoML answers, since a bigger model knows more.
questions.why: The problem is stale source material, and retrieval over the current documents supplies the latest facts at question time, whereas AutoML would need retraining every time the handbook changes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to AI how you would choose between Model Garden, Agent Search and AutoML for a business need, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the business needs. If they want to pick a ready-made model to generate or summarize text, I would point to Model Garden, which is a catalog of models we can browse and deploy without building one ourselves. If they want answers grounded in their own documents, I would use Agent Search, which retrieves relevant passages and gives them to a model, so answers come from current sources. If they have a specific prediction and a set of examples labeled with the right answers, I would consider AutoML, which trains a custom model with little code. The tradeoff with Agent Search is that answer quality depends on how well the documents are organized and kept up to date. The tradeoff with AutoML is that it needs enough good labeled data, and without it the model will not be reliable.
rubricPoints: Model Garden is a catalog for selecting and deploying existing models.
Agent Search grounds answers in the organization's own documents through retrieval.
AutoML trains a custom model from labeled examples with little code.
Each option has a limit, such as document quality or the need for good labeled data.

suggested.rationale: Matching a business scenario to the right product is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers generative AI products.

lessons.plain: Imagine a capable new hire who has never read your company's policy binder. If you ask a question, they might guess. A better setup lets them look up the right pages first, then answer using only those pages. That pattern is called retrieval-augmented generation, often shortened to RAG. Google Cloud offers ready-made RAG through Agent Search, which handles the lookup and answering for you, and RAG APIs, which are building blocks for assembling your own version. For a business, the value is answers based on the company's own documents, with the sources visible, instead of answers drawn only from general training.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a chatbot that answers employee HR questions using only its HR policy documents. Before reading anything else, what do you think would go wrong if the chatbot answered from its general training alone, and what would you add to fix it?
lessons.teach:
RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation. It is a method in which, when a question arrives, the system first retrieves relevant passages from a collection of documents, then passes those passages to a generative model together with the question. The model writes its answer based on that supplied text. The collection of documents is often called a data store, and retrieval usually works by splitting files into smaller pieces called chunks, converting each chunk into a numerical representation called an embedding that captures its meaning, and finding the chunks whose meaning is closest to the question. Grounding means the answer is tied to source text that a person can check.

The reason this works is that the model does not need to have memorized your data. It only needs to read the few passages that matter for the current question, and it can point to them.

Google Cloud offers two shapes of this. Prebuilt RAG, such as Agent Search, is a managed service: you connect your data sources, and the service indexes, retrieves, and generates answers with sources, with little engineering work. RAG APIs are lower-level building blocks that your own application calls, so your team controls chunking, ranking, and answer format, at the cost of more engineering effort.

Worked example: a support team wants answers drawn from 2,000 product manuals. Step one, the manuals are connected to a managed index. Step two, an agent asks how to reset a router. Step three, the service retrieves the three passages most relevant to resetting. Step four, the model writes a short answer and links the manual page it used. Step five, the agent opens the link to confirm.

Common mistake: assuming RAG makes answers always correct. If the documents are outdated, or retrieval picks the wrong chunk, the model can still give a fluent, confident, wrong answer.

Consequence in a running system: if the index is stale, every answer is stale too, yet the output still looks trustworthy. Keeping the source documents current is part of the design, not an afterthought.

questions.prompt: A clinic connects 900 internal policy PDFs to a managed prebuilt RAG service such as Agent Search. Step one: the PDFs are connected to the index. Step two: a nurse asks how many consecutive hours a shift may run. Step three: [missing]. Step four: the model writes a short answer and cites the policy section it used. Step five: the nurse opens the cited section to confirm the number.
choices: The service splits the PDFs into chunks, converts each into an embedding, and retrieves the chunks whose meaning is closest to the shift-length question
The service ranks all 900 PDFs by file size and sends the largest one to the model
The nurse's question is deleted because the service only answers questions about product manuals
The model is retrained on the 900 PDFs so it knows the shift limit without looking anything up
questions.why: Before the model writes anything, the system must retrieve the passages closest in meaning to the question, which is done by chunking, embedding, and finding nearest matches.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does grounding mean for an answer produced by a RAG system?
choices: The model has permanently memorized the documents and no longer needs them
The answer is tied to source text that a person can check
The answer is shortened so it fits in a single sentence
The answer is translated into the language of the documents before it is shown
questions.why: Grounding means the answer is linked to source passages a person can inspect, which is what makes checking possible.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm with a two-person IT team wants staff to ask questions over 300 shipping contracts and get answers with links to the clauses used, quickly and with little custom engineering. Which offering best fits?
choices: Retrain a generative model on the 300 contracts so retrieval is unnecessary
Ask a generative model to answer from general knowledge and attach no sources
Build a custom application on RAG APIs so the team controls chunking, ranking, and answer format
Prebuilt managed RAG such as Agent Search
questions.why: A managed prebuilt RAG service indexes sources and returns sourced answers with little engineering, which suits a small team, while RAG APIs demand more engineering effort.

questions.prompt: A utility's RAG assistant was built from a tariff collection indexed 14 months ago. It now answers with fluent, confidently cited rates that were replaced last quarter. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The index is stale, so answers reflect outdated passages
Grounding guarantees correctness, so the citations prove the cited rates are still in force today
The embeddings were probably generated in a different language from the tariff documents
The model is too large and needs a smaller version to stop making up rates
questions.why: A RAG answer is only as current as its indexed sources, and fluent citations do not reveal that the source itself is out of date.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks why we would choose a prebuilt RAG service instead of building our own pipeline with RAG APIs. Explain the choice to a teammate in your own words, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of the prebuilt option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the prebuilt service when the goal is a working search-and-answer experience over our documents quickly, with little engineering effort. It handles connecting data, indexing, retrieving relevant passages, and generating answers with sources. The tradeoff is control. We get less say over how documents are split into chunks, how results are ranked, and how answers are formatted, so an unusual document layout or a very specific ranking rule might not fit. The RAG APIs give us those levers, but we would then own the pipeline, its tuning, and its upkeep. So I would choose prebuilt when speed and low maintenance matter most, and the building blocks when our content or workflow needs custom behavior.
rubricPoints: Defines RAG as retrieving relevant documents at question time and grounding the answer in them
Distinguishes the prebuilt managed service from lower-level RAG API building blocks
Names a concrete tradeoff such as less control over chunking or ranking versus more engineering effort
Notes that answers are only as current and correct as the source documents

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a prebuilt RAG service and building blocks in a business scenario is best practised by reasoning through the situation, which this lesson sets up with a guess prompt and an explanation task.

lessons.plain: Imagine an assistant that does more than write an answer. It reads your question, looks something up in your company's records, takes a step such as updating a booking, and then reports back. That is the idea behind an AI agent. Google Cloud's Agent Platform is where a business builds its own agents: it chooses a model, connects the agent to its own information and systems, and sets rules for what the agent may do. For a non-engineer, the key question is simple: does this task need the AI to look things up or act, not just talk?
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants an AI that answers 'where is my order?' by checking its own order system and then acting, such as moving a delivery date. Is a text-writing model on its own enough, or is something more needed? Explain your reasoning in a sentence or two.
lessons.teach:
An agent is an AI system that works toward a goal across several steps rather than producing one reply. A model is the generative AI engine that reads text and produces text. A tool is anything outside the model that the agent can call, such as a search over company documents, a lookup in an order database, or an action like sending a message. A custom agent is one a business designs for its own tasks, with its own instructions, tools and data. Agent Platform is Google Cloud's environment for building such agents. From a business view, its main functions are: choosing a model from a catalogue of options (Model Garden), giving the agent grounded access to company information through search (Agent Search), and training a specialised model on labelled examples when a general model is not accurate enough (AutoML).

Why it works: a model on its own knows only what it was trained on and cannot see today's order status. Tools fill that gap. The agent decides which tool to use, reads the result, and continues until the task is finished or it hands off to a person.

Worked example: a customer writes 'Where is my refund?' Step 1: the agent reads the message and finds the order number on the customer's account. Step 2: it calls the order-lookup tool. Step 3: it reads the refund status from the returns records. Step 4: it replies with the status and expected date. Step 5: the refund exceeds the policy limit, so the agent passes the case to a human with a short summary.

Common mistake: treating a custom agent as a chatbot with a longer prompt. Without tools and company data, the model answers from general knowledge and may confidently state a wrong refund date.

Consequence: an agent that can take actions can also take wrong ones, so its access should be limited to what the task needs, and high-impact steps should need a human check. The business value of a custom agent lies in automating multi-step work that depends on the company's own data, not in producing clever text.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain builds a custom agent to handle guests who want to move their stay. The agent may approve price differences up to 150 dollars on its own. Anything above that needs front-desk staff. Work through this example. Step 1: the agent reads the guest's message 'Can I move my Friday check-in to Saturday?' and finds the reservation. Step 2: it calls the room-availability tool and confirms a Saturday room of the same type is free, with a price difference of 210 dollars. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: it sends the guest a message saying the change is with the front desk. Which action belongs in the missing step 3?
choices: Confirms the Saturday change to the guest right away and asks staff to review the price later
Compares the 210 dollar difference with the 150 dollar limit and hands the case to front-desk staff with a short summary, rather than confirming it
Asks the underlying model to estimate the new price from general knowledge without calling any tool
Sends the guest the old price so the conversation can end before any change is made
questions.why: The agent must check the action against its approval limit using the tool results, and because 210 is above 150 it hands the case to a person with a summary, which is the handoff pattern the teaching text describes for high-impact steps.

questions.prompt: A parts supplier builds a custom agent that answers 'Is part 4471 in stock?' by querying its warehouse inventory system. In this design, which piece is the tool?
choices: The general product knowledge stored inside the underlying language model
The customer's chat message asking about the part
The warehouse inventory lookup that the agent can call from outside the model
The written instructions telling the agent to stay polite with customers
questions.why: A tool is anything outside the model that the agent can call, and the inventory lookup is an external system the agent queries, while the other options are instructions, model knowledge, or input.

questions.prompt: A clinic deploys a custom agent for appointment questions. It has instructions and a language model but no connection to the scheduling system. A patient asks whether a Tuesday 9am slot is free. What is the most likely failure?
choices: The agent answers from general knowledge and may confidently state a wrong availability
The agent forwards the question to the scheduling software vendor for an answer
The agent checks the schedule and correctly reports the slot is free
The agent refuses every question automatically because it has no tools
questions.why: Without tools and company data the model answers from general knowledge, which can produce a confident but wrong answer, as the teaching text warns about custom agents that are really just chatbots with prompts.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's custom agent can read shipment records and reschedule pickups. Which access design best follows the principle that an agent's access should be limited to what the task needs?
choices: Allow it to read shipment records and reschedule routine pickups, and require staff sign-off before changing high-value freight
Give the agent full administrator rights across every company system so it never has to stop mid-task
Remove all its tools so that it cannot take any wrong action
Connect it to every internal database so it can answer any future question without asking
questions.why: The teaching text says an agent that can act can also act wrongly, so access should match the task and high-impact steps should need a human check, which the second option does while the others grant excess access or remove the agent's purpose.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a custom agent built on Agent Platform is, when a business should build one instead of using a plain model, and one limit or tradeoff they should weigh.
lessons.modelAnswer: A custom agent is an AI system a business configures for its own multi-step task. It uses a model to reason, plus tools such as a search over company documents or a lookup in an order system, so it can answer with current facts and take steps like updating a record. Agent Platform is where we would pick the model, connect our data through search, and set the agent's instructions. We should build one when the work involves several lookups or actions, such as handling refund questions, rather than just drafting text. The main tradeoff is risk and effort: the agent can act wrongly, so we must limit its permissions, test it against real cases, and route high-impact decisions to a person. It also needs good data behind it, because a poorly connected agent will sound confident and still be wrong.
rubricPoints: Defines a custom agent as a model plus tools and business data working toward a task over several steps
Explains why tools and company data are needed, since a model alone cannot see current records
Names a suitable use case where the task requires lookups or actions, not only text generation
States a limit or tradeoff such as action risk, permission scope, data quality, or the need for human escalation

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a business scenario about when a custom agent fits adds more than reading, since the objective is recognising fit and value.

lessons.plain: An agent is an AI model that can do more than write text: it can look things up and take actions. To do that it uses tools, which are connections to things outside the model, such as a database, a document library, or another company's service. A tool lets the agent interact with the outside world instead of relying only on what it memorised during training. This objective is about recognising the main kinds of tools and knowing what each one is for, so you can match a business need to the right kind.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks a support chatbot 'where is my order right now?' The chatbot has no access to the warehouse system. What would the company need to give the chatbot so it can answer correctly, and who should control what it is allowed to look up?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a model that can decide to act. A tool is anything outside the model that the agent can call to read or change information, such as a booking system, a document collection, or a calculator. Four kinds come up in Google Cloud's agent material. An extension is a connector to an external service that the platform manages for you: the model chooses it and the platform makes the call. A function is a capability you define yourself by naming it, describing its purpose, and listing its inputs. The model replies with a request to run it, your own application runs it, and the result goes back into the conversation. A data store is a collection of your documents that the agent searches, so its answers rest on your facts rather than memory. A plugin is a general term for a packaged add-on that gives an agent one more tool. Focus on what it does, not its packaging.

Why it works: the model never touches the outside system directly. It produces a structured request, something outside the model executes it, and the result returns so the model can answer with it.

Worked example: a shipping assistant receives 'Where is order 4417?' Step 1: the model recognises it needs live order status. Step 2: it selects a function named get_order_status with order_id 4417. Step 3: your application calls the internal order system and receives 'in transit, arrives Tuesday'. Step 4: the model writes the reply using that result. If the question were 'What is our return policy?', searching a data store of policy documents would be the better tool.

Common mistake: assuming the model queries the database itself. In reality your code does, so an agent's answer is only as reliable as the tool result it received. A function that changes data needs permission checks in your code, because the model's wording cannot enforce them.

questions.prompt: A university HR assistant answers staff questions about leave rules. A staff member asks: 'What notice do I have to give for parental leave?' Worked through: Step 1: the model recognises that the answer depends on written policy, not general knowledge. Step 2: the model selects the data store named staff_handbook and issues the search 'parental leave notice period'. Step 3: [MISSING]. Step 4: the model writes its reply using the returned passages and cites the handbook section. Which sentence correctly fills the missing Step 3?
choices: The model calls a function named update_policy to confirm the notice period with the HR director.
The model reads the entire handbook from its training memory and checks the notice period from there.
The data store searches the indexed handbook documents and returns the passages that match the query.
Your application edits the handbook so that the notice period matches what the staff member expects.
questions.why: A data store is a searchable collection of your own documents, so the matching passages it returns are the facts the model's answer must rest on.

questions.prompt: A freight company wants its agent to fetch current shipping rates from a carrier's service. The platform already manages the connector, the model decides when to use it, and the platform makes the call. Which tool type fits this description?
choices: A function, because the company writes its own definition of the rate lookup.
A calculator, because the agent is working out a price from numbers.
An extension, because it is a connector to an external service that the platform manages and calls for you.
A data store, because the rates are kept in a set of documents the agent searches.
questions.why: An extension is a managed connector to an outside service where the platform makes the call, which matches the freight rate case.

questions.prompt: A subscription business gives its agent a function called cancel_subscription that takes a customer_id. The team adds an instruction telling the model to cancel only for verified customers, and assumes this stops unauthorised cancellations. What is the flaw?
choices: The model should be allowed to verify customers itself, since it reads the conversation.
The instruction is written as a wording rule, but the model's wording cannot enforce permissions; the check must be in the application code that runs the function.
Nothing is wrong, because data stores enforce cancellations automatically.
Functions cannot take a customer_id, so the instruction is never reached.
questions.why: The model only produces a request, and the application that executes a data-changing function must enforce the permission check, because model wording cannot do it.

questions.prompt: A bike rental company's agent is asked whether bike 12 is free this afternoon. It calls the inventory system, which returns no status because of a timeout. What should the agent's answer be based on?
choices: A statement that availability could not be confirmed, because the tool gave it no result to rely on.
A confident yes, because bikes are normally free in the afternoon.
Its guess from how often bike 12 was booked last week, since that pattern is usually reliable.
A repeat of whatever it said in an earlier conversation about bike 12.
questions.why: An agent's answer is only as reliable as the tool result it received, so with no result it should say it could not confirm availability rather than invent one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a function and a data store as ways an agent uses tools, and name one limit or tradeoff of letting an agent call a function that changes data.
lessons.modelAnswer: A data store is a set of documents the agent searches so its answers are grounded in company material, such as policies or manuals. It is good for questions about knowledge that changes slowly, but the agent only reads it; it cannot act. A function is an action you define, such as get_order_status or issue_refund. The model asks for it with specific inputs, your application runs it, and the result returns to the model. Functions are good for live data and for doing things. The main tradeoff of letting an agent call a function that changes data is risk: the model can request the wrong action or pass the wrong input, and it can be tricked by unusual user wording. So the application should validate inputs, check the user's permissions in its own code, limit the action's scope, and often ask a human to confirm before anything irreversible happens.
rubricPoints: A data store provides searchable reference documents for grounding answers, and the agent only reads it.
A function is a developer-defined action: the model requests it, the application executes it, and the result returns.
An extension is a connector to an external service that the platform manages.
A limit of function-based changes is that the model can request wrong or unsafe actions, so the application must validate and authorise them.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between tool types from a business scenario is an exam-style reasoning skill that benefits most from working through situations.

lessons.plain: An AI agent is a model-driven program that does more than answer questions. It takes actions, such as looking up an order or booking a slot. To act, it needs tools: defined ways to reach things outside itself, like a database, a web service, or a stack of documents. This objective is about recognising which kind of tool fits a business need and which Google Cloud product offers it. Some tools you write yourself. Others come pre-built, so you can connect an agent to a data source or service without writing the connector. Choosing well is a business decision as much as a technical one, because it shapes how much you build, how fast you ship, and how much control you keep over the data the agent touches.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks a support assistant 'Where is my order?' The answer lives in a live order database. Would you give the assistant a document search tool, or a way to call a function that queries the order system? Why?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a model that can decide to use tools. A tool is a capability outside the model, such as a database query, an API call, or a search over stored content. The model does not run the tool itself; it requests it, and the surrounding system carries it out and returns the result. A function is a tool your team defines: you describe its inputs and outputs, and the model asks for it to be run with specific values. An extension is a connection to an external service that the agent can call through a managed integration. A plugin is a packaged, reusable connector, often pre-built. A data store is an indexed collection of your documents or records that the agent can search so its answers are grounded in your content. Retrieval over a data store is read-only: it finds information but does not change anything.

Worked example. A retailer wants an assistant that answers order-status questions and product-manual questions. Step 1: the model reads 'Where is my order?' and recognises it needs live order data. Step 2: it requests a function the team wrote, which queries the order system with the order number. Step 3: the function returns the status, and the model phrases the answer. Step 4: for 'How do I reset this device?', the model searches a data store indexing the manual and answers from the retrieved passages. Two tool types, each matched to a need.

Common mistake: treating a data store as an action tool. A data store lets the agent read and retrieve. If the task is to cancel or change an order, you need a function or extension that performs a write, with its own permission checks.

Consequence: if the wrong tool is chosen, the agent either refuses the task or, worse, reports an action as done when nothing changed. Matching each task to a tool that can actually perform it is what keeps the agent's answers true.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain sets up an agent that handles two guest requests. Request A is 'Is a sea-view room free on 12 May?' Traced: the model recognises that live availability is needed and requests a function the team wrote, which queries the booking system for that date. The function returns the availability and the model phrases the answer. Request B is 'Cancel my booking 8841.' Traced: the model recognises that this changes a record and requests a function with the booking number and a cancel action. Step 3 for Request B is missing. Which step completes the trace?
choices: The model searches a data store of the hotel's policy documents and tells the guest the booking is cancelled.
The function carries out the cancellation under its own permission checks and returns a confirmation, and the model reports the booking as cancelled only after that confirmation comes back.
The model writes the cancellation directly into the document index so that the next search reflects it.
The model tells the guest the booking is cancelled as soon as it makes the function request, since the request was made.
questions.why: A cancellation changes a record, so it must be performed by a function with its own permission checks, and the model should report success only once the function confirms the change.

questions.prompt: Which tool type lets an agent search an indexed collection of a company's documents so its answers are grounded in that content, without changing anything?
choices: An extension that calls an external service through a managed integration
A data store, which is read-only retrieval over indexed content
A function the team writes, which takes inputs and performs a write
A plugin that is a packaged connector for an outside application
questions.why: A data store is an indexed collection the agent can search, and retrieval over it is read-only, so it finds information without changing anything.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's agent is asked to change the delivery address on shipment 55102. The team connects only a data store of shipping manuals. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The agent refuses the task and asks the user to wait, because data stores always block write requests.
The agent updates the address in the manuals, which then propagates to the shipment record automatically.
The agent may report the address as changed when nothing in the shipment system was updated, because a data store cannot perform a write.
The agent changes the address correctly, since searching a data store also edits the records it indexes.
questions.why: A data store is read-only, so the address change cannot happen, and an agent that reports it as done has given a false answer.

questions.prompt: A bank wants its agent to fetch the current exchange rate from an outside rate service, using a managed integration that the platform maintains rather than code the bank writes itself. Which tool type fits best?
choices: A function the bank's team defines with its own input and output description
An extension, which is a connection to an external service the agent calls through a managed integration
A packaged, reusable connector that the bank copies into its own code
A data store indexing the bank's historical rate reports
questions.why: An extension is defined as a connection to an external service called through a managed integration, which matches this need better than a team-written function or a data store.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an AI agent uses tools to reach outside data. Use one example where the agent must change a record, say which tool type you would choose and why, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: An agent is a model that decides when it needs something outside itself, and then asks a tool to get it. The model doesn't query the database directly. It requests a function or extension with specific inputs, the surrounding system runs it, and the result comes back for the model to use. For reading information, such as answering from product manuals, a data store is a good fit: it indexes content and retrieves matching passages, grounding the answer. But a data store only reads. If the task is to change a record, like cancelling an order, I'd use a function or an extension that performs the write, with its own permission checks. The tradeoff is that a custom function means we build and maintain the integration ourselves, while a pre-built connector is faster to adopt but gives us less control over exactly what it can do.
rubricPoints: An agent uses tools by requesting them; the surrounding system executes them and returns results
Data stores are for retrieving and grounding answers, not for performing actions
Functions and extensions can perform actions, and need permission controls
Pre-built connectors trade speed of adoption against control and customisation

suggested.rationale: Matching a business task to the right tool type is best practised by reasoning through a realistic scenario with reads and writes, which no current mission covers.

lessons.plain: Google offers more than one place to work with generative AI, and picking the right one depends on what you are building. Some tools are for trying a model out: you type a request, see what comes back, and tune it quickly. Others are for building a working assistant that does things, such as looking up records or changing an order, inside a company's systems and under its security rules. This lesson helps you tell these two situations apart, so you choose the place that matches the job rather than the one you happen to have open.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a quick tool that drafts product descriptions from a short brief, and a second team wants a chatbot that checks live stock levels and places orders. Which kind of Google Cloud tool would you guess suits each team, and what in each description made you choose that?
lessons.teach:
Google AI Studio is a web workspace for working directly with Google's Gemini models. You write a prompt, adjust settings such as how varied the answers should be, compare outputs, and can obtain a key to call the model from your own code. Its purpose is exploring and prototyping how a model behaves. Agent Studio belongs to Google Cloud's Agent Platform. It is for building an agent, meaning a system that does more than answer: it takes steps, such as reading a database or calling an external tool, and it runs inside enterprise controls for access, data handling, and monitoring. A useful test is what must happen after the model responds. If a person will review plain text, the prototyping workspace fits. If the system must act on business systems for someone, it needs the agent-building environment.

The reason this works is that the two tools sit at different layers. One gives you direct access to a model. The other gives you a governed place to connect a model to tools and data and run it for an organisation.

Worked example. Team one wants a tool that drafts marketing taglines. Step one: the job is text generation. Step two: no internal system is touched. Step three: a person reviews every output. Choice: Google AI Studio. Team two wants an assistant that reads order status from the warehouse database and opens a return request. Step one: the assistant must read and write business data. Step two: it needs defined tools and access rules. Step three: the company needs an audit trail. Choice: Agent Studio.

Common mistake: choosing the quick prototyping tool because it is faster, then trying to add live data access and permissions later in code that was never designed for governance. A prototype with an API key pasted into a script can be copied into production, leaking the key or letting the model act with no record of what it did.

The decision turns on whether the output stays as words for a person to use, or must act on business systems under company controls.

questions.prompt: A furniture retailer wants a tool that writes product descriptions. Step one: the job is text generation. Step two: no internal system is read or changed. Step three: ______. Choice: Google AI Studio. Which completion fits step three?
choices: A merchandiser reads each description before it goes live
The company needs an audit trail of every tool call the model makes
The model must query the warehouse database to check stock counts before writing
The model pushes each description straight into the live product catalogue
questions.why: A person reviewing plain text output is the test that points to the prototyping workspace, while the other three describe the model acting on business systems, which points to Agent Studio.

questions.prompt: In the teaching text's sense, what is the main difference in purpose between Google AI Studio and Agent Studio?
choices: Google AI Studio is for production use, while Agent Studio is for free experiments
Google AI Studio is for exploring how a model responds, while Agent Studio builds a governed system that takes steps across tools and data
The two tools are interchangeable and differ only in price
Agent Studio is for editing images, while Google AI Studio is for writing text
questions.why: The text says AI Studio gives direct access to a model for exploring and prototyping, while Agent Studio gives a governed place to connect a model to tools and data and run it for an organisation.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance claims team wants a model that reads a submitted claim form, looks up the policy status in their claims database, and marks the claim approved in that database, with a record of who approved each claim. Which tool fits?
choices: Google AI Studio, because an API key can be stored in a script
Either tool, because the choice only affects how fast the prototype runs
Google AI Studio, because prompts are quick to test there
Agent Studio, because the system must act on business records under access rules and keep an audit trail
questions.why: Acting on business systems for someone under company controls, including access rules and monitoring, is the situation the text assigns to Agent Studio.

questions.prompt: A team prototyped a support assistant in Google AI Studio and pasted the model access key directly into a script. They now want the assistant to update customer accounts. What is the main risk the teaching text warns about?
choices: Google AI Studio cannot produce text, so the assistant will fail to respond
Moving to production makes the prototype compliant automatically
The key may leak, and the model could act on accounts with no record of what it did
The model will answer more slowly than it did in the prototype
questions.why: The text's common mistake is carrying a quick prototype with a pasted key into production, which risks key leakage and unrecorded actions because governance was never designed in.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Google AI Studio and Agent Studio for a new project, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you would make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the system has to do after the model responds. If the output is text that a person reads, checks, and uses themselves, Google AI Studio is the right place to explore prompts and test how the model behaves. It is fast and simple for prototyping. The tradeoff is that it is not built to connect the model to live company data and tools with enterprise access rules and audit records. If the system must look things up in business systems and take actions on someone's behalf, I would choose Agent Studio on the Agent Platform, because it is designed for building agents with tools, data connections, and governance. The tradeoff there is more setup and more design work before the first test. So I would prototype quickly in AI Studio if I only need to learn what the model can do, but I would not move a system that acts on company data into production without the agent environment and its controls.
rubricPoints: Google AI Studio is for exploring and prototyping model behaviour with prompts.
Agent Studio is for building agents that use tools and data under enterprise controls.
The deciding question is whether the output stays as text or must act on business systems.
A named tradeoff, such as speed versus governance and setup effort.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between the two tools is best practised by reasoning through short exam-style scenarios where the deciding detail must be spotted.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large AI model trained on vast amounts of text, images or other data, and then used for many different tasks. Its limitations are the predictable ways it falls short. It only knows what its training data contained, that data was collected up to a cutoff date, it can reflect unfair patterns from the data, it can state invented facts with confidence, and it can fail on unusual inputs. Spotting which limitation is at play is the first step, because each one has a different cause. Think of a very well-read assistant who finished learning on a fixed date and has never seen your company's files.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks a chatbot, built on a model trained in 2023, about a tax rule that changed in 2025, and the bot answers confidently with the old rule. Which limitation is most likely at work, and why might the bot sound so sure of itself?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data, and each common limitation has a specific cause. Data dependency means the output is only as good and as complete as the data the model learned from; it cannot reliably answer about topics that were rare, missing, or absent from training. Knowledge cutoff means the model's built-in knowledge stops at the date its training data was collected, so it does not know later events unless new information is supplied. Bias is a systematic tilt in outputs that comes from skewed training data. Fairness asks whether that tilt treats different groups of people unequally. Hallucination is a fluent, confident answer that is not supported by fact, because the model generates likely-sounding text rather than checking a source. Edge cases are unusual or rare inputs, such as odd phrasing, unfamiliar formats, or ambiguous requests, where behaviour becomes unreliable.

Worked example: a support assistant is asked, in a regional dialect, for the warranty period of a product released last month. Step one: the product is absent from training data, so this is data dependency. Step two: the release came after the training date, so this is knowledge cutoff. Step three: the dialect is uncommon, so this is an edge case. Step four: if the model invents a number that appears in no source, that is a hallucination. One question can show four limitations at once.

Common mistake: treating one limitation as the whole story, or assuming a fluent answer is a verified one. Fluency is not evidence of accuracy.

Consequence: in a live customer system, a wrong warranty figure sent confidently creates refunds, complaints and legal exposure, which is why identifying the limitation matters before choosing any fix. Each limitation is a diagnosis, and the diagnosis comes before the remedy.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's driver chatbot is asked, in a rural dialect, whether a depot opened last quarter accepts refrigerated freight. Step one: the depot opened after the model's training data was collected, so the model has no record of it. This is a knowledge cutoff. Step two: the dialect is uncommon in the training data, so this is an edge case. Step three is the one left for you: the model replies with a confident yes and a capacity figure that appears in no source it was given. Step four: the driver dispatches a refrigerated load to a depot that cannot take it. Which limitation does step three name?
choices: Bias: the model favours refrigerated freight because its training data over-represents certain regions.
Fairness: the chatbot gives drivers in rural areas answers that are less accurate than those given to city drivers.
Hallucination: the model generated a fluent, confident figure that no source supports, rather than checking one.
Data dependency: the depot's freight rules were rare in training data, so the model had too little to learn from.
questions.why: A confident, fluent figure that no source backs is the defining mark of a hallucination, which is the step the question leaves to you.

questions.prompt: An insurer's claims assistant gives systematically lower approval estimates to applicants whose names suggest one ethnic group, even when income and claim history are identical. Which limitation does this most directly describe?
choices: Knowledge cutoff: the model's built-in knowledge stops before recent policy changes.
Fairness concern: a systematic tilt in outputs that treats one group of people unequally.
Edge case: the applicants' names are unusual inputs that the model handles unreliably.
Hallucination: the model invents approval figures that have no basis in any record.
questions.why: A systematic tilt that treats a group unequally is a fairness problem rooted in bias, while the other three options describe different limitations.

questions.prompt: A hotel-review summariser is asked about a food festival that was held last weekend. It confidently describes a festival held two years ago in the same town. Which diagnosis is most accurate, and what is the common mistake to avoid?
choices: Hallucination only: the answer is wrong, so this is simply invented text with no other cause.
Bias: the town's older festivals are over-represented in the training data, tilting the answer.
Knowledge cutoff: the festival post-dates training, so the model answers from older data it did hold.
Edge case: the question is short, which makes the model's reply unreliable.
questions.why: The event happened after the training data was collected, so the model can only answer from older knowledge, and treating it as just a hallucination misses the cause.

questions.prompt: A forms-processing model reads dates on paper forms. It misreads dates written in a day-first layout with a two-digit year, a layout that appeared rarely in its training examples. Which limitation best fits?
choices: Hallucination: the model invents a date that appears in no source document.
Fairness: the reader treats forms from one region less accurately than others.
Edge case: an unusual, rare input format where the model's behaviour becomes unreliable.
Knowledge cutoff: the model stopped learning before the forms were printed.
questions.why: A rarely seen input layout is an edge case, because the model's behaviour becomes unreliable on unusual inputs rather than on knowledge or fairness grounds.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell a knowledge cutoff problem apart from a hallucination when a model gives a wrong answer, and name one limit of that test.
lessons.modelAnswer: A knowledge cutoff problem is about time. The model lacks information created after its training data was collected, so the answer may have been correct when training ended. I would check when the fact changed. If it changed after the cutoff, the cause is most likely the cutoff. A hallucination is about invention. The model produces a confident claim that no source supports, and this can happen even with older facts, such as a made-up citation or a number that appears nowhere. A quick test is to ask whether the claim was ever true and whether it can be checked against a source. The limit of this test is that I may not know the cutoff date precisely, and a wrong answer about older facts could still come from either cause. So I would verify the claim against a source before deciding which limitation it is.
rubricPoints: Knowledge cutoff is about time: information created after the training data was collected is missing from the model.
A hallucination is a confident claim with no supporting source, and it can occur even for older facts.
A useful test checks when the fact changed and whether the claim can be verified against a source.
The test has a limit: the cutoff date may be uncertain, so verification is needed before concluding.

suggested.rationale: Identifying which limitation explains a failure is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no listed mission covers this directly.

lessons.plain: Large language models sometimes give answers that are out of date, made up, or missing your company's private facts. Several practices address this. Grounding means tying the model's answer to trusted source material you supply. Retrieval-augmented generation means first looking up relevant documents and handing them to the model along with the question. Prompt engineering means writing clearer instructions and examples in the request, without changing the model. Fine-tuning means further training the model on your own examples. Human in the loop means a person checks or approves outputs before they reach customers or drive decisions. Each practice fixes a different problem, so the real skill is matching the problem to the right fix.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot for a shipping company quotes last year's prices and invents a refund policy that does not exist. Which single practice would you try first to stop the invented policy, and why?
lessons.teach: A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data before anyone adapts it to a job. Its knowledge stops at a knowledge cutoff, and when it lacks an answer it may produce a hallucination, which is a fluent but false statement. Each practice targets a different cause. Grounding ties an answer to trusted sources you supply, such as your own documents. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is one way to ground: a search step fetches relevant passages, and those passages are added to the prompt before the model writes. Prompt engineering changes the instructions and examples in the request, with no change to the model. Fine-tuning runs extra training on your own labelled examples, which changes the model's behaviour and style. Human in the loop means a person reviews, approves or corrects outputs before they go further. Why it works: a model writes from patterns it has seen, so putting the right facts in front of it at answer time makes those facts the likely pattern to copy. Worked example: a shipping company's chatbot is asked whether a parcel that arrived three days late qualifies for a refund. Step 1, the system searches the current policy documents and finds the late-delivery refund section. Step 2, it adds that text to the prompt with the instruction to answer only from these passages, and to say so and offer a human agent if they do not cover the question. Step 3, the model writes the reply from that passage. Step 4, because refunds involve money, a human reviews the first replies during a new policy rollout. Common mistake: assuming fine-tuning teaches the model today's prices. Training fixes patterns at a point in time, so changing facts go stale again, and retraining every time is slow and costly. Retrieval suits facts that change. Consequence: without grounding, the bot quotes last year's prices and invents a policy, creating refund disputes that the support team then has to unwind. The right fix matches the problem: stale or private facts call for grounding or RAG, unclear output format calls for prompt engineering, a consistent specialised style calls for fine-tuning, and high-stakes decisions call for human review.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs an assistant that answers customers' questions about mortgage rates. Its rate sheet changes every week. Here is how one question is handled. Step 1: the system searches the current rate sheet and finds the 30-year fixed section. Step 2: it adds that text to the prompt with the instruction to answer only from it. Step 3: this step is left blank for you to fill. Step 4: a loan officer checks any reply that quotes a rate before the customer sees it. Which choice correctly fills step 3?
choices: The model answers from what it absorbed during training, and the retrieved passage is discarded.
The model writes the reply using the retrieved passage as its source of facts.
Step 4 is skipped, because adding the passage to the prompt already guarantees the rate is correct.
The bank retrains the model on the new rate sheet so the model remembers this week's rate.
questions.why: Step 3 is the generation step: the model writes the answer from the passage that retrieval placed in the prompt, which is what grounding means here.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants its model to return every answer as a fixed structure with the fields named order_id, status and eta, in that order, with no extra text. Which practice most directly addresses this need without changing the model itself?
choices: Fine-tuning the model on a year of past customer emails
Adding a human reviewer to read every answer after it is sent
Prompt engineering, by stating the required fields and format in the instructions and giving one example
Retrieval-augmented generation that searches the firm's shipping database
questions.why: Prompt engineering changes the instructions and examples in the request and needs no change to the model, so specifying the output format there addresses an unclear output format directly.

questions.prompt: A retailer fine-tuned a model on last quarter's product prices. Now the model quotes those old prices when customers ask about current ones. Which explanation and fix are correct?
choices: The model needs a larger context window, so the fix is to paste the whole catalogue into every request.
Fine-tuning failed to run, so the fix is to repeat the same training job until the prices update.
Fine-tuning fixes patterns at a point in time, so changing prices go stale; the fix is grounding or RAG that retrieves current prices at answer time.
Human review is missing, so the fix is to have staff approve each price before it is shown.
questions.why: Training captures facts as they were when training happened, so frequently changing facts need retrieval at answer time rather than more training.

questions.prompt: An insurance company uses a model to draft decisions on claims. Claims above 5,000 pounds could lead to a large payout or a denial that a customer may dispute. Which practice best fits the high stakes?
choices: Human in the loop, where a claims handler reviews and approves each draft above the threshold before it goes further.
Grounding the model in the policy wording, with no review step, since sources make it accurate.
Fine-tuning on the company's old claim letters so the style is consistent.
Prompt engineering that tells the model to be careful with large sums.
questions.why: When a decision has high stakes, a person should review, approve or correct the output before it takes effect, which is the human-in-the-loop practice.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would choose between grounding or RAG, prompt engineering, and fine-tuning for a chatbot that gives wrong answers. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would try first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what is actually wrong. If the bot gives wrong answers about facts that change, like prices or policies, I would ground it: retrieve the current policy text and have the model answer only from it, with a fallback to a human when the text does not cover the question. If the answers contain the right facts but have the wrong format or tone, I would try prompt engineering first, because it is cheap and needs no training. I would reach for fine-tuning only when the style or a specialised pattern stays wrong after good prompting, since it takes curated examples and effort to keep current. The tradeoff with retrieval is that answer quality now depends on search quality. If the wrong passage is retrieved, the model will confidently answer from the wrong text. So I would measure what the search returns and keep human review on refunds and other money decisions.
rubricPoints: Match the technique to the specific limitation: stale or private facts call for grounding or RAG, while format or tone problems call for prompt engineering.
Fine-tuning changes behaviour and style, and it is slower and costlier than retrieval to keep current when facts change.
Retrieval quality limits the answer, because a wrong retrieved passage produces a confident wrong answer.
Human in the loop is needed for high-stakes outputs whichever technique is used.

suggested.rationale: Choosing the right fix for a described limitation is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission or planned engine covers generative AI.

lessons.plain: Once a generative AI model is in use, the work does not stop. Its answers can get worse over time, the provider may release new versions, security fixes arrive, and the people using it change what they ask. Continuous monitoring and evaluation means regularly checking how the model behaves against goals the business has set, such as accuracy, speed, cost, and safety, and acting when the numbers slip. It is closer to a car's dashboard and scheduled service than to a single inspection on the day you buy it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team launched a generative AI assistant last year. It still responds quickly and never shows errors, but customers say its answers are getting less useful. What would you check first, and why would uptime dashboards miss the problem?
lessons.teach:
Monitoring means checking a live system on a schedule against targets chosen in advance. For a generative AI model, those targets are usually key performance indicators, or KPIs: measurable numbers that matter to the business, such as the share of answers a reviewer rates as correct, the rate at which users escalate to a human, response time, and cost per request. Evaluation is the matching test: running the model on a fixed set of representative inputs and scoring the outputs the same way each time, so results from different weeks can be compared.

Several terms matter here. A model version is a fixed snapshot of a model. Pinning means staying on one named version so its behavior does not change under you. An automatic upgrade means the provider moves your traffic to a newer version without your review. Drift is the slow gap that opens between the conditions the model was checked under and the conditions it now faces, such as new products, new customer questions, or changed source documents. Security patches fix vulnerabilities in the serving stack and must be applied and tested too.

Why it works: a model that was good at launch can become worse without any change to your code, because the world and the inputs move. Measuring the same KPIs on the same test set over time is the only reliable way to see that happen.

Worked example. A support assistant tracks a KPI of reviewer-rated helpful answers, with a target of 88 percent on a weekly sample of 200 real questions. Week one scores 92 percent. The provider then upgrades the model automatically. Week three scores 81 percent, below the threshold, so an alert fires. The team checks the version log and sees that traffic moved to the new version on Monday. They rerun the old and new versions on the same 200 questions and find the new one handles refund questions poorly. They pin the previous version, revise the prompts, and re-evaluate before moving forward.

Common mistake: watching only uptime and latency. Those stay green while answer quality decays, and a one-time evaluation at launch is not monitoring at all.

In a running system this matters because a silent quality drop reaches customers before anyone notices. A wrong refund answer may be given to thousands of people before the weekly sample catches it.

questions.prompt: A freight company runs a shipping-status chatbot. Its weekly KPI is the share of reviewer-rated correct answers from a sample of 150 real customer questions, with a target of 85 percent. Last week it scored 91 percent. On Tuesday the vendor automatically upgraded the model, and this week the score fell to 79 percent, so an alert fired. The team checked the version log and confirmed traffic moved to the new version on Tuesday. They then ran the old and new versions on the same fixed 150 questions and found the new one answers customs-hold questions poorly. They pinned the previous version and revised the prompts. Next step:
choices: They re-evaluated the revised setup on the same fixed 150-question set to confirm the score recovers to target before moving forward.
They deleted the weekly log so the upgrade history would not affect future audits.
They switched to a fresh, different set of questions so the new results would look better and skipped the side-by-side comparison.
They accepted the new version because its uptime and response time were still green on the dashboard.
questions.why: Re-running the revised setup on the same fixed test set is what lets the team compare the score fairly against the earlier results and confirm the fix worked.

questions.prompt: A retail bank's fraud-explanation assistant has been pinned to model version 4.2 for six months. What does pinning accomplish?
choices: It keeps the assistant on one named snapshot so its behavior does not change without the team's review.
It encrypts the model so that no one outside the bank can read its weights.
It removes the need for a regular test set because the model can never change.
It lets the provider move traffic to newer versions overnight so the bank gets fixes sooner.
questions.why: Pinning means staying on one named, fixed version so the model's behavior stays the same until the team deliberately chooses to move.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling bot's dashboard shows 99.9 percent uptime and 300 ms latency every week, but its answer quality was evaluated only once, at launch. Why is this not adequate monitoring?
choices: Uptime and latency are never measured in a live production system.
Dashboards are not an acceptable place to record monitoring results.
Uptime and latency can stay green while answer quality declines, and a single launch check cannot show changes over time.
A latency under 500 ms is too slow to count as a healthy target.
questions.why: Monitoring means tracking quality KPIs on a schedule against a fixed test set, because infrastructure metrics can look healthy while the answers get worse.

questions.prompt: A recruiting firm's résumé-summary model was accurate at launch. Two years later, incoming job postings use different skill terms, its accuracy has slipped, and no code has changed. Which term best names this situation?
choices: An automatic upgrade, where the provider moves traffic to a newer version without review.
Drift, the gap that opens between the conditions the model was checked under and the conditions it now faces.
Pinning, the practice of staying on one named model version.
A security patch, a fix for a vulnerability in the serving stack.
questions.why: Drift describes the widening gap between launch-time conditions and current inputs, which can reduce quality even when the code and model version are unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a generative AI model needs ongoing monitoring after launch, and name one real limit or tradeoff of letting the provider automatically upgrade the model version.
lessons.modelAnswer: A model that worked well at launch can get worse later without anyone touching our code. The inputs change as customers ask new kinds of questions, the source documents we rely on get updated, and the provider may release new versions. So we track a few KPIs, such as the share of answers reviewers rate as correct and how often users escalate to a person, and we run the same fixed test set on a schedule so the numbers are comparable week to week. Uptime and latency alone would hide quality problems. The tradeoff with automatic upgrades is that a newer version can be better on average yet worse on a specific task we depend on, like refund questions, and we may not know until the numbers drop. That is why I would prefer to pin a known version, test a new one side by side, and then move traffic deliberately.
rubricPoints: Ongoing monitoring is needed because quality can drift as inputs, sources, or model versions change
