Use KPIs measured on a fixed test set so results over time are comparable
Uptime and latency do not show answer quality
Automatic upgrades can improve averages while hurting a specific task, and may go unnoticed
Pinning a version and testing new versions side by side is a safer way to adopt upgrades

suggested.rationale: Setting thresholds and alerts on a quality metric is the hands-on skill behind catching drops in KPIs, which this planned engine would practice.

lessons.plain: A prompt is the text you send to an AI language model to ask it for something. Prompt engineering means deliberately writing and adjusting that text, including the instructions, examples, and background it contains, so the model gives answers that are more useful and predictable. It is a bit like briefing a new colleague: the clearer the brief, the closer the result. It does not change the model itself, and it matters because the same model can produce very different output depending on how it is asked.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you asked the same AI model two different ways to summarise a customer complaint, what would you expect to change in the answers, and what would stay the same?
lessons.teach:
A large language model (LLM) is a model trained on very large amounts of text to predict and generate text. A prompt is the input you give it: the instructions, any examples, the role you assign, and any source material that arrive before it writes. Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and refining that input so the model's output is more useful, accurate, and consistent for a given task. It changes what you send, not the model's internal weights, so nothing is retrained.

Why it works: an LLM continues whatever pattern the input sets up. It does not know what you intended unless the prompt says so. Stating the role, the task, the output format, the constraints, and a sample or two narrows the range of plausible continuations toward the one you want.

Worked example: a support team wants a summary of a customer email. Step 1, the vague prompt 'Summarise this email.' leaves the model to guess length, tone, and audience. Step 2, the output is a long paragraph that mixes the complaint with the request. Step 3, the improved prompt 'You are a support analyst. In three bullet points, list the customer's problem, the requested action, and the urgency. Email: ...' gives a role, a fixed structure, and a clear scope, so the output is short and comparable across emails.

Common mistake: treating prompt engineering as a one-off trick that guarantees correct answers. A better prompt lowers error rates, but it does not remove hallucinations (confident but false statements) or knowledge that is out of date. Those need other techniques, such as grounding the model in trusted data.

Consequence in a running system: the prompt effectively becomes part of the application's behaviour. A small wording change can alter the output format and break any downstream code that reads it, so prompts should be versioned and tested the way code is.

Prompt engineering is therefore a practical, low-cost lever for shaping LLM behaviour, and its value is capped by what the model already knows.

questions.prompt: A recruiting firm wants an LLM to score job applications. Step 1: the prompt 'Rate this CV.' returns ratings on different scales, sometimes a number, sometimes a paragraph. Step 2: the team adds a role ('You are a recruiter screening for junior data analysts') and a fixed output format (a JSON object with the keys score_1_to_5 and reason). Step 3: the team adds two sample CVs with the ratings a human reviewer gave them. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the process the way the teaching text recommends?
choices: Switch to a larger model, since a bigger model needs fewer prompt details.
Retrain the model on the firm's past CVs so its weights learn the scoring rule.
Version the prompt, then run it against a test set of CVs with known ratings and check the outputs for consistency before release.
Raise the model's randomness setting so the ratings vary more and look less mechanical.
questions.why: The teaching text says prompts should be versioned and tested like code, and a test set with known answers is how you check that a prompt change keeps outputs consistent.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines prompt engineering?
choices: Training a new language model on a company's private documents so it learns the company's vocabulary.
Connecting a model to a live database so it can answer questions about current stock levels.
Designing and refining the input sent to an LLM so its output is more useful and consistent, without changing the model's internal weights.
Measuring how many tokens a model can process in a single request before it truncates the reply.
questions.why: Prompt engineering is defined as shaping the input (instructions, examples, role, source material) to improve output, and it leaves the model's weights untouched.

questions.prompt: A retail team's assistant gives confidently wrong answers about this quarter's shipping fees, which changed last week. The team rewrites the prompt with a clearer role and format, but the answers stay wrong. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The model needs more randomness in its settings so it will guess the new fees more creatively.
The prompt cannot supply knowledge the model does not have, so the team needs a technique that brings in trusted, current data.
The model's format rules are conflicting, so the team should remove the role from the prompt entirely.
The prompt has not yet been made specific enough, so the team should keep adding instructions until the fees appear.
questions.why: Prompt engineering lowers error rates but is capped by what the model already knows, so out-of-date or missing facts call for grounding in trusted data.

questions.prompt: A developer's application reads the model's reply and expects exactly three bullet points. The developer edits the prompt from 'Return three bullet points' to 'Give a short summary,' and the application starts failing. What explains this?
choices: The model ran out of training data, so it stopped following instructions in the prompt.
The model's weights were changed by the edit, so its outputs no longer match the old version.
The application's network connection dropped during the longer reply.
The output format changed, and the prompt effectively became part of the application's behaviour, so the downstream code broke.
questions.why: A small wording change alters the output format, and any code that parses that format can break, which is why prompts should be versioned and tested.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what prompt engineering is and why it matters when using a large language model, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Prompt engineering is designing the input we send a large language model: the instructions, the role, the output format, any examples, and any background material. The model's behaviour is shaped by that text, because it continues the pattern the input sets up, so careful wording can make answers more relevant, consistently structured, and easier to check. It matters because changing a prompt is fast and cheap compared with retraining a model. The main limit is that it cannot add knowledge the model lacks or guarantee facts. A well-written prompt can still produce a confident wrong answer, and a prompt that works today may behave differently after the model is updated. So for accuracy about recent or company-specific information, we pair prompting with techniques such as grounding, and we test prompts the way we test code.
rubricPoints: Defines a prompt as the input text, including instructions, examples and context.
Explains prompt engineering as designing and refining that input without retraining the model.
Says why it matters: output quality, format and consistency depend heavily on the prompt.
Names a limit: prompting cannot supply missing knowledge or guarantee factual accuracy.
Notes that prompts can change behaviour after model updates, so they should be tested and versioned.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the idea and its limits to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission practises prompt design.

lessons.plain: Prompting techniques are different ways of writing the instructions you give a generative AI model so it produces a better answer, without changing the model itself. Some techniques give the model no examples at all, some show it one or several examples of the task, some tell it to take on a persona such as a careful editor, and some split a big job into a sequence of smaller prompts where each step feeds the next. Choosing the right one is a practical, low-cost decision: you match the technique to how hard the task is and how consistent the output needs to be.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team wants a model to label each customer email as billing, technical or other. Before reading anything, would you put a few labelled example emails in the prompt, or just describe the labels and ask? Why?
lessons.teach:
Zero-shot prompting means asking the model to do a task with no examples, relying on what it already learned in training. One-shot prompting includes exactly one worked example in the prompt. Few-shot prompting includes several examples, usually a handful. Role prompting tells the model to act as a particular persona, such as a billing specialist, which shapes its vocabulary, focus and assumptions. Prompt chaining splits a task into a sequence of prompts, where the output of one prompt becomes the input to the next.

These work because a language model predicts likely continuations of text. An example shows the exact format and label set, which narrows the guesses. A role shifts the register and focus. A chain keeps each step simple, so each intermediate result can be checked.

Worked example. Start zero-shot: 'Label this email billing, technical or other: My card was charged twice.' The answer is billing, which is fine. Now try an ambiguous email: 'The app logs me out and my invoice is wrong.' The model may pick either label arbitrarily. Switch to few-shot by adding three labelled emails in the same format, one of them an ambiguous case labelled with a stated rule. The output now uses only the three labels and follows the pattern. For a harder task, chain two prompts: the first extracts the main complaint, the second labels that complaint.

Common mistake: assuming more examples always help. Examples that are wrong, or that are mostly from one label, push the model toward that label.

Consequence in a running system: every example is sent again with each request, so few-shot increases token count, cost and latency per call. Each chained step is another model call, and an error in an early step carries into every later step.

A prompting technique is a design choice that trades effort and cost against consistency, and you pick it by looking at the task.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm, FreightLine, wants each shipment message sorted as carrier, customer or weather. Their engineer chains two prompts. Prompt A reads the message and writes the main delay cause in one sentence. Prompt B takes that sentence and returns one label. The team runs 50 sample messages through both prompts, but nobody checks Prompt A's sentences before Prompt B runs on them. The plan is missing one step. Which one?
choices: Adding three more labelled examples to Prompt B so it becomes few-shot
Merging both prompts into one so the system makes only one model call
Checking Prompt A's sentences for accuracy before they feed Prompt B, because an early error carries into every later label
Giving Prompt B the role of a freight dispatcher
questions.why: A chain keeps each step simple so that each intermediate result can be checked, and an error in an early step carries into every later step, so the missing step is checking Prompt A's output before it reaches Prompt B.

questions.prompt: A bakery's sales team pastes one sample product tagline into the prompt and asks the model to write a new tagline in the same style. Which prompting technique is this?
choices: Prompt chaining
Zero-shot prompting
One-shot prompting
Few-shot prompting
questions.why: One-shot prompting includes exactly one example in the prompt, and this prompt includes exactly one sample tagline.

questions.prompt: A county library wants its question-answering assistant to reply about overdue fees in the voice of a patient, careful librarian, and it adds that instruction to the prompt without any examples. Which technique is the library using to shape the replies?
choices: Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Role prompting
Prompt chaining
questions.why: Role prompting tells the model to act as a particular persona, which shapes its vocabulary, focus and assumptions, and the library's instruction names a persona rather than providing examples.

questions.prompt: A team adds twelve labelled examples to its classification prompt, but all twelve are labelled 'billing'. Accuracy on the other labels then drops. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Role prompting overrode the label set
The examples are mostly from one label, which pulls the model toward that label
Each example adds a chained step that fails on its own
Few-shot prompts only work with an odd number of examples
questions.why: The teaching text notes that examples mostly from one label push the model toward that label, so the skewed example set is the likely cause of the drop.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose few-shot prompting over zero-shot, and name one limit or tradeoff of few-shot prompting.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with zero-shot for simple, well-understood tasks, because the prompt is short and cheap. I move to few-shot when the output format or label scheme is specific to our product, or when the model keeps getting edge cases wrong, since a few examples show it exactly what we mean. The tradeoff is that every example is sent again with each request, so it adds tokens, cost and latency to every call. Examples also bias the output: if most of them come from one category, the model tends to over-pick that category. So I choose a small, varied, correct set and test it against a sample of real inputs before relying on it.
rubricPoints: Zero-shot gives the model no examples and relies on its general knowledge.
Few-shot adds several examples that show the format and labels, which helps with consistency.
Role prompting sets a persona that shapes tone and focus, and prompt chaining splits a task into steps whose outputs feed the next prompt.
A named limit of few-shot, such as extra tokens, cost and latency, or bias from unrepresentative examples.
A sensible selection rule: match the technique to task difficulty and how consistent the output must be.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario asking which technique fits a given task adds the most here, since no listed mission or planned engine covers prompting.

lessons.plain: Some questions are too hard to answer in one jump, so a prompt can ask a language model to slow down and work in visible stages. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write out its working steps before giving a final answer, which tends to help with arithmetic, logic and multi-step questions. ReAct prompting goes a step further: the model alternates between deciding what it still needs and taking an action, such as looking something up with a tool, then reading the result before choosing its next move. Both are prompt-level techniques, so they change how the model is asked to work, not what facts it knows.
lessons.guessPrompt: A language model gets a multi-step word problem wrong when asked only for the final number. What single change to the prompt might help, and why would asking for the intermediate steps help?
lessons.teach:
Chain-of-thought prompting means asking a model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer. The chain is the sequence of linked steps, each building on the last. It helps because a language model produces its answer one token (a small piece of text) at a time, so writing steps gives it a longer path where each small step is easier to get right than a single leap. Worked example: you have 5 crates of 12 bottles and use 14 bottles. Step 1: 5 times 12 is 60. Step 2: 60 minus 14 is 46. Final answer: 46. The common mistake is to assume visible steps make the facts true. Chain-of-thought improves reasoning over facts already in the prompt or the model's memory; it does not supply missing or recent facts, so the model can still write confident, wrong steps.

ReAct prompting, short for reason and act, interleaves three kinds of text: a thought about what is needed, an action such as calling a search or lookup tool, and an observation, which is the tool's result fed back into the conversation. The loop repeats until the model can give a final answer. Use it when the answer depends on information the model lacks or that changes over time, such as an order's current status. Each action is a real call, so it adds latency and cost, and if the tool can change data, a wrong action can change a live system. Pick chain-of-thought for pure reasoning over known facts, and ReAct when the problem needs outside data.

questions.prompt: A call centre has 4 teams of 6 agents. 3 agents are on leave today. Each available agent can handle 20 calls. A chain-of-thought answer to how many calls can be handled today goes like this. Step 1: 4 times 6 is 24 agents on the roster. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: 21 times 20 is 420 calls. Final answer: 420.
choices: 21 plus 20 is 41 agents needed
Step 2 can be skipped because the call total is already known
24 divided by 3 is 8 agents on leave
24 minus 3 is 21 agents available today
questions.why: Step 2 subtracts the 3 agents on leave from the 24 on the roster, leaving the 21 who actually take calls, which is the number Step 3 multiplies.

questions.prompt: A retailer asks a model to work out a 15 percent discount on a 240 dollar jacket, and both the price and the rate are written in the prompt. Which technique fits best?
choices: ReAct prompting, because the model must call a tool to do any arithmetic
Fine-tuning, because the model needs new training to handle percentages
Chain-of-thought prompting, because every fact needed is already in the prompt
Grounding against a live price feed, because the price may have changed
questions.why: Chain-of-thought suits pure reasoning over facts already supplied, and this problem needs no outside or changing data.

questions.prompt: A model reasons step by step about whether a parcel is out for delivery and writes clear, logical steps, but the parcel's status changed this morning and its answer is wrong. What is the best explanation?
choices: Chain-of-thought does not supply recent or missing facts, so clear steps can still rest on stale information
Visible steps prove the facts are true, so the courier must be wrong about the status
The steps were too short, so the model needed many more of them
The model should have been fine-tuned on this morning's status before answering
questions.why: Chain-of-thought improves reasoning over facts the model already has, but it cannot add recent facts, so confident steps can still be wrong.

questions.prompt: A travel app's assistant must check live seat availability and then book a seat for a customer using ReAct prompting. Which risk matters most to plan for?
choices: Observations from the seat lookup must be stored as fine-tuning data
The model cannot use observations, so it will always book the first seat it sees
The booking step is a real call that changes live data, so a wrong action can alter the actual reservation system
The thought text may be too long for the customer to read comfortably
questions.why: In ReAct each action is a real call, so a wrong booking action can change a live system, and each call also adds latency and cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose chain-of-thought prompting over ReAct prompting, and name one limit of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use chain-of-thought when the question is a multi-step reasoning problem and all the facts are already in the prompt, such as working out a total from given prices and quantities. Asking the model to show its steps makes the arithmetic or logic easier to check. The limit is that it cannot add facts it does not have, so it can still reason confidently from a wrong assumption. I would use ReAct when the answer depends on live or private data, such as an order's current status. The model thinks, calls a lookup tool, reads the result and continues. Its limit is cost and risk: every action adds latency and a tool call, and if the tool can write to a system, a mistaken action has real effects, so such tools should be read-only or gated by a person.
rubricPoints: Chain-of-thought asks for intermediate steps and suits multi-step reasoning over facts already in the prompt.
ReAct alternates thought, action and observation, which suits questions needing outside or current data.
Chain-of-thought cannot supply missing or recent facts and can still be confidently wrong.
ReAct adds latency, cost and risk, because tool calls can change live systems.

suggested.rationale: Matching a short exam-style scenario to the right technique adds the most, since the skill is choosing between the two approaches.

lessons.plain: Grounding means tying a language model's answers to real, checkable information you supply or can look up, instead of letting it answer only from what it absorbed during training. A model can sound confident while being wrong, a bit like a student answering from memory in an exam with no notes. Grounding gives it the notes. The useful question is where those notes come from: the company's own records, a partner's data, or the broad public world. Each source changes what the answer can be trusted for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer asks an AI support bot 'What is my current account balance?' The bot has no access to your billing system. Why would it be a bad idea to let the bot answer from memory, and what would it need in order to answer correctly?
lessons.teach:
Grounding is the practice of giving a language model specific, verifiable source material and having it base its answer on that material. A large language model is a system that produces text from a prompt, and it learns patterns from training data that stops at a fixed point in time. It cannot see your private records. When it lacks an answer, it may still produce a fluent guess, which is called a hallucination.

Why it works: when the source text is placed in the request, the model's job shifts from recalling facts to reading and summarising them, which it does far more reliably. Grounding does not make the model perfect, but it gives the answer something concrete to be checked against.

The three source types differ in who owns them and how they are controlled. First-party enterprise data is your organisation's own material, such as product manuals, order records or policy documents. You control it, and it is often sensitive. Third-party data comes from an outside provider you have a relationship with, such as a supplier's price feed; you depend on its accuracy and licence terms. World data is broad public information, such as general web content. It is wide and current, but it has not been vetted for your situation.

Worked example: a warehouse assistant is asked, 'What is the return window for item 4471?' Step one: the system looks up item 4471 in the company's own product policy store, which is first-party data. Step two: it retrieves the returns clause. Step three: the model writes an answer that quotes that clause. If the store has no entry, the correct behaviour is to say so rather than guess.

Common mistake: assuming that grounding on public web results makes an answer about your own business correct. In a running system, a bot grounded only on world data may quote a competitor's return policy to your customer, which is wrong and can create real liability. The right source depends on whose facts the question concerns, so match each source to the owner of the truth.

questions.prompt: A regional water utility runs an assistant that answers customers asking when planned maintenance will affect their street. The utility's own maintenance calendar lists each street with its dates. Worked example: Step one, the system searches the utility's maintenance calendar for the customer's street, which is first-party data. Step two, it retrieves the matching calendar entry. Step three is missing. Step four, the answer is sent to the customer. For a customer on Hollow Lane, the calendar entry reads Tuesday 14 March, 08:00 to 12:00. What belongs in the missing step three?
choices: The assistant asks a national weather service for likely outage times and uses that figure instead of the calendar.
The model writes an answer that quotes the calendar entry, and if no entry exists it says so rather than guessing.
The model writes an answer from its training memory of typical maintenance patterns in cities like this one.
The assistant averages the start times of past outages on Hollow Lane and presents that average as the schedule.
questions.why: Grounding means the model's answer is written from the retrieved source text, so step three is where it quotes the calendar entry and admits when no entry exists.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does grounding a language model mean?
choices: Retraining the model's internal weights on a company's private records so it memorises them.
Lowering the model's randomness setting so that each answer comes out identical every time.
Limiting the model to short, one-sentence replies so that it cannot wander off topic.
Giving the model specific, checkable source material and having it base its answer on that material.
questions.why: Grounding places verifiable source text in the request so the answer can be checked against it; the other options describe fine-tuning, a sampling setting, and a length limit.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's assistant answers customer questions using a freight rate feed from a carrier the company has a contract with. Which source type does this feed represent?
choices: World data, because the rate feed is published openly on the internet.
Hallucinated data, because the model generated the rates from its training patterns.
First-party data, because the company uses the feed every day in its own operations.
Third-party data, because an outside provider supplies it and you depend on its accuracy and licence terms.
questions.why: Third-party data comes from an outside provider you have a relationship with, so the company depends on that provider's accuracy and terms, which matches the feed described.

questions.prompt: A retailer's support bot is grounded only on general web search results. It tells a customer the store has a 30-day return window, but the store's actual window is 14 days. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The bot was not grounded on the retailer's own policy, so it quoted public web terms that are not this store's terms.
The bot's randomness setting was too low, so it repeated stale wording from an old page.
The model's answer was cut off by a length limit, so the number was misreported.
The bot correctly used the store's policy, but the customer misread the clause.
questions.why: World data is broad and public but not vetted for this business, so a bot grounded only on it can quote terms belonging to other sellers rather than the store's own first-party policy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why grounding a support bot on the company's own policy documents is different from grounding it on public web search results. Name one limit or tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Grounding on our own policy documents means the bot answers from the source that actually governs our customers, so its answers about returns and warranties match what we will honour. The limit is coverage and freshness: the bot only knows what we have loaded, so if a policy document is missing or out of date, it can be wrong or silent, and the documents may contain sensitive data we must protect. Grounding on public web results is broad and current, so it can answer general questions, but it reflects other companies' rules and unvetted sources. Its tradeoff is that it can sound authoritative about our business while describing the wrong policy. For a question about our own terms, the web is the wrong source, and I would route it to the company's own documents instead.
rubricPoints: Grounding supplies verifiable source material so the model answers from it rather than from memory.
First-party data is the organisation's own and governs its answers, but its coverage and freshness are limited by what was loaded.
Public world data is broad and current but unvetted for the organisation's specific facts, so it can mislead on company-specific questions.
The source should match the owner of the truth for the question being asked.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why the source of grounding data changes what an answer can be trusted for, which is best practised by saying it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: Retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, is a way to have an AI writing tool answer from a set of documents you choose, instead of only from what it absorbed during training. Before the model writes a reply, a separate search step finds the passages most relevant to the question and hands them to the model along with the question. The model then writes its answer using those passages. The effect is that answers can reflect current or private information the model never saw during training, and the answer can point back to its source. RAG does not permanently teach the model anything new.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's chatbot is asked about a return policy that was changed last month, and the model was trained a year ago. Without any other change, what would you expect it to do, and what extra step might help?
lessons.teach:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a pattern in which a generative model answers using text fetched at question time. A retrieval step, a search over a collection of documents such as manuals, policies or product records, selects the passages most likely to be relevant. Those passages are placed into the prompt next to the user's question, and the model generates its answer from that combined input. The model's weights do not change. Only the material it sees for this one request changes.

It works because a language model's built-in knowledge is frozen at its training cutoff and is blended from many sources, so it can be out of date or vague on specific facts. Supplying the relevant text in the prompt lets the model work from the source rather than from memory, which tends to reduce invented details and makes it possible to show where each claim came from.

Worked example: a user asks, 'What is the refund window for online orders?' Step 1, the search step scores the policy library and returns the paragraph titled 'Online returns', which says 30 days. Step 2, the system builds a prompt containing that paragraph and the question. Step 3, the model writes 'Online orders can be refunded within 30 days,' and the system can cite the paragraph.

Common mistake: assuming RAG guarantees a correct answer. If retrieval returns the wrong paragraph, or nothing relevant, the model can still answer confidently from it or fill the gap with invention.

In a running system, RAG adds a search call to every request, so it adds latency and cost, and the document index must be refreshed when policies change or the answers go stale.

questions.prompt: A university IT help desk uses a RAG assistant for student questions. A student asks, 'How long does a lost student ID replacement take?' Step 1: the search step scores the help desk documents and returns the passage titled 'Lost ID cards', which says replacements are issued within 5 working days at the Registrar counter. Step 2: [MISSING STEP]. Step 3: the model writes 'Lost student IDs are replaced within 5 working days at the Registrar counter' and the system cites the passage. Which choice correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: The system deletes the 'Lost ID cards' passage from the index so the model cannot be misled later.
The system sends the question to the model first with no passage, and only searches if the model says it is unsure.
The system asks the model to retrain on the ID card policy so its weights change before it answers.
The system places the retrieved passage and the student's question together into the prompt that the model will read.
questions.why: In RAG the retrieved text is placed into the prompt alongside the question, which is the step that lets the model answer from the source rather than from memory.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm adds RAG to its internal chatbot so it can answer questions about shipping rules. Which statement best describes what RAG changes?
choices: It updates the model's weights each night with the newest shipping rules.
It supplies relevant rule passages inside the prompt for each request, while the model's weights stay the same.
It swaps the language model for a plain keyword search that produces no generated text.
It changes only the randomness setting of the model's output.
questions.why: RAG works by adding retrieved text to the prompt for one request; the model's weights are not changed by the retrieval step.

questions.prompt: A legal-services company uses RAG to answer questions about contract notice periods. For one question, the search step returns a clause from an unrelated lease agreement, and the model answers confidently with a notice period from that lease. What is the best explanation?
choices: RAG guarantees a correct answer, so the lease must actually apply to the question.
The model ignored the question entirely because the notice period setting was too high.
Retrieval passed wrong material into the prompt, and a model given wrong or no relevant text can still answer confidently from it or invent details.
The model's weights were corrupted during the last retrieval, so it reads the lease as a contract.
questions.why: RAG does not guarantee correctness; if retrieval returns the wrong or no relevant passage, the model can still produce a confident but wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A regional grocery chain runs a RAG assistant that answers questions about store opening hours from a document index. The chain changes its holiday hours, but the index is not refreshed for six weeks, and customers receive the old hours. What is the most direct cause and consequence?
choices: The model's weights drifted during the six weeks, so the assistant must be retrained before it can answer.
The retrieval step is working correctly, so the old hours are being invented by the model from memory.
The search call added latency to each request, which is why customers received the wrong hours.
The index holds outdated text, so the answers go stale until the index is refreshed with the new hours.
questions.why: RAG answers are only as current as the indexed documents, so an index that is not refreshed when policies change will keep returning stale information.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never heard of RAG what it changes about a model's answers, and name one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: RAG changes the source of the answer for each request. Before the model writes, a search step pulls the passages from our own documents that look most relevant to the question, and those passages go into the prompt with the question. So the model answers from current text we chose, not only from what it learned in training, which helps with recent policy changes and company-specific facts, and it lets us cite the source. The model's weights don't change, so nothing is permanently learned. The main limit is that the answer is only as good as retrieval: if the search returns the wrong or no relevant passage, the model can still give a wrong answer with confidence. There is also added latency and cost for the search, and the document index has to be kept up to date.
rubricPoints: States that RAG retrieves relevant documents at question time and adds them to the prompt
Explains that this lets answers reflect current or private information beyond the training data
Notes that model weights are not changed and nothing is permanently learned
Names a limit: poor or missing retrieval can still produce wrong answers, plus added latency and index maintenance

suggested.rationale: Explaining the search-then-generate flow and its limits back to a teammate is the core skill, and no current mission practises it.

lessons.plain: Grounding means tying a language model's answer to real source material, either documents you choose or current information, so it answers from evidence rather than only from what it absorbed during training. Google Cloud offers several ready-made ways to do this. Some find and answer from your own company documents, some give you building blocks to wire retrieval into your own application, and one lets the model use fresh public web search results. Knowing which option fits which situation is the goal of this lesson.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support bot answers customers using only what the model learned during training, and it confidently quotes last year's return policy. Before any teaching, which fix would you expect to help most: connecting the bot to the current policy documents, or rewording the bot's instructions? Say why in one sentence.
lessons.teach: Grounding means supplying a language model with trusted source material at answer time, so its reply is anchored to that material instead of only to patterns it absorbed in training. Retrieval-augmented generation, usually shortened to RAG, is the most common way to do this. The system first retrieves relevant passages from a store of documents, typically a search index built from your files, and then places those passages into the prompt so the model writes its answer from them. Google Cloud offers three grounding routes that matter for this objective. First, Vertex AI Agent Search is a prebuilt RAG option inside the Vertex AI Agent Builder family. You point it at your documents, and it handles ingestion, indexing and retrieval for you, returning answers with citations. Second, the RAG APIs, offered through the Vertex AI RAG Engine, are building blocks. You call them from your own application and keep control over how documents are split into chunks, retrieved and passed to the model. Third, Grounding with Google Search lets a Gemini model use live public web results as sources. That suits current events and general public facts, not private company data. Worked example: a staff member asks about a travel policy updated last week. Agent Search indexes the policy folder, retrieves the new section, and the model answers while citing it. The common mistake is choosing Google Search grounding because it is easy. It cannot read your internal policy, so the answer will be generic or wrong. The consequence in a running system is that if the index is not refreshed after the policy changes, the assistant confidently cites the old version, so refresh schedules are part of the design. Grounding reduces unsupported answers but does not eliminate them.

questions.prompt: A regional clinic group wants a chatbot that answers nurses' questions from its drug formulary, a document listing which medicines the group stocks and covers. The formulary is revised every month. The team uploads the current PDF files to Vertex AI Agent Search, which splits them into passages, builds a search index (a stored, searchable copy of the content), and returns answers with citations. Step three, which the team skips, is what keeps answers correct after each monthly revision.
choices: Switch to Grounding with Google Search so the model reads the latest public drug information online
Lower the model's randomness setting so that the answers stop changing between questions
Fine-tune the model on the formulary so it memorises the drug list permanently
Re-index the formulary after each monthly revision so retrieval finds the new version rather than the old one
questions.why: Agent Search only retrieves from the index it has built, so the index must be refreshed after each revision or the assistant will keep citing the superseded formulary.

questions.prompt: A logistics company wants its assistant to answer questions about a port strike that was reported in public news outlets this morning. Which Google Cloud grounding route fits this need best, and why?
choices: Fine-tuning the model on last month's news, because training updates the model's knowledge in real time
RAG APIs, because they let the company's developers choose how news articles are chunked
Vertex AI Agent Search, because it indexes the company's own files and cites them
Grounding with Google Search, because it lets a Gemini model use live public web results as sources
questions.why: Grounding with Google Search is the route built for current public events, using live web results rather than private company files or a stored index.

questions.prompt: An insurer is building its own claims application. Its developers want to decide how each claim document is split into chunks, which chunks get retrieved, and how they are passed to the model. Which Google Cloud offering matches this design?
choices: Vertex AI Agent Search, which hides ingestion and retrieval behind a prebuilt service
The RAG APIs through the Vertex AI RAG Engine, which are building blocks the application calls directly
Grounding with Google Search, which controls retrieval through live web queries
A prompt that tells the model to be careful about claim details
questions.why: The RAG APIs are building blocks called from your own application, so the developers keep control of chunking, retrieval and how passages reach the model.

questions.prompt: A university library builds an assistant with Agent Search over its licensed journal archive. The index was built in March. In June the library replaced several archived articles with corrected versions, and the index was not rebuilt. What is the most likely result?
choices: The assistant cannot answer any question, because a stale index causes the whole system to fail
Grounding guarantees the answers are correct, so the June changes have no effect
The assistant may confidently cite the superseded articles, because retrieval still returns the old passages
The assistant automatically detects the replaced articles and updates its index overnight
questions.why: Retrieval only returns what the index holds, so without a refresh the model answers from and cites the outdated versions, and grounding reduces but does not eliminate such errors.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to add a company-policy assistant and says Google Search grounding will cover it. In your own words, explain which Google Cloud grounding offering you would choose instead for private documents, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not use Google Search grounding here, because it searches the public web and cannot read our internal policy documents. For private files I would use Vertex AI Agent Search, which is the prebuilt option: we point it at the policy folder, it builds the index and retrieves matching passages, and the model answers with citations back to the source. The tradeoff is less control, since we accept its default chunking and retrieval behaviour rather than tuning every step. If we needed custom retrieval logic, I would consider the RAG APIs instead, which give more control but mean we build and maintain more of the pipeline ourselves. Either way, the index has to be refreshed when policies change, or the assistant will keep quoting stale rules.
rubricPoints: Matches Google Search grounding to public web or current information, not private company documents
Identifies Agent Search as the prebuilt RAG option for your own documents
Notes that the RAG APIs trade extra control for more build and maintenance work
States a limit such as the index going stale or the reduced control of a prebuilt option

suggested.rationale: This objective is a product catalogue of which offering fits which situation, so reading the distinctions and then explaining them is the most efficient route, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When you ask a generative AI model for an answer, it does not look up one fixed reply. It builds the answer one small piece at a time, and several settings decide how it picks those pieces and how long it keeps going. Some settings make answers more predictable, some make them more varied, some cap how long they can get, and some decide which kinds of content get filtered out. Knowing what each setting does lets you explain why the same question can get a dry answer one day and a rambling one the next, and helps you pick the right setting for a business need instead of treating the model as a black box.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you asked a text-writing model the same question five times and got five slightly different answers, which single setting would you most suspect controls how much those answers vary, and why?
lessons.teach:
Text models write output one token at a time. A token is a small chunk of text, often a word or part of one, and at each step the model estimates which token should come next. Sampling parameters are settings that control how that estimate becomes a real choice and how much text gets produced.

Temperature controls randomness. Low values make the model almost always pick the most likely next token, so answers are steadier. Higher values let it pick less likely tokens, so answers vary more.

Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, limits the candidate pool. The model ranks possible next tokens by probability, keeps the smallest group whose probabilities sum to the top-p value, and chooses only from that group.

Token count and output length set limits. A maximum output setting is a hard cap that stops generation even mid-sentence. The input prompt also uses the model's fixed context window, so a long prompt leaves less room for the reply.

Safety settings are thresholds for filtering output by harm category. Stricter thresholds block more content; looser ones block less. They change what gets through, not how well the model reasons.

Example: a support team wants short, steady refund replies. They set temperature low, top-p moderate, and a 120-token output cap. A reply that would have run 400 tokens is cut off at 120, so the team either raises the cap or asks for brevity in the prompt.

Common mistake: treating these settings as accuracy controls. Lower temperature makes the model repeat its most likely answer, which can still be wrong. Sampling settings shape how an answer is picked, not which facts the model knows; grounding addresses that.

In a live product, a cap that is too low ships truncated answers that look broken, and an overly strict safety threshold can block legitimate content.

questions.prompt: A claims-intake team at an insurance firm uses a text model with a fixed context window of 8,000 tokens. Their policy excerpt in the prompt is 6,500 tokens, and they want a summary of up to 2,000 tokens. Step 1: confirm the window is fixed at 8,000 tokens. Step 2: measure the input, which is 6,500 tokens. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: set the output cap no higher than the room found in step 3. Which choice completes step 3?
choices: Multiply the input by a top-p value of 0.9 to estimate how many tokens the reply will need.
Add the 2,000-token target to the input, giving 8,500 tokens, which shows the window is large enough.
Raise the temperature so the model writes a shorter summary that fits.
Subtract the input from the window: 8,000 minus 6,500 leaves 1,500 tokens for the reply.
questions.why: The prompt and the reply share the same fixed context window, so the room left for the reply is the window size minus the input length, which is 1,500 tokens here.

questions.prompt: A bank's marketing team describes temperature as the setting that decides how many tokens a reply may contain. Which statement correctly corrects this?
choices: Temperature sets the list of harm categories that the safety filter checks.
Temperature sets a hard cap on output length, so it stops generation mid-sentence.
Temperature decides which facts the model knows, so higher values make answers more accurate.
Temperature controls randomness: low values make the model usually pick its most likely next token, and higher values allow less likely tokens to be picked.
questions.why: The teaching text defines temperature as the randomness control, and output length is set by a separate maximum output setting, not by temperature.

questions.prompt: A bank's marketing team sets temperature to its lowest value to brainstorm slogans, then gets nearly the same slogan on every run. What is the most likely explanation and fix?
choices: The safety threshold is too strict, so the model keeps returning one blocked slogan; loosen the threshold.
The output cap is too low, so each slogan is cut off and looks identical; raise the cap.
The top-p value is too high, so the model has too many tokens to choose from; lower it to zero.
Low temperature makes the model favour its most likely next token, which reduces variety; raise the temperature to get more varied slogans.
questions.why: Low temperature narrows the choice toward the most likely token, so repeated outputs are expected, and raising temperature widens the variety of picks.

questions.prompt: A hospital's internal assistant gives a wrong medication dose even with temperature set to 0.1 and top-p set to 0.5. Which diagnosis best matches the teaching text?
choices: The sampling settings shape how an answer is picked, not which facts the model knows, so the fix is to supply the verified source the answer must come from, which is grounding.
The safety setting is blocking the correct dose, so the thresholds should be made stricter.
The output cap is cutting the dose off, so the cap should be removed entirely.
The sampling settings are too conservative, so the model should be given a higher temperature to find the right dose.
questions.why: The teaching text states that sampling parameters do not change the facts a model knows, and that grounding is the technique that addresses missing or wrong knowledge.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what temperature, top-p, the output length cap, and safety settings each control, and name one limit or tradeoff of adjusting them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Think of the model writing one piece at a time, choosing from a ranked list of likely next tokens. Temperature sets how adventurous that choice is: low means it nearly always takes the top option, so output is steady but can feel repetitive; high means more variety and more chance of an odd or wrong pick. Top-p narrows the list first by keeping only the smallest set of top candidates whose probabilities add up to the chosen value. The output length setting is a hard stop, so a low value truncates answers mid-sentence, and the input prompt uses the same context window, so a long prompt leaves less room for the reply. Safety settings filter what gets through by harm category, and tightening them can block legitimate content. The limit to remember is that none of these add knowledge or fix hallucinations. If an answer must match company policy, we need grounding, not a different temperature.
rubricPoints: Temperature controls how random or varied token choice is, with low values giving steadier output.
Top-p limits the candidate tokens to the smallest group whose probabilities reach the chosen value.
The output length cap is a hard stop that can truncate answers, and input tokens share the context window.
Safety settings filter output by harm category and do not improve accuracy; tradeoffs include blocking legitimate content.

suggested.rationale: These are parameter definitions and console-level settings best learned by reading and then reasoning about them, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model sampling.

lessons.plain: Generative AI is software that creates new content, such as sentences, pictures, or program code, by learning patterns from a large body of examples. Businesses use it for different jobs, and those jobs fall into a few families: producing written text, producing images, producing code, and tailoring output to a particular person. Recognizing which family a business problem belongs to is the first step in deciding whether generative AI fits it at all. Think of it like a skilled assistant who has read a huge library: good at drafting and remixing, but not automatically aware of your private facts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer support team wants a tool that reads a customer's complaint and drafts a polite reply for an agent to review. Before reading anything else, which family of generative AI does this fall into, and what is one reason a human should still review the draft?
lessons.teach:
Generative AI means models that produce new output, such as text, images, or code, in response to a prompt, which is the instruction or input a user gives the model. Most of these tools are built on foundation models, which are large models trained on very broad data and then adapted to many tasks.

Text generation produces written language, such as summaries, drafts, or rewrites. Image generation produces pictures from a written description or edits an existing one. Code generation produces program source code, or explains and fixes code that already exists. Personalized user needs means shaping output to one person or context, such as a reply that uses a customer's past orders. Personalization is a purpose that usually sits on top of one of the other three types.

Why it works: the model has learned statistical patterns from many examples, so it predicts a plausible text, picture, or program from the prompt. It does not check facts unless the system supplies them.

Worked example: a retailer wants a product description for a new jacket. Step 1: the output is a paragraph, so this is text generation. Step 2: the copy should reflect the buyer's region and past purchases, so personalization sits on top. Step 3: a waterproof rating is a factual claim, so a person must verify it before publishing. The fit is text generation with personalization and a human check.

Common mistake: choosing a type because it sounds impressive, such as image generation for a legal label that must be exact, instead of asking whether the output must be precise.

Consequence: generated code can look correct and still contain bugs or security flaws, so it must pass the same tests and review as human-written code. The output type therefore tells you which checks matter most.

questions.prompt: A parcel company wants a tool that writes a delay notice for each customer. Each notice must use the customer's first name and the delivery window promised in that customer's account. Steps 1 and 3 are given below, and you supply Step 2. Step 1: the output is a message paragraph, so this is text generation. Step 2: (you fill this in, stating which type or layer applies because of the customer's name and window). Step 3: the revised delivery date is a factual claim, so a staff member must verify it before the notice is sent. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Personalization sits on top of text generation, because each notice is shaped to one customer's name and promised window
No personalization is needed, because one identical template sent to everyone is always the most accurate
Code generation, because the tool pulls the data from the account database
Image generation, because the notice could include a map of the route
questions.why: Personalization is a purpose layered on a base output type, and here the notice is shaped to one customer's name and window while the base output remains a text paragraph.

questions.prompt: A small software firm has a tool that reads a broken function in the firm's own codebase, explains what the bug is, and proposes a corrected version. Which output type does this tool fit?
choices: Image generation, since the explanation is shown as a diagram
Text generation with personalization only, since it targets one developer
Personalized user needs as a standalone type, separate from the other three
Code generation, since it explains and fixes code that already exists
questions.why: The teaching text lists code generation as covering both producing new source code and explaining or fixing code that already exists, which is exactly this case.

questions.prompt: A clinic team says the code its AI tool generated looks tidy and passed a quick glance, so they plan to skip their usual tests and peer review. What is the main risk of this plan?
choices: Generated code is exempt from review because a model rather than a person wrote it
Generated code can look correct and still contain bugs or security flaws, so it must pass the same tests and review as human-written code
Generated code is always rejected by the compiler, so no tests are needed
Tests only matter for image output, not for program source code
questions.why: The teaching text warns that generated code can look correct while hiding bugs or security flaws, so it must go through the same tests and review as human-written code.

questions.prompt: A credit union wants one web banner picture made from a short text description, and a disclosure paragraph that states an exact interest rate. Which pairing best fits the teaching?
choices: Text generation for the banner, and code generation for the interest rate
Image generation for both pieces, since both are visual layouts of numbers
Image generation for the banner, and a person verifies the exact interest rate because it is a factual claim
Personalization for both pieces, since the rate should match each reader
questions.why: The banner is a picture produced from a description, so image generation fits, while the exact rate is a factual claim that the teaching says a person must verify before publishing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the four types of generative AI solutions (text, image, code, and personalized user needs), and name one limit or tradeoff that applies to at least one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Generative AI solutions fall into four families based on what they produce. Text generation writes drafts, summaries, and rewrites. Image generation creates or edits pictures from a description. Code generation writes or explains program code. Personalized user needs is a purpose rather than a format: it adapts output to one person's context, like a recommendation or a reply using their history. The main limit is that these models predict plausible output rather than verify facts, so a draft can sound confident and still be wrong. For example, a generated product claim or a line of code needs a human check before it reaches customers. Personalization adds a tradeoff too, because using customer data raises privacy questions that must be handled before the feature ships. So the type tells you what to produce, and the limit tells you what to check.
rubricPoints: Names the four types and says what each produces
Explains that personalization is a purpose layered on another output type
States a limit such as plausible-but-unverified output
Connects the limit or tradeoff to a concrete check or review step

suggested.rationale: This objective is a set of categories and definitions that the teaching text covers fully, and no listed mission or planned engine practices generative AI solution types.

lessons.plain: Before a company builds anything with generative AI, it has to know what the system must achieve and what it is allowed to do. Business requirements are the outcomes people need: which problem is being solved, for whom, how much value it should bring, how fast, and how much risk is acceptable. Technical constraints are the limits of the environment the system must work within: how fast answers must arrive, how much data exists and how clean it is, which existing systems it must connect to, and what privacy or location rules apply. Good planning starts with both lists, because the same idea can be sensible for one organization and impractical for another.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank wants a gen AI tool that answers customer questions in a live chat window. Name two things you would need to know before deciding whether the idea is workable, and say why each one matters.
lessons.teach:
A business requirement is a statement of what the organization needs from a solution, written as an outcome. It names the users, the measurable improvement (for example, cutting average reply drafting time by a set share), and what a failure would cost. A technical constraint is a limit that the design has to respect, imposed by data, infrastructure, security, or time. Common constraints include latency, which is the delay between a request and its answer; throughput, which is how many requests the system must handle at peak; data availability and quality; integration with existing systems; data residency, meaning where data is legally or contractually allowed to be stored; and cost per request.

Requirements decide which kind of solution fits and how much accuracy matters. Constraints decide what is feasible. A requirement checked against no constraints produces a plan that cannot be built, and a constraint considered with no requirement produces a capable system that nobody needs.

Worked example. A regional airline wants an assistant that drafts replies to customer emails. Step one, the requirement: drafting time should drop by 40 percent, and a human must approve every reply, because a wrong refund promise is expensive. Step two, the constraints: emails contain personal data, so it must stay in an approved cloud region; the team has 3,000 past replies of uneven quality; and drafts must land in the existing ticketing tool. Step three, the conclusion: the approval step comes from the requirement, and the data cleaning and privacy work come from the constraints.

Common mistake: starting from the technology ('we need a chatbot') and treating constraints as details to fix later. Consequence: a live chat assistant whose answers take twenty seconds to arrive will be abandoned by customers even when the answers are good, because the latency constraint was never tested against the requirement.

Requirements say what success looks like, and constraints say what is possible. A plan is sound only when both are written down and checked against each other.

questions.prompt: A property management firm wants a tool that drafts summaries of maintenance requests for landlords. Requirement: summary time should fall by 30 percent, and a staff member must review each summary before it is sent, because a wrong summary of a legal notice can start a dispute. Constraints: tenant records must stay in the firm's home-country region; the firm has 800 past summaries of mixed quality; summaries must be written into its existing property software; and a landlord's dashboard loads each summary on demand, so each one must return within about three seconds. Steps one and two are done. Step three: the team should conclude that ______.
choices: the review step comes from the constraints and the regional storage limit comes from the requirement, so the two are reversed

the review step comes from the requirement, and the regional storage, data-quality and response-time limits come from the constraints, so each must be checked against the 30 percent target before building
the three-second limit can be ignored, because a staff member reviews every summary before it goes out
the 800 past summaries can be used as they are, since uneven quality does not affect a requirement about drafting time
questions.why: The requirement determines the approval step and the constraints determine what is feasible, and the plan is sound only when both are checked against each other.

questions.prompt: A card company's fraud-alert tool must answer each transaction within 200 milliseconds and must handle 5,000 transactions per second at peak. Which term names the 200-millisecond limit?
choices: cost per request
latency, the delay between a request and its answer
throughput, how many requests must be handled at peak
data residency, where data is allowed to be stored
questions.why: Latency is the delay between a request and its answer, so a 200-millisecond limit on each response is a latency constraint.

questions.prompt: A retailer's product-description generator writes accurate text, but the team never checked the cost per request against the 400,000 descriptions it must produce each month. The budget is exceeded in the first week. Which statement best explains the failure?
choices: The team wrote a requirement but never checked cost per request against the volume it must serve, so the plan was never tested against its constraints
Customers rejected the product because of its writing style
The model's accuracy was too low to be useful
The team should have chosen a larger model regardless of cost
questions.why: A plan is sound only when requirements and constraints are both written down and checked against each other, and the cost constraint was never tested against the volume the requirement demanded.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm states: 'Dispatchers should spend 25 percent less time on rerouting, and a missed reroute costs a full day's delivery.' Which category does this statement belong to?
choices: business requirement, because it names the users, a measurable improvement and the cost of failure
both, because it mentions a cost
neither, because it describes a process rather than a need
technical constraint, because it names a data limit
questions.why: A business requirement is written as an outcome that names the users, a measurable improvement and what failure would cost, and this statement does all three.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a gen AI idea is ready to build. Name the business requirements and technical constraints you would check first, and describe one tradeoff where a requirement and a constraint pull in opposite directions.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing the business requirement as a measurable outcome: who uses the tool, what should improve, by how much, and what a wrong answer would cost. Then I would check the technical constraints that decide feasibility: how quickly answers must arrive, whether there is enough clean data to ground the answers, which systems it must connect to, and whether personal data has to stay in a particular region. The main tradeoff is usually quality against speed and cost. A larger model may give better answers, but it can be slower and more expensive per request. If the requirement is an instant reply in a live chat, I would accept a smaller model or a narrower scope and state that choice explicitly. The idea is not ready until the requirements and constraints have been checked against each other.
rubricPoints: Defines business requirements as measurable outcomes tied to users and risk
Defines technical constraints such as latency, data quality, integration, and data residency
Explains that requirements decide what fits and constraints decide what is feasible
Gives a concrete tradeoff, such as quality against speed or cost, and how it would be resolved

suggested.rationale: Explaining requirements against constraints back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers gen AI business planning.

lessons.plain: Choosing the right generative AI solution means matching a real business problem to the kind of AI tool that fits it, instead of adopting AI because it is fashionable. Generative AI is software that produces new content such as text, images or code by predicting likely output from patterns it learned in training data. A company might want faster customer replies, a summary of long documents, or product descriptions. Each need points toward a different approach: a ready-made model used as is, a model guided with clear instructions and trusted company documents, or a model adapted with extra training. The skill is asking what the problem actually requires before choosing the tool.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small clinic wants a tool that drafts friendly appointment reminder messages. Another company wants a tool that answers staff questions accurately using its own 500-page policy manual. Do you think both need the same kind of AI solution? Which one would you expect to need company data, and why?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can handle many tasks without being built for one of them. Prompting means writing clear instructions and examples in the request. Grounding means supplying trusted documents at the moment of the question so answers draw on them. Fine-tuning means running extra training on example data so the model's behavior changes. Hallucination means the model produces output that sounds confident but is false.

Worked example: an insurance team wants short summaries of adjuster notes. Step one: summarizing text is general language work, so a foundation model is a candidate. Step two: the facts are already inside each note, so the notes can be passed in with the request; grounding or prompting is enough and no custom training is needed. Step three: summaries feed decisions, so a person reviews them before use. Step four: the notes contain personal data, so the team checks how the provider handles that data before going ahead.

Common mistake: starting from the technology ('we need a chatbot') instead of the outcome and how success will be measured. Teams also jump to fine-tuning when grounding would solve the problem more cheaply.

Consequence: a custom model costs more to build and maintain, and must be retrained when policies change, while a grounded solution can be updated by changing the documents.

questions.prompt: A freight company with 40 dispatchers wants a tool that answers questions about its routing rules. The rules are kept in a 200-page manual that the operations office revises every quarter. The team works through four steps. Step one: answering questions from a written manual is language work, so a foundation model (a large general-purpose model that can handle many tasks without being built for one) is a candidate. Step two: the manual is trusted text that changes often, so the current manual is supplied with each question (grounding, meaning trusted documents are provided at the moment of the question) instead of running custom training. Step three: [left blank for you to complete]. Step four: dispatchers act on the answers, so a supervisor spot-checks a sample each week before the team relies on the tool. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Set the measure of success first, such as how many dispatcher questions still go up to a supervisor, and record that figure before launch so the change can be compared afterward.
Skip the weekly spot-checks in step four because the manual is trusted text and the answers will be correct.
Choose the model with the largest number of parameters before anything else, since bigger models rarely produce false answers.
Fine-tune the model on last year's dispatcher chat logs so it learns the routing rules directly, which is cheaper than grounding.
questions.why: The teaching text says teams should start from the outcome and how success will be measured, and the other choices either jump to custom training (which the text says is costlier when grounding would solve the problem) or remove the human review the text requires.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants an assistant that answers customer questions about its return policy, which the legal team rewrites every few weeks. Which approach best fits this need?
choices: Build the chatbot first and decide later how to tell whether customers were helped by it.
Write one prompt that states the policy from memory and leave it unchanged for the life of the product.
Supply the current policy text with each customer question (grounding), so a policy update only means changing the document.
Fine-tune a model on two years of past customer emails so the policy is memorized inside the model, then retrain whenever the rules change.
questions.why: Grounding supplies trusted, current documents at the moment of the question, so the answers follow the latest policy without retraining, which matches the teaching text's point that grounded solutions update by changing documents.

questions.prompt: A bank fine-tuned a model on 5,000 internal policy documents. Six months later the policies were rewritten. What is the most accurate consequence?
choices: The model must be retrained on the rewritten policies to change its behavior, which adds build and maintenance cost.
The bank only needs to edit a header in the training file and redeploy the model the same day.
The model stops producing hallucinations, because it was trained on verified policy text and will not drift from it.
Nothing changes, because fine-tuned behavior is stored in the documents and updates on its own.
questions.why: The teaching text says a custom model costs more to build and maintain and must be retrained when policies change, so the rewritten policies require new training rather than a simple edit.

questions.prompt: A startup says 'we need a chatbot' and begins building before naming any business outcome. What is the main risk?
choices: Chatbots always cost more than search tools, so the budget will run out before launch.
The team cannot tell what success looks like, and may jump to custom training when grounding would do.
The team must publish its model weights publicly before launch.
Foundation models cannot be used for any chat interface at all.
questions.why: The teaching text names starting from the technology instead of the outcome and how success will be measured as the common mistake, and notes that teams often jump to fine-tuning when grounding would solve the problem more cheaply.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between using a ready-made generative AI model with grounding and building a customized model for a business problem. Name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the business outcome and what counts as success, then ask whether the task is general, such as drafting or summarizing, or depends on our own knowledge. If a ready-made model can do the task with our documents supplied at question time, that is usually cheaper and faster to launch, and we can update it by changing the documents. I only consider customizing the model when grounding does not reach the required quality or style, because that means more data preparation, training cost, and ongoing retraining. The main tradeoff of the simpler route is that output quality depends on the documents we provide and the model can still hallucinate, so we keep a human review step for high-stakes answers. Data sensitivity and cost also shape the decision before we commit.
rubricPoints: Starts from the business outcome and success measure, not the technology
Distinguishes general tasks from tasks needing company-specific knowledge
Explains that grounding or prompting is usually cheaper than customization
Names a real limit, such as hallucination or ongoing retraining cost
Mentions data sensitivity or human review as part of the decision

suggested.rationale: Choosing a solution is a judgment task best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style business scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: Putting generative AI into a company is a sequence of decisions, not a single purchase. Generative AI means software that produces new text, images or code from a prompt. Integrating it means taking that capability from an idea to a working tool people rely on: deciding what problem it solves, checking the information it needs, testing it on a small scope, protecting the data and customers involved, and then watching how it performs over time. Think of a kitchen adding a new dish: it plans the menu, tests the recipe, trains staff, and keeps checking quality before the dish reaches every table.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retail company wants a chatbot that answers customer questions about their orders. Before anyone builds anything, what do you think should happen first, and why would building the chatbot straight away be risky?
lessons.teach:
The steps to integrate generative AI into an organization form a repeatable path from a business problem to a monitored production system. A business problem is the specific pain point or goal, such as slow replies to customers. Readiness means checking whether the data, people and rules needed are in place. A pilot is a small, time-limited trial with real users and clear success measures. Governance is the set of owners, policies and review steps that decide who is accountable for what the system outputs. Pseudonymizing data means replacing names and identifiers with stand-in codes. In broad order, the steps are: define the problem and how success will be measured; check data readiness, including quality, bias and privacy; choose an approach, such as an off-the-shelf model or one given trusted company documents at question time; run a pilot; add security and responsible-AI controls; then deploy, monitor and improve.

The order matters because each step reduces a costly risk before the next, bigger spend. If you cannot say what success looks like, you cannot tell whether a pilot worked.

Worked example: a support team wants draft replies to customer emails. Step one: the goal is to cut average first-reply time from two days to four hours, tracked weekly. Step two: past emails are checked, and because some contain personal data, names are pseudonymized before use. Step three: the team chooses a model and supplies its help-center articles as trusted context. Step four: five agents use it for two weeks on one product line. Step five: a named manager approves every reply before it reaches a customer. Step six: after launch, the team tracks accuracy complaints and reply times, and updates its instructions when quality drifts.

Common mistake: starting with the model and searching for a use for it afterwards. The result is a demo nobody needs, with no measure to judge it.

Consequence in a running system: without governance, wrong answers reach customers with no owner to fix them, which damages trust and can create legal exposure.

Integration is a loop, not a straight line, because monitoring results feed back into how the problem is defined.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union wants gen AI to draft replies to member questions about loan terms. Step one: the goal is to cut the average reply time from 24 hours to 2 hours, tracked weekly. Step two: 18 months of member chat logs are checked, and account numbers are pseudonymized before use. Step three: the team picks an off-the-shelf model and gives it the credit union's current loan policy documents as trusted context.
