scenarios.title: Harbor Lantern Logistics: The Refund Policy Chatbot
scenarios.scenario: Harbor Lantern Logistics is a fictional freight company that runs a customer chat assistant built on a large language model (LLM, a model trained on very large amounts of text to predict and generate language). Customers use it to ask about shipping rates, delivery windows, and the company's refund policy. During testing, the team found three problems. First, the assistant confidently described a refund window that the company retired last year. Second, when a customer asked whether container HL-4471 was delayed at the Ridgemouth port today, the assistant gave a plausible-sounding answer that it had no real basis for. Third, the same policy question sometimes got noticeably different wording from one chat to the next, which worries the support managers. The team lead asks you to advise on three points. 1. The assistant quotes an out-of-date refund window. Name the foundation model limitation involved, name the Google Cloud-recommended practice that addresses it, and explain in plain terms how that practice changes the assistant's answer. 2. For the container delay question, decide whether the needed information is first-party enterprise data, third-party data, or world data, and explain which grounding approach or Google Cloud grounding offering would fit, giving your reason. 3. The support managers want policy answers to be consistent and predictable rather than varied. Identify the sampling setting that most directly controls this, explain what it does, and say what the team should keep watching over time to confirm the assistant stays accurate.
subParts: Outdated refund window: limitation, practice, and effect on the answer
Container delay: data type and grounding fit
Consistency of policy answers: sampling setting and ongoing monitoring
modelAnswer: The limitation is a knowledge cutoff, meaning the model only knows what was in its training data up to a certain date, so it cannot know that the refund window changed later. A related issue is that the model may state the old window with confidence, which is a hallucination (an answer that sounds fluent and certain but is not supported by facts). The recommended practice is grounding, which means connecting the model to a trusted source of facts and having it base its answer on that source. A common form is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where the system first searches the company's current policy documents for passages relevant to the question, then passes those passages to the model together with the question. With the current policy supplied, the assistant states the current window and can point to the document it used, instead of relying on memory. Prompt engineering (writing clear instructions to the model) can also help by telling it to answer only from the supplied text, but it does not give the model new facts by itself.

The container delay is information about one specific shipment that changes by the hour. Harbor Lantern's own tracking system holds this, so it is first-party enterprise data (data the company owns and generates itself). Third-party data would come from an outside provider, such as a carrier or port authority feed, and world data is general public knowledge such as broad news or facts available on the open web. The best fit is grounding with first-party enterprise data, typically through a RAG pipeline that retrieves the latest tracking record for HL-4471 and gives it to the model at question time. If the team wanted to include public port news, Grounding with Google Search would address world data, but it would not reliably know the internal status of one container, so it should not be the main source here. The key reason is that a model cannot know a live shipment status from training alone; it must be given the current record.

The setting that most directly controls consistency is temperature. Temperature is a sampling parameter, meaning a setting that controls how the model picks each next word (token, a small chunk of text) from its possible options. A low temperature makes the model choose the most likely words, so repeated answers to the same question tend to match. A high temperature allows more varied choices, which suits brainstorming but not policy wording. Top-p (a setting that limits choices to the smallest group of likely words whose combined probability reaches a threshold) also affects variety, and output length or token count limits how long an answer can run, but temperature is the primary lever for consistency. The team should keep monitoring over time, tracking key performance indicators (KPIs, measurable targets such as the share of answers that match the current policy), checking for drift (a gradual decline in accuracy as the world or the company's documents change), and recording the model version so changes can be traced. Human in the loop review of a sample of answers, where staff check outputs and feed corrections back, is a standard safeguard alongside these measures.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Parcel's Claims Assistant
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional mid-sized parcel delivery company with about 900 staff. Its customer service team handles roughly 4,000 damage and lost-parcel claims each month. Each claim has a free-text case note written by an agent, which often includes the customer's full name, home address, phone number, and sometimes a medical or health detail when a fragile item was for a patient. Leadership wants a generative AI solution, meaning a system that produces new content such as text, images, or code from a prompt, to draft a reply to the customer and to write a two-sentence summary of each case for the team lead. The IT lead, Priya, must recommend a plan to the executive group that covers the type of solution, the privacy handling, and how the company will know whether it worked. Answer each sub-task as a short, self-contained recommendation. 1. Identify which type of generative AI solution fits this need (text generation, image generation, code generation, or a personalized solution that adapts output to each user) and give two business requirements and one technical constraint that drove your choice. 2. Explain how the team should handle the personal data in the case notes before the notes reach the model, distinguishing between data anonymization and pseudonymization and stating which one suits a case where the team must still link a reply back to the right customer record. 3. Name one technique the company can use to measure whether the initiative is delivering business impact, and say what it would show that a simple usage count would not.
subParts: Choosing the solution type with business requirements and a technical constraint
Handling personal data: anonymization versus pseudonymization
Measuring business impact beyond usage counts
modelAnswer: Text generation is the right type because the output needed is written language: a draft customer reply and a short case summary. Two business requirements that drive this choice are that replies must reach customers within one working day and that agents must keep control of what is sent, so the output should be a draft a person reviews rather than an automatic send. One technical constraint is that the case notes are free text in English and some other languages, so the model must handle varied, messy input; another valid constraint is that the notes contain sensitive data, which limits where the data can be processed. Image generation does not match the need, and code generation would only matter if the team were building tools rather than writing customer messages. A personalized solution is a possible later step, but the first need is drafting text, not adapting a product.

Anonymization means removing or altering identifying details so thoroughly that no one, including the company, can work out who the person is again. Pseudonymization means replacing direct identifiers, such as a name or account number, with a stand-in code, and keeping a separate, protected lookup table that links the code back to the real person. Because the team must still send each reply to the correct customer record, anonymization is the wrong choice, since it removes the link permanently. Pseudonymization suits this case: the model sees a case code and the event description, and the mapping table stays in a restricted system. Health details still need care, since they are sensitive even with a code attached, so the team should limit what goes into the prompt to what the reply actually needs. A common mistake is to think that replacing the name is enough while the address and phone number remain in the free text; the team should scan for those fields too.

A useful measure is a before-and-after comparison of a business outcome, such as the average time from claim received to first reply, the share of drafts agents accept with light edits, or customer satisfaction scores on replies, compared with a control group that still uses the old process. A simple usage count, such as how many drafts the tool produced, only shows that people used the tool. It does not show whether replies got faster, more accurate, or better received, and it could rise even if the tool made work slower because agents had to rewrite poor drafts. Pairing the comparison with a quality check, such as a sample of replies reviewed for accuracy and tone, shows whether speed came at the cost of errors.
